question_text:
A 35-year-old man is admitted to the cardiology ward after presenting to the emergency department with syncope. He has had several episodes of syncope. These have largely happened when he has been exerting himself, most recently when he was running to catch the bus. He is currently pain-free and has never suffered from any chest pain.

His electrocardiogram shows ST elevation and negative T waves in leads V1, V2 and V3.

What is the most likely finding on further investigation?
options_json: ["Mutation in the calsequestrin 2 gene", "Mutation in the cardiac ryanodine receptor gene", "Mutation in the gene encoding the myocardial potassium ion channel", "Mutation in the gene encoding the myocardial sodium ion channel", "Mutation in the gene encoding the sarcomere"]
answer_text: Mutation in the gene encoding the myocardial sodium ion channel
explanation_text:
Mutations in the SCN5A gene (which encode the myocardial sodium ion channel protein are the most common gene abnormality seen in Brugada syndrome

There are several cardiac conditions with a genetic basis which can cause syncope. This syncope may be arrhythmogenic or obstructive in nature. Hence, it is the ECG changes here that point towards a particular diagnosis. The presence of an ST elevation and negative T waves in V1-3 is typical for Brugada syndrome. A partial right bundle branch block is associated. The ECG changes may be more apparent following the administration of flecainide or ajmaline.

Mutation in the gene encoding the myocardial sodium ion channel

is the correct answer. Around 20-40% of patients with Brugada syndrome have a mutation in the SCN5A gene which encodes the myocardial sodium ion channel protein. Patients are managed with the insertion of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Mutation in the gene encoding the sarcomere

is incorrect. This would be suggestive of hypertrophic (obstructive) cardiomyopathy (HCM). This can present with syncope. However, the ECG findings seen here are not typical making this answer incorrect. In HCM, common ECG findings are left ventricular hypertrophy and deep, narrow Q waves in the lateral +/- inferior leads.

Mutation in the cardiac ryanodine receptor gene

is incorrect. This is the most common genetic variant causing an autosomal dominant form of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. In this condition, a resting ECG is usually normal.

Mutation in the calsequestrin 2 gene

is incorrect. This is the most common genetic variant causing an autosomal recessive form of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Mutation in the gene encoding the myocardial potassium ion channel

is incorrect. Problems with myocardial potassium ion channels play a major factor in congenital long QT syndrome. From the physiology, remember that repolarisation is due to potassium shifts, and therefore if this is disrupted, repolarisation is delayed and therefore the T wave is also delayed. This patient's ECG did not show a prolonged QT interval so this answer is incorrect.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman who is pregnant at 38 weeks gestation develops spontaneous labour. She has a history of pre-eclampsia. Her blood pressure is 180/115 mmHg.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	105 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	95 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	14.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

A decision is made to start the patient on magnesium sulphate.

Shortly after administering the magnesium sulphate, the patient develops respiratory depression with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute.

What treatment is urgently required?
options_json: ["Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP)", "Calcium gluconate", "Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)", "Intubation and ventilation", "Naloxone"]
explanation_text:
Magnesium sulphate - monitor reflexes + respiratory rate

The patient has several features of severe pre-eclampsia, namely a very high blood pressure (> 160/110 mmHg) and the presence of thrombocytopenia. Urgent delivery and magnesium sulphate are therefore indicated. Magnesium sulphate is used to both prevent seizures in patients with severe pre-eclampsia and treat seizures once they develop.

Symptoms of magnesium sulfate toxicity include loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest. Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first sign of magnesium toxicity.

The patient in this case has therefore likely developed magnesium sulphate toxicity due to the presence of respiratory depression.

Calcium gluconate

is correct. Calcium gluconate is the first-line treatment for magnesium sulphate induced respiratory depression.

Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP)

is incorrect. This is used to treat acute hypercapnic respiratory failure.

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)

is incorrect. In general patients with poor respiratory drive require invasive ventilation.

Intubation and ventilation

is incorrect. Although this may be required, non-invasive strategies should be pursued first e.g. calcium gluconate.

Naloxone

is incorrect. Opioid-induced respiratory depression is potentially fatal but may be reversed by the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone, an agent with a short elimination half-life (30 min). Although this remains within the differential diagnosis, and a careful drug history should be elicited, the history is more in keeping with magnesium sulphate toxicity.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman is referred to the respiratory clinic by her general practitioner. She has been experiencing exertional dyspnoea for 6 months.

She undergoes transthoracic echocardiography and subsequently right heart catheterisation which shows the following:


Pulmonary artery systolic pressure	51mmHg	(15-25)
Pulmonary artery diastolic pressure	30mmHg	(8-15)
Mean pulmonary artery pressure	37mmHg	(10-20)

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Acute vasodilator testing", "Add a calcium channel blocker", "Add a prostacyclin analogue", "Add an endothelin receptor antagonist", "CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA)"]
explanation_text:
Acute vasodilator testing should be used in patients with pulmonary artery hypertension to determine which patient show a significant fall in pulmonary arterial pressure following vasodilators and help guide treatment

This woman has presented with pulmonary artery hypertension. This classically presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea in young females. This is confirmed by the raised pulmonary pressures on right heart catheterisation. The first step in management is to perform an acute vasodilator test. If responsive, oral calcium channel blockers may be prescribed.

A calcium channel blocker can be used first-line once a response has been demonstrated on acute vasodilator testing, however as this has not been performed yet, this answer is incorrect.

A prostacyclin analogue may be indicated if no response is shown on acute vasodilator testing, however as this has not been performed yet, this answer is incorrect.

Similarly, endothelin receptor antagonists may be indicated but only once acute vasodilator testing has shown no response.

Pulmonary emboli are a cause of raised pulmonary artery pressures however due to the chronic nature of this woman's symptoms, this is unlikely to be the case. A CTPA is not routinely required to diagnose pulmonary artery hypertension.

question_text:
An 84-year-old female with a background of osteoporosis is given an infusion of pamidronate. A week later she presents to her GP complaining of paraesthesia. On examination she has hyperreflexia and carpopedal spasm.

Given the electrolyte abnormality she is likely to have developed, what ECG abnormality is most associated with this?
options_json: ["Atrioventricular node block", "Delta waves", "Tented T waves", "Long QT", "Atrial flutter"]
explanation_text:
A QT interval of greater than 0.44 seconds is associated with the development of ventricular arrhythmia, syncope and sudden cardiac death.

Long QT causes:

electrolyte abnormalities: hypokalemia and hypocalcemia
drugs: tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines, erythromycin, clarithromycin, amiodarone, haloperidol
congenital long QT syndromes: more than 10 different types recognised
myocardial infarction/significant active myocardial ischemia
cerebrovascular accident (subarachnoid haemorrhage)
hypothermia

Hyperreflexia and carpopedal spasm indicate neuromuscular irritability which is a feature of hypocalcaemia. Chvostek's sign can also be elicited by tapping over the facial nerve at the angle of the jaw. A positive result would involve ipsilateral twitching of the muscles around the nose and lips.

question_text:
A 56-year-old woman presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue over the past few months. She has no chest pain and no significant past medical history.

On examination, the chest is clear. The pulmonary component of the second heart sound is accentuated. Given the suspected diagnosis, vasodilator testing is arranged, to which the patient has a negative response.

What would be the single best initial treatment?
options_json: ["Digoxin", "Diltiazem", "Furosemide", "Nifedipine", "Sildenafil"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with negative response to vasodilator testing should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. Often combination therapy is required

The diagnosis here is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), given the symptoms of progressive breathlessness and fatigue and the heart sound findings. Vasodilator testing is used to identify the small subset of patients who respond to oral calcium-channel blockers. The vast majority of patients have a negative response to vasodilator testing, as in the scenario above. These patients should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. The only suitable medication in this scenario is sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor.

Digoxin is occasionally used as an adjunct in a select group of patients with PAH - those with refractory right heart failure or supraventricular arrhythmias. It is not routinely used, and in the scenario above, sildenafil remains the best choice initially.

Diltiazem is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker and may have been used if the patient had a positive response to vasodilator testing. A rate-limiting blocker would be more suitable in patients with higher baseline heart rates.

Furosemide is a loop diuretic and is sometimes used as an adjunct to relieve fluid retention associated with right heart failure. It is not directly a first-line treatment option for PAH.

Nifedipine is a non-rate-limiting calcium channel blocker and would be used if the patient had a positive response to vasodilator testing. In the scenario above, as testing was negative, sildenafil is most appropriate.

question_text: A 41-year-old man is admitted with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a dry cough and reports that the pain is relieved by sitting forward. For the past three days he has been experiencing flu-like symptoms. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely finding on ECG?
options_json: ["Large S wave in lead I, a large Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III", "Atrial fibrillation", "Widespread ST elevation", "ST segment depression in the anterior leads", "Hyperacute T waves"]
explanation_text:
Global ST and PR segment changes: think pericarditis

The correct answer in this case is

widespread ST elevation

. The patient's presentation of left-sided pleuritic chest pain that is relieved by sitting forward, dry cough, and recent flu-like symptoms are suggestive of pericarditis. In pericarditis, the most common ECG finding is widespread ST elevation.

Large S wave in lead I, a large Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III

(S1Q3T3 pattern) is associated with acute pulmonary embolism. While the patient does present with pleuritic chest pain, which can also be seen in pulmonary embolism, the relief of pain by sitting forward and recent flu-like symptoms make pericarditis more likely than pulmonary embolism.

Atrial fibrillation

is an irregularly irregular heart rhythm that can be associated with various cardiac conditions but is not specific to pericarditis. The patient's symptoms do not suggest atrial fibrillation as the primary cause of his chest pain.

ST segment depression in the anterior leads

typically indicates myocardial ischemia or injury involving the anterior wall of the heart. This can be seen in conditions like angina or myocardial infarction. However, given the patient's description of pleuritic chest pain that improves with sitting forward and recent flu-like symptoms, pericarditis remains more likely.

Hyperacute T waves

are an early sign of myocardial infarction (MI), occurring before ST-segment elevation becomes apparent. They represent a very early stage of MI and may progress to ST elevation if not treated promptly. Although MI could potentially present with chest pain, this patient's clinical features such as pleuritic nature of pain and relief on sitting forward point towards pericarditis rather than MI as the cause for his symptoms.

question_text:
A 35-year-old female delivers a newborn at 30 weeks of gestation. During the first trimester, the mother suffered from fever and joint pain for one week. At that time, she only received symptomatic treatment. Today, the patient delivered a premature baby via normal vaginal delivery. On examination of the newborn continuous machine-like murmur is heard in the left infraclavicular space.

Which of the following drugs can treat the underlying condition of the newborn baby if the symptoms persist after one week?
options_json: ["Indapamide", "Ibuprofen", "Mifepristone", "Progesterone", "Prostaglandin"]
explanation_text:
Preterm infants with haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus 1 week after birth - give ibuprofen/indomethacin to promote duct closure

This newborn is suffering from

patent ductus arteriosus (PDA),

a non-cyanotic congenital heart disorder. It is a type of left-to-right shunt in which blood passes from the aorta to the pulmonary vessel via the patent ductus arteriosus. Newborns may have a normal presentation, but on auscultation, a

continuous machine-like murmur

is characteristic.

Indomethacin or ibuprofen

is used for treating the patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn.

Prostaglandins can keep the ductus arteriosus open. They are used to keep the ductus arteriosus open in cyanotic disorders like transposition of great vessels (TGA) until the definitive surgery is performed.

Mifepristone is an anti-progesterone drug. It is used along with misoprostol to terminate labour. It does not close the patent ductus arteriosus.

Indapamide is a thiazide diuretic. It does not treat patent ductus arteriosus.

Progesterone is a sex hormone in females. It does not close the patent ductus arteriosus.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man attends his GP with a 4-week history of intermittent palpitations.

He notes no obvious trigger. They can occur at rest, and usually last only for 30 seconds. He denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. They occur 2-3 times per week.

On examination, his heart sounds are normal and his pulse is regular.

His full blood count, CRP, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, bone profile, and thyroid function are all within normal limits.

His 12 lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. He was not symptomatic whilst recording.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options_json: ["24 hour Holter monitor", "72 hour Holter monitor", "Echocardiogram", "Exercise ECG testing", "Implantable loop recorder"]
explanation_text:
Palpitations should first be investigated with a Holter monitor after initial bloods/ECG

72 hour Holter monitor

is correct. This patient is experiencing palpitations but the 12-lead ECG and blood tests are unremarkable. To capture the heart rhythm during these episodes of palpitations, ambulatory ECG monitoring will be required. This is most often in the form of a Holter monitor and can be performed over 24, 48, or 72 hours depending on the frequency of symptoms. This patient's symptoms are every few days, so a longer duration of monitoring will be required.

24 hour Holter monitor

is incorrect. This patient does need a Holter monitor as the next step in investigation, however monitoring for only 24 hours in this case is likely to miss the episodes, as they are occurring every few days. A 72 hour monitoring period would be more appropriate.

Echocardiogram

is incorrect. This would give structural information about the heart, rather than any rhythm disturbances. An echocardiogram can comment if the rhythm is regular or irregular, but it will not give detailed information about the rhythm. Additionally, it is important to sample the rhythm over a longer period to ensure information is gathered at the time the patient is symptomatic, which realistically may not occur during a short echocardiogram.

Exercise ECG testing

is incorrect. Exercise ECG testing is used to investigate for ischaemic heart disease or exercise-induced arrhythmias. There is no suggestion in the question that these palpitations are related to exercise, so this test will be of little value.

Implantable loop recorder

is incorrect. This is a much more invasive test, but may be required subsequently if the Holter monitor is unable to explain the episodes but the clinical suspicion for arrhythmias remains high.

question_text: A 54-year-old man with hypertension is reviewed in clinic. He complains that over the past two months he has developed ankle swelling. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
options_json: ["Amlodipine", "Perindopril", "Indapamide", "Losartan", "Diltiazem"]
explanation_text:
Calcium channel blockers - side-effects: headache, flushing, ankle oedema

Amlodipine

is the archetypal dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and peripheral ankle oedema is its hallmark adverse effect, occurring in up to 10–15 % of patients. The drug selectively relaxes precapillary arterioles, increasing hydrostatic pressure within capillaries while leaving post-capillary venous tone unchanged. This pressure gradient pushes fluid into the interstitial space, producing painless, pitting oedema that typically appears after a few weeks of therapy and is bilateral. The phenomenon is dose-related, improves on stopping the drug or switching to a different antihypertensive class, and is not due to salt and water retention, so diuretics are usually ineffective. Recognising this mechanism allows the clinician to reassure the patient and alter therapy appropriately.

Perindopril

, an ACE inhibitor, more commonly causes cough, taste disturbance and, rarely, angio-oedema rather than dependent peripheral oedema. In fact, by reducing afterload and promoting natriuresis, ACE inhibitors can improve congestive ankle swelling secondary to heart failure. Consequently, although perindopril is a very widely used antihypertensive, it is not usually implicated when isolated ankle swelling develops in an otherwise well patient.

Indapamide

is a thiazide-like diuretic. Its recognised adverse effects include hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and a mild photosensitive rash. It promotes renal sodium and water loss, so it would be expected to relieve, not precipitate, peripheral oedema. Ankle swelling developing while on indapamide should prompt the clinician to look for another cause, such as concomitant amlodipine therapy or underlying cardiac disease.

Losartan

, an angiotensin II receptor blocker, shares many side-effects with ACE inhibitors but ankle oedema is not a characteristic problem. By blocking the renin–angiotensin pathway it tends to reduce venous and arterial pressures and is sometimes used as part of combination therapy precisely because it does not exacerbate dihydropyridine-induced swelling.

Diltiazem

is a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker with more pronounced effects on the myocardium and cardiac conduction than on peripheral vasculature. Although mild ankle oedema can occur, it is far less common than with dihydropyridines like amlodipine. Bradycardia, constipation and worsening of heart failure in susceptible patients are considerably more typical. Therefore, in a patient presenting primarily with ankle swelling after starting antihypertensive therapy, diltiazem is a less likely culprit than amlodipine.

question_text: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a friend from work. Around 30 minutes ago she developed a 'fluttering' in her chest. She reports feeling 'a bit faint' but denies any chest pain or shortness of breath. An ECG shows a regular tachycardia of 166 bpm with a QRS duration of 0.11s. Blood pressure is 102/68 mmHg and oxygen saturations are 99% on room air. What is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Intravenous magnesium sulphate", "Direct current cardioversion", "Intravenous adenosine 3mg", "Intravenous adenosine 6mg", "Carotid sinus massage"]
explanation_text:
The first-line management of SVT is vagal manoeuvres: e.g. Valsalva manoeuvre or carotid sinus massage

The first-line management of supraventricular tachycardia are vagal manoeuvres such as carotid sinus massage. Only if these fail should adenosine be given. There are no indications for direct current cardioversion as per the ALS guidelines.

question_text: A 35-year-old man who is an intravenous drug user is admitted to hospital. He has had three previous admissions with infective endocarditis but presents on this occasion feeling generally unwell, complaining of upper abdominal discomfort and leg swelling. On examination he has an elevated jugular venous pressure, tender hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema. A diagnosis of tricuspid regurgitation is suspected. Which one of the following additional features would be most supportive of this diagnosis?
options_json: ["Split first heart sound", "Early diastolic murmur", "Left parasternal heave", "Wide pulse pressure", "Cannon 'a' waves"]
explanation_text:
Left parasternal heave is a feature of tricuspid regurgitation

Left parasternal heave

is indeed the correct answer as it is a characteristic finding in tricuspid regurgitation. The right ventricle hypertrophies and dilates in response to the volume overload caused by tricuspid regurgitation, leading to a palpable left parasternal heave. This is particularly relevant in this case of a patient with likely right-sided endocarditis secondary to intravenous drug use, which commonly affects the tricuspid valve.

Split first heart sound

is not specifically associated with tricuspid regurgitation. While heart sound abnormalities can occur in tricuspid valve disease, a split first heart sound is more commonly associated with conditions affecting left-sided valve timing or conduction delays.

Early diastolic murmur

is characteristic of aortic regurgitation or pulmonary regurgitation, not tricuspid regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation typically produces a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo's sign).

Wide pulse pressure

is a feature of aortic regurgitation where there is a high systolic pressure and low diastolic pressure due to backward flow through the incompetent aortic valve. This is not a feature of right-sided valve disease such as tricuspid regurgitation.

Cannon 'a' waves

in the jugular venous pulse are seen in complete heart block or when the atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve. While jugular venous distension is common in tricuspid regurgitation, cannon waves are not a typical feature and instead you would expect prominent v waves.

question_text:
A 28-year-old man attends his GP for evaluation due to recent episodes of exertional chest pain and occasional palpitations. He reports a family history of sudden cardiac death, with his father passing away at the age of 40. Although he is currently asymptomatic, an echocardiogram has revealed hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

What echocardiographic finding would be indicative of the poorest prognosis in this patient?
options_json: ["Ejection fraction of 60%", "Left atrial enlargement", "Left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradient of 25 mmHg", "Mitral regurgitation", "Septal wall thickness of 3.5 cm"]
explanation_text:
HOCM - poor prognostic factor on echo = septal wall thickness of > 3cm

A

septal wall thickness of 3.5 cm

, indicates a poorer prognosis in patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). The thickened septum (> 3cm) can impede the outflow of blood from the left ventricle, resulting in diminished cardiac output and clinical manifestations including chest pain, dyspnoea, and syncope. In extreme cases, this obstruction may precipitate sudden cardiac death. Consequently, a septal wall thickness measurement of > 3cm would portend a less favourable prognosis when compared to the alternatives listed.

Ejection fraction of 60%

reflects normal systolic function and is generally considered prognostically advantageous. Within the context of HOCM, ejection fraction alone does not correlate with adverse outcomes. It is often preserved or even augmented in HOCM and therefore is not conventionally employed as a prognostic indicator.

While

left atrial enlargement

may develop in HOCM due to heightened pressures during ventricular filling, it does not have a direct correlation with poor prognosis. Although left atrial enlargement arises as a consequence of increased filling pressures and may be implicated in an elevated risk for atrial arrhythmias—which could indirectly affect prognosis—it is not a primary prognostic factor.

The

left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradient of 25 mmHg

quantifies the level of obstruction within the left ventricular outflow tract. It offers some insight into the severity of this obstruction. While an LVOT gradient has some prognostic implications, a moderate gradient such as 25 mmHg is typically less determinative for prognosis than septal wall thickness, which more accurately reflects the degree of myocardial hypertrophy and its associated complications in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Therefore, despite its value in assessing obstruction, the severity of the LVOT gradient has less influence on long-term outcomes and clinical management compared to septal wall thickness.

Although

mitral regurgitation

may occur alongside HOCM, it is not principally used as an indicator of poor prognosis. Mitral valve abnormalities are usually secondary to hypertrophic alterations within the heart muscle itself. Notwithstanding that severe mitral regurgitation might exacerbate cardiac dysfunction and increase symptomatology among HOCM patients, it does not primarily dictate prognosis.

question_text:
An elderly patient on the oncology ward has a cardiac arrest. You start compressions and the resuscitation team are contacted. Assessment of the rhythm shows ventricular tachycardia (VT). Three cycles of CPR are performed and successive shocks given.

After the third shock which two medications are indicated in the ALS protocol?
options_json: ["Amiodarone 300mg and adrenaline 100mg", "Amiodarone 300mg and adrenaline 10mg", "Amiodarone 300mg and adrenaline 1mg", "Amiodarone 300mg and adrenaline 0.01g", "Lidocaine 1mg and adrenaline 10mg"]
explanation_text:
The recommended dose of adrenaline to give during advanced ALS is 1mg

If identified in hospital these patients should be treated with a shock of a minimum of 150 joules (unless the defibrillator model states otherwise). Compressions at a rate of 30:2 should be restarted for 2 minutes and assessment of the rhythm again thereafter. If VF or pVT persists a second shock should be given. The previous steps should be repeated until the third shock where 1mg IV of adrenaline and 300mg IV of amiodarone should be given while still performing CPR. Afterwards, 1mg of adrenaline should be continued to be given after every other shock. The 2nd dose of amiodarone should be considered after a total of 5 defibrillation attempts.

In circumstances where amiodarone is unavailable lidocaine can be used.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman has 2 years of progressive fatigue, leg swelling, and episodic palpitations. Her history includes rheumatic fever, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Her pulse is 72 bpm, and her BP is 110/70 mmHg. A low-pitched diastolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. It is louder on inspiration. She has bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, and her jugular venous pulse (JVP) shows a slow 'y' descent.

Investigations:


NT-proBNP	663 ng/L	(< 400)

What process best describes her JVP waveform findings?
options_json: ["Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve", "Contraction and increased pressure of the right atrium", "Fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole", "Opening of the tricuspid valve and filling of the right ventricle", "Right ventricular contraction and closure of the tricuspid valve"]
answer_text: Opening of the tricuspid valve and filling of the right ventricle
explanation_text:
JVP: y descent = opening of tricuspid valve

Opening of the tricuspid valve and filling of the right ventricle

is the correct answer. This patient has clinical features of tricuspid stenosis, indicated by the presence of a low-pitched diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration. She also has features of right-sided heart failure, evidenced by bilateral oedema and a raised NT-proBNP. Her history of rheumatic fever is highly relevant, as rheumatic heart disease is a recognised cause of isolated tricuspid stenosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. The y descent in the JVP represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens in early diastole. In tricuspid stenosis, the valve opening is narrowed and obstructed, so the flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle is delayed and slowed. This causes a characteristic slow and blunted y descent on JVP tracing. Therefore, the slow y descent seen here corresponds to the opening of the tricuspid valve and filling of the right ventricle, which is impaired due to stenosis.

Atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve

is incorrect as this describes the v wave. In this patient, the abnormality described is due to impaired opening of the tricuspid valve, causing a slow y descent. Abnormal v waves include large v waves, which may occur in tricuspid regurgitation. This would present with a pansystolic murmur, which is not the case here.

Contraction and increased pressure of the right atrium

is incorrect as this describes the a wave. In this patient, the abnormality described reflects impaired right ventricular filling through a stenotic tricuspid valve instead. Abnormalities of the a waves include 'cannon' a waves, which occur when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (e.g. in complete heart block), or absent a waves in atrial fibrillation. These features are not described here.

Fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole

is incorrect as this describes the x descent. Here, the abnormality described is a slow y descent, which describes impaired right ventricular filling via a stenotic tricuspid valve. Abnormalities of the x descent instead include deep x descents, which can be seen in constrictive pericarditis, alongside deep y descents and a JVP which paradoxically rises on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign). These features are not relevant here.

Right ventricular contraction and closure of the tricuspid valve

is incorrect, as this corresponds with the c wave. The main abnormality described here is a slow y descent due to impaired ventricular filling through a stenotic tricuspid valve. The c wave is generally small and often not visible. In tricuspid regurgitation, prominent CV waves may occur, which represent merged c and v waves. This is associated with a pansystolic murmur, which is not seen here.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset swelling of his lips and tongue. He denies any rash, itching, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. He has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis. One week ago, his GP changed one of his antihypertensive medications during a routine medication review.

On examination, he has isolated, non-tender swelling of the lips and tongue. There is no stridor, urticaria, or wheeze.

Observations:

BP: 140/85 mmHg
HR: 78 bpm
SpO₂: 98% on room air
RR: 18 breaths/min
Temperature: 36.8°C

Which medication is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options_json: ["Amlodipine", "Bisoprolol", "Doxazosin", "Eplerenone", "Losartan"]
explanation_text:
Drug-induced angioedema without urticaria is most frequently associated with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or, less frequently, angiotensin II receptor blockers

The correct answer is

losartan.

This patient presents with angioedema—acute, painless, non-pruritic swelling of subcutaneous or submucosal tissues, typically affecting the face, lips, tongue, or airway. He has no signs of urticaria or anaphylaxis, and the recent change in antihypertensive medication strongly suggests a drug-induced cause. Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) like losartan are a recognised but less common cause of angioedema compared to ACE inhibitors. The mechanism is not fully understood but may be independent of bradykinin accumulation. ARB-induced angioedema can occur even in patients who have previously tolerated ACE inhibitors. Management includes discontinuation of the offending agent and airway monitoring.

Amlodipine

is incorrect. Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. Angioedema is extremely rare but has been reported. However, angioedema is far less commonly associated with amlodipine than with ACE inhibitors or ARBs. Given the overall rarity, it is unlikely to be the most likely cause here as compared to an ARB.

Bisoprolol

is incorrect. Bisoprolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker used for hypertension and heart failure. It can cause bradycardia and fatigue but is not a known cause of angioedema. Of note, beta-blockers may impair the response to anaphylaxis but do not typically induce angioedema themselves.

Doxazosin

is incorrect. Doxazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker used to treat hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. While it may cause postural hypotension or dizziness, it is not associated with angioedema.

Eplerenone

is incorrect. Eplerenone is a selective aldosterone antagonist used in hypertension and heart failure. Its side effects include hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia (though less than spironolactone), but angioedema is not a recognised complication.

question_text: A 42-year-old man of Afro-Caribbean origin is diagnosed as having hypertension. Secondary causes of hypertension have been excluded. What is the most appropriate initial drug therapy?
options_json: ["Losartan", "Bisoprolol", "Indapamide", "Ramipril", "Amlodipine"]
explanation_text:
ACE inhibitors have reduced efficacy in black patients and are therefore not used first-line

The correct answer is

Amlodipine

. Amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker (CCB), is the recommended first-line antihypertensive treatment in people of African or Caribbean family origin of any age according to NICE guidelines. This recommendation is based on evidence demonstrating that CCBs and thiazide-type diuretics have greater antihypertensive efficacy than ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) in this population group.

Losartan

, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), is not the initial drug of choice for hypertension in Afro-Caribbean patients. ARBs are less effective as monotherapy in black patients compared with white patients due to a lower renin profile.

Bisoprolol

, a beta-blocker, is not recommended as first-line therapy for hypertension unless there are compelling indications such as heart failure or angina. Beta-blockers have been shown to be less effective at reducing stroke risk and all-cause mortality compared to other antihypertensive classes.

Indapamide

, a thiazide-like diuretic, could also be considered as a first-line antihypertensive treatment in black patients according to NICE guidelines. However, it's generally used when calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.

Ramipril

, an ACE inhibitor, has been found less effective as monotherapy in black hypertensive patients compared with white hypertensive patients due to differences in renin profiles between these population groups. It would therefore not be the most appropriate initial drug therapy for this patient.

question_text:
You receive an emergency bleep to a 52-year-old woman who was admitted 6 hours ago with atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response.

On arrival, you find her sweaty, tachypnoeic, and hypotensive. You note bibasal crepitations on auscultation of the chest with irregular tachycardia. Cardiac monitoring shows atrial fibrillation at a rate of 140-170 bpm.

A decision is made to perform emergency DC cardioversion. The on-call anaesthetist is in attendance to support with sedation and airway.

Synchronised DC cardioversion takes place as per the tachyarrhythmia advanced life support algorithm.

Which part of the QRS complex is used for synchronisation?
options_json: ["P wave", "Q wave", "R wave", "S wave", "T wave"]
explanation_text:
Electrical cardioversion is synchronised to the R wave

This woman is showing signs of shock and heart failure in association with atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. These are two unstable, adverse features of tachyarrhythmias that require emergency, synchronised DC cardioversion.

Prior to a shock being delivered, the 'sync' button should always be pressed to ensure that the shock occurs at the correct time in the QRS complex.

DC cardioversion is synchronised to the R wave to minimise the risk of inducing ventricular fibrillation. Non-synchronised DC cardioversion is defibrillation and should only be used in cardiac arrest scenarios for shockable rhythms (ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia).

answer_text: Lengthening of the PR interval on ECG
explanation_text:
Infective endocarditis - indications for surgery:

Lengthening of the PR interval is likely to represent an aortic root abscess which will require surgical intervention.

question_text:
A 35-year-old woman is visiting the pulmonary hypertension (PAH) clinic. She is experiencing worsening shortness of breath even after starting medications. As a result, she was prescribed a combination of tadalafil and bosentan as standard therapy. However, due to her liver function being deranged, bosentan was replaced with ambrisentan.

The patient was informed that the new medication is not recommended during pregnancy because of its teratogenic effects. The most common side effects of this drug are lower limb oedema, headache, and anaemia.

What is this new medication's mechanism of action?
options_json: ["Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker", "Endothelin receptor A antagonist", "Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor", "Prostacyclin receptor agonist", "Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator"]
explanation_text:
Ambrisentan - endothelin receptor A antagonist

Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare condition that is most commonly found in young to middle-aged women. A diagnosis of idiopathic PAH is based on several investigations, including autoimmune screens, echocardiogram, cross-sectional imaging, and right heart catheterisation.

In patients with idiopathic PAH, a selective

endothelin receptor A antagonist

, such as ambrisentan, is typically started along with a phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor (PDE5-i) such as tadalafil when vasoreactivity testing is negative. It should be noted that bosentan has a higher incidence of causing deranged liver function compared to ambrisentan. A common side effect of these medications is peripheral oedema. Additionally, endothelial receptor antagonists have teratogenic effects, and should not be used during pregnancy.

For patients with PAH who have tested positive for vasoreactivity during a right heart catheterisation, a

dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker

, such as amlodipine, is used. A positive vasoreactivity test is defined as a reduction in mean pulmonary artery pressure by ≥ 10-mmHg to reach an absolute value ≤ 40-mmHg, with increased or unchanged cardiac output. Calcium channel blockers alone typically suffice for positive vasoreactivity testers. If amlodipine is to be stopped, a gradual dose reduction is advised due to the possible haemodynamic worsening due to a withdrawal effect.

A

PDE5-i

such as tadalafil is used in patients with PAH either alone or in combination with endothelial receptor antagonists for initial treatment when they are non-responders to vasoreactivity testing. However, PDE5-i medications should not be used in combination with either nitrates or soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators due to the risk of systemic hypotension. Side effects include headache, hypotension, and flushing.

In patients with PAH who experience clinical deterioration or have an initial presentation suggesting severe pulmonary hypertension, a

prostacyclin receptor agonist

such as selexipag is used in combination with PDE5-i inhibitors and endothelin receptor antagonists. However, its use would depend on individual patient factors. The side effects of selexipag include headache, diarrhoea, nausea, and jaw pain. It should not be used during pregnancy.

A

soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator

such as riociguat is used in place of PDE5-i in certain patients with PAH, i.e., clinical deterioration despite double or triple combination therapy. These medications would not be used as initial standard therapy. Riociguat cannot be used in combination with PDE5-i due to the risk of systemic hypotension. Side effects of riociguat include hypotension, peripheral oedema, and anaemia. It is not advised for use during pregnancy.

question_text: A 59-year-old female is admitted to the Emergency Department with a 30 minute history of central chest pain radiating to her left arm. An ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely to be affected?
options_json: ["Right coronary", "Left anterior descending", "Left main stem", "Left circumflex", "Anterior interventricular"]
explanation_text:
Inferior MI - right coronary artery lesion

The correct answer is the

Right coronary artery

. ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF on an ECG indicates an inferior wall myocardial infarction. This is most commonly due to occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA). The RCA supplies blood to the inferior part of the heart, which corresponds to these ECG leads.

The

Left anterior descending artery (LAD)

is not the correct answer. Occlusion of this artery typically results in ST segment elevation in the anterior precordial leads V1-V4, as it supplies blood to the anterior wall and septum of the heart.

Similarly, occlusion of the

Left main stem

would cause widespread ST-segment elevation across multiple leads (I, aVL and V1-V6) because it gives rise to both LAD and LCX arteries. Thus supplying a significant portion of myocardium including anterior, lateral and septal regions.

The

Left circumflex artery (LCX)

primarily supplies blood to the lateral wall of the heart. Therefore, occlusion typically results in ST segment elevation in leads I, aVL or V5-V6 that correspond to this region.

Lastly, there is no such named vessel as an '

Anterior interventricular

' artery within the human coronary circulation. The term may be mistaken for Anterior Interventricular Branch which is another name for Left Anterior Descending Artery discussed above.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man has been admitted to the coronary care unit after suffering from an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). He is awaiting primary percutaneous coronary intervention.

The nurse bleeps you because he now is having episodes of dizziness, but remains alert and talking. You ask them to do a set of observations and an electrocardiogram (ECG) while you arrive on the ward. He is attached to a cardiac monitor for you to review on arrival as well.

What particular arrhythmia is this patient at risk of developing?
options_json: ["Ventricular fibrillation", "Ventricular tachycardia", "Atrioventricular block", "Cardiogenic shock", "Atrial fibrillation"]
explanation_text:
AV block can occur following an inferior MI

This is a case of an inferior ST-elevation MI causing a bradyarrhythmia soon after myocardial injury.

The atrioventricular (AV) node is supplied by the AV nodal artery, which is a branch of the right coronary artery in 90% of people. The other 10% come from the left circumflex artery.

It manifests itself as a second or third-degree heart block with moderate bradycardia and a junctional escape rhythm on the ECG.

Treatment would follow the standard adult resuscitation guidelines for bradyarrhythmias.

Looking at the alternatives:

Ventricular fibrillation is the most common cause of death post-MI. There would be no cardiac output seen with this rhythm and is exclusively seen in cardiac arrest situations.

Ventricular tachycardia is another common tachyarrhythmia seen post-MI. It would present similar to this case, however, AV block is more common given the type of myocardial infarction the patient had.

Cardiogenic shock can occur post-MI if the ventricular ejection fraction is significantly affected. Patients tend to have low blood pressure, are peripherally cool with a reduced capillary refill time and have an elevated JVP. The JVP is often a differentiator between this and septic or hypovolaemic shock.

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is common post any type of MI. In post-MI patients, AF is usually transient and only short term treatment is needed in the aftermath of an acute event.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to exertional dyspnea that has progressed over the last year. She can hardly walk a block without stopping to rest. On physical examination, the patient has a loud second heart sound over the left upper sternal border, increased jugular venous pressure, and a palpable right ventricular impulse. Chest x-ray shows clear lungs.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
options_json: ["Aortic stenosis", "Hypertensive heart disease", "Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy", "Left bundle branch block", "Pulmonary hypertension"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary hypertension is a cause of a loud S2 (due to a loud P2)

Pulmonary hypertension commonly presents with progressive dyspnea, and patients may also experience exertional angina or syncope. Physical examination reveals a loud pulmonic component (P2) of S2, caused by forceful pulmonic valve closure in the setting of high pulmonary arterial pressure.

Aortic stenosis is common in elderly and presents with systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border. It presents with soft S2, not loud S2.

Hypertensive heart disease causes left ventricular hypertrophy, leading to impaired ventricular compliance and diastolic heart failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy presents with crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard at the left sternal border.

Left bundle branch block can delay the closure of the aortic valve, leading to later occurrence of the aortic component (A2) of S2 and narrowed or paradoxical splitting.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man attends the clinic with recurrent episodes of collapse. These are often preceded by heart palpitations described as a rapid heart rate. On examination, heart sounds were normal. there was no evidence of heart murmurs, and he was euvolaemic.

An ECG is performed in the clinic:


ECG	Convex ST-segment elevation in V1-V3 followed by a negative T wave; Partial right bundle branch block; QTc 410 ms

You order a cardiac genetic panel.

A mutation in which gene is expected?
options_json: ["CAV3", "MYBPC3", "MYH7", "SCN5A", "TTR"]
explanation_text:
Mutations in the SCN5A gene (which encode the myocardial sodium ion channel protein are the most common gene abnormality seen in Brugada syndrome

SCN5A

is correct. The clinical and electrocardiographic features are highly suggestive of Brugada syndrome.  A large number of variants exist however around 20-40% of cases are caused by a mutation in the SCN5A gene which encodes the myocardial sodium ion channel protein.

CAV3

is incorrect.  Mutations in this gene are associated with hereditary long QT syndrome. The normal QTc makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

MYBPC3

is incorrect. Nearly 70% of all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) mutations can be found in the sarcomere genes MYH7 and MYBPC3 (encoding for cardiac myosin binding protein C). The ECG features, in this case, are not suggestive of HCM. HCM results in left ventricular hypertrophy, T wave inversion in the precordial leads, and deep, narrow ('dagger-like') Q waves in the lateral (I, aVL, V5-6) +/- inferior (II, III, aVF) leads.

MYH7

is incorrect. Nearly 70% of all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) mutations can be found in the sarcomere genes MYH7 and MYBPC3 (encoding for cardiac myosin binding protein C). The ECG features, in this case, are not suggestive of HCM (as discussed above).

TTR

is incorrect. Mutations in TTR are associated with transthyretin amyloidosis. Classical electrocardiogram (ECG) findings in cardiac amyloidosis include that of low voltage complexes with increased left ventricular wall thickness on echocardiography. The absence of these features in this case makes cardiac amyloidosis a less likely diagnosis.

His departmental echocardiogram shows he has a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35%. Which of the following statements most accurately counsels this patient as regard to his driving?
options_json: ["An LVEF of < 40% bars him from driving a lorry, even if he becomes asymptomatic with treatment", "His symptoms bar him from driving both a lorry and a car", "The implantation of a CRT-defibrillator would allow him to drive in 6 weeks' time", "He does not need to inform the DVLA", "An LVEF of < 40% bars him from driving a lorry only if associated with incapacity"]

question_text:
A 54-year-old man with known ischaemic heart disease presents with acute onset palpitations and shortness of breath.

He is found to be in a tachyarrhythmia with evidence of instability and therefore electro-cardioversion is attempted. Unfortunately, this fails to restore sinus rhythm and so amiodarone is given IV whilst a cardiology opinion is sought.

Due to its half-life time an initial loading dose is required followed by a continuous infusion over 24 hours which, once started, reverts the patient into sinus rhythm.

How long is the half-life of this antiarrhythmic agent?
options_json: ["Approximately 2-10 mins", "Approximately 2-3 days", "Approximately 2-4 hours", "Approximately 20-100 days", "Unpredictable half-life (mins to months)"]
explanation_text:
Amiodarone has a long half-life - it is highly lipophilic and widely absorbed by tissue, which reduces its bioavailability in serum. Therefore, a prolonged loading regime is required to achieve stable therapeutic levels

Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent that can be used in the management of most atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmia, particularly in patients with known cardiac failure. Amiodarone has several undesirable features including a very long half-life of

approximately 20-100 days

. As with most drugs that have a very long half-life this means a loading dose is required.

Medications with a half-life as short as

2-10 mins

are extremely rare as most of a drug would be eliminated in under an hour, making their use very limited.

Drugs commonly have a half-life of

2-3 days

but would rarely require a loading dose for this period. Amiodarone has a much longer half-life with approximately 20 days being the shortest period for 50% of the drug to be eliminated.

A half-life of

2-4 hours

would be considered relatively short and therefore a loading dose would not be required for medications with this property. Metoprolol is a good example of an antiarrhythmic drug with a half-life such as this. It is therefore a suitable drug to trial for rate control in stable tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation as any adverse effects will be short-lived.

Medications with such a wide range of half-life

(mins to months)

would be unsuitable to use as their unpredictability would mean the correct dosing for patients would not be possible to achieve.

question_text:
A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of three days of fever, malaise and shortness of breath. He has poor dentition and underwent a tooth extraction ten days previous to this attendance. He has a past medical history of hypertension. He is on regular amlodipine. He smokes three cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol at weekends.

His observations are heart rate 111 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 21/minute, oxygen saturations 96% on room air and temperature 38.3ºC.

On examination, chest auscultation was normal. Heart sounds were present with the addition of an early diastolic murmur heard loudest in expiration at the lower left sternal edge. There was no peripheral oedema. Erythematous lesions were noted on the palms of both hands, which were non-tender.

Urinalysis was unremarkable.


Hb	131 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	389 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	14.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.1 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	76 mg/L	(< 5)

An ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia.

Plain radiography of the chest was normal.

Given the history and the likely diagnosis, what organism is most likely to be responsible?
options_json: ["Eikenella corrodens", "Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus", "Staphylococcus aureus", "Streptococcus sanguinis", "Streptococcus bovis"]
explanation_text:
Patients with very poor dental hygiene may develop endocarditis secondary to Viridans streptococci e.g.

Streptococcus sanguinis

is the right answer. The diagnosis is infective endocarditis as evidenced by the clinical presentation of fever in combination with aortic regurgitation and Janeway lesions. This is most likely as a result of dental surgery in the context of poor dentition. Patients with very poor dental hygiene may develop endocarditis secondary to viridans streptococci e.g.

Streptococcus sanguinis

.

Eikenella corrodens

is incorrect. This is an organism that is part of the HACEK (

Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella

) group of fastidious gram-negative bacteria that are an unusual cause of endocarditis. These were historically felt to be a common cause of endocarditis but in more recent times have been recognised to be much rarer. They are a cause of 'culture-negative' endocarditis, which means they do not produce a colony on regular agar plates but rather require a specific nutrient.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

is incorrect. This is a possible cause of endocarditis but is typically associated with intravenous drug use and right-sided endocarditis.

Staphylococcus aureus

is incorrect. This is the most common cause of endocarditis but the history of poor dentition and preceding dental work, in this case, makes viridans streptococci species a more likely cause of infection.

Streptococcus bovis

is incorrect. There is a postulated associated between colorectal cancer and the development of endocarditis caused by

Streptococcus bovis

. However, there is nothing in this scenario to suggest an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer.

question_text:
A 41-year-old male is diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. He undergoes vasodilator testing with intravenous epoprostenol to which he has a positive response.

What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for his condition?
options_json: ["Sildenafil", "Treprostinil", "Bosentan", "Isosorbide mononitrate", "Nifedipine"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with positive response to vasodilator testing should be treated with calcium channel blockers

Patients who test positive to vasodilator testing are typically treated with calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, diltiazem and increasingly amlodipine, making option 5 the correct answer.

Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor used in patients who test negative to vasodilators.

Treprostinil is a  prostacyclin analogue used in patients who do not respond to acute vasodilator testing.

Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist also used for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension who are negative during vasodilator testing.

Isosorbide mononitrate is used in the treatment of angina not pulmonary arterial hypertension.

question_text:
A 60-year-old male who recently underwent cardiac surgery presents with fever, fatigue, and weight loss. The patient was discharged after a successful mitral valve replacement 4 months ago and as such an urgent echocardiogram is performed.

The echo confirms the presence of a new valvular lesion, and a diagnosis of endocarditis is made. Three sets of blood cultures are taken.

Which organism is most likely to be responsible for the patient's diagnosis?
options_json: ["Staphylococcus aureus", "Staphylococcus bovis", "Staphylococcus epidermidis", "Streptococcus mitis", "Streptococcus viridans"]
explanation_text:
Most common cause of endocarditis:

Staphylococcus aureus

is now the most common cause of infective endocarditis particularly in acute presentations and intravenous drug users. Although the patient has recently undergone valve replacement surgery it was over 2 months ago and so the spectrum of organisms that cause endocarditis return to normal. Therefore,

Staphylococcus epidermidis

not the most likely organism.

Streptococcus bovis

is part of the natural bowel flora and can result in endocarditis, but is not as common as

Staphylococcus aureus

.

Streptococcus bovis

is associated with colon cancer and, if found to be a causative agent of endocarditis, should prompt urgent investigation as the bacteria may have been released into the bloodstream due to a colon tract breakdown.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is the most common cause of endocarditis post valvular surgery but only for 2 months post-procedure. After this point

Staphylococcus aureus

becomes the more likely organism.

Streptococcus mitis

is one of the most notable viridans streptococci and is found in the mouth. This organism is therefore associated with endocarditis following dental procedures or in patients with poor dental hygiene.

Streptococcus viridans

previously was the most common cause of infective endocarditis, however this is no longer the case except in developing countries.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with chest pain. He has a history of previous ST-elevation myocardial infarction and angioplasty.

He describes periods of worsening stable angina limiting his exercise tolerance. His resting heart rate is 60bpm. Recent echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50-55%.

Current medications include amlodipine 10mg OD and bisoprolol 10mg OD.

What is the most appropriate medication to initiate while awaiting further investigation?
options_json: ["Change amlodipine to diltiazem", "Change bisoprolol to sotalol", "Isosorbide mononitrate (immediate release) BD at 0800 and 1400", "Isosorbide mononitrate (immediate release) at 0800 and 2200", "Ivabradine"]
answer_text: Isosorbide mononitrate (immediate release) BD at 0800 and 1400
explanation_text:
Asymmetric dosing regimes should be used for standard-release ISMN to prevent nitrate tolerance

This scenario describes a situation where a patient with stable angina is experiencing progressive symptoms while on maximum doses of dual anti-anginal therapy with a beta-blocker (bisoprolol) and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine).

NICE guidelines recommend commencing a third agent while awaiting specialist assessment in this situation. We are to consider: a long-acting nitrate, ranolazine, ivabradine or nicorandil.

Isosorbide mononitrate

(ISMN) is a long-acting nitrate that causes nitric oxide release resulting in vascular smooth muscle relaxation and subsequent vasodilation. Its principal mechanism in reducing anginal symptoms is venous dilation and consequently reduced preload and reducing myocardial oxygen demand. It can also dilate epicardial coronary arteries thereby increasing coronary arterial flow.

Evidence shows that continuous nitrate therapy produces tolerance with loss of pharmacological effect on repeated doses. Consequently, NICE recommend that a 'nitrate-free period' of 10-14 hours is maintained. Given that ISMN in the immediate release form acts for ~6 hours, dosing at 0800 and 1400 helps to safely maintain the nitrate-free period as recommended by NICE.

Dosing at

0800 and 2200

would leave a 12 hour total period between doses, but given the fact that the immediate release form acts for up to 6 hours, tolerance is more likely to develop. This would reduce drug efficacy after each subsequent dose.

Ivabradine

is recommended by NICE in patients who experience angina despite beta-blocker/calcium channel blocker monotherapy, or have NYHA II-IV symptoms with an ejection fraction <35% on optimal heart failure therapy. The only significant trial data is in patient cohorts with heart rates over 70bpm. This patient's resting heart rate and good LV function precludes him from ivabradine therapy.

Diltiazem

is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker and risks atrioventricular blockade when used in conjunction with a beta-blocker.

Sotalol

is a nonselective beta-blocker that is used in maintaining sinus rhythm in patients with atrial fibrillation as well as in reducing the frequency of both supraventricular and ventricular tachyarrhythmia. It has no place in the management of angina.

question_text: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the Emergency Room following a collapse at church. ECG reveals dissociation between the P and QRS complexes with a rate of 40 / minute. Which one of the following clinical findings may also be found?
options_json: ["Loud S1", "Narrow pulse pressure", "Giant v waveforms in the JVP", "Variable intensity of S1", "Soft S2"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block causes a variable intensity of S1

The correct answer is

variable intensity of S1

. In complete heart block (third-degree AV block), there is complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity. This means the P waves and QRS complexes occur independently of each other. When atrial contraction (P wave) occurs very close to ventricular contraction (QRS complex), the S1 heart sound will be louder due to higher ventricular end-diastolic volume. Conversely, when atrial contraction occurs far from ventricular contraction, S1 will be softer. This creates characteristic variation in S1 intensity.

Loud S1

is typically associated with conditions like mitral stenosis or short PR interval, not complete heart block. A consistently loud S1 would not be expected.

Narrow pulse pressure

is not a typical finding in complete heart block. The slow heart rate actually tends to cause an increased pulse pressure due to increased stroke volume.

Giant v waveforms in the JVP

are typically seen in tricuspid regurgitation, not complete heart block. The JVP may show cannon a waves due to atrial contraction against closed AV valves.

Soft S2

is not a characteristic finding of complete heart block. S2 intensity is more related to semilunar valve closure and arterial pressure than to AV conduction.

The bradycardia of 40/min and dissociated P waves and QRS complexes are classic ECG findings of complete heart block, which requires urgent temporary pacing followed by permanent pacemaker insertion in most cases.

question_text:
A 68-year-old woman presents with progressive shortness of breath. She has been feeling increasingly out of breath when doing jobs around the house over the past few months, to the point where she is now breathless on walking 5m. She denies any chest pain, cough, fevers or weight loss - if anything, she's put weight on! She has a background of hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

On examination, she has fine crepitations at both bases on auscultation, her JVP (jugular venous pressure) is raised to 4 cm above her clavicle, and she has some mild pitting oedema at her ankles. She has a regular pulse at around 70bpm, a central capillary refill time of less than 2 seconds, and moist oral mucosa.

An echocardiogram finds an ejection fraction of 40%, yet her NT-pro-BNP (N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide) is within the normal range at 240.

What could be the cause of this spurious result?
options_json: ["Her heart failure is already well-managed", "She is obese", "She is under the age of 70", "She has hypertension", "She is female"]
explanation_text:

question_text:
A 75-year-old man is admitted after feeling faint and complaining of palpitations. An ECG taken in the department shows a ventricular tachyarrhythmia. His blood pressure is stable. Treatment with IV amiodarone is commenced, with a loading dose being given initially.

What is the reason for the loading dose being given?
options_json: ["Autoinduction of the P450 system by amiodarone", "High ventricular rate leading to rapid dilution", "Long half-life of amiodarone", "Reduce the risk of extravasation injury", "Amiodarone exhibiting zero-order kinetics"]
explanation_text:
Amiodarone has a long half-life - it is highly lipophilic and widely absorbed by tissue, which reduces its bioavailability in serum. Therefore, a prolonged loading regime is required to achieve stable therapeutic levels

The correct answer is the

Long half-life of amiodarone

. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug with a long half-life, ranging from 25 to 100 days. The purpose of giving a loading dose is to achieve therapeutic levels more quickly, which helps to control ventricular tachyarrhythmia promptly. By administering a larger initial dose, the time required to reach steady-state concentrations in the body is significantly reduced.

The option

Autoinduction of the P450 system by amiodarone

is incorrect because amiodarone does not autoinduce its own metabolism in the liver. In fact, it inhibits various cytochrome P450 enzymes (e.g., CYP3A4 and CYP2C9), leading to potential drug interactions with other medications metabolized by these enzymes.

High ventricular rate leading to rapid dilution

is also incorrect. While high ventricular rates can lead to hemodynamic instability and decreased perfusion, this does not directly relate to the need for a loading dose of amiodarone. The loading dose is given due to its long half-life rather than any effect on dilution within the bloodstream.

The option

Reduce the risk of extravasation injury

is not correct as well. Extravasation injury refers to damage caused by leakage of medication into surrounding tissues during administration. A loading dose has no direct impact on reducing this risk; instead, proper IV insertion technique and close monitoring during administration are important measures for preventing extravasation injury.

Finally,

Amiodarone exhibiting zero-order kinetics

is an incorrect choice. Zero-order kinetics refers to drugs that have a constant rate of elimination regardless of their concentration in the bloodstream. Amiodarone follows first-order kinetics, meaning that its rate of elimination is proportional to its concentration in the blood. The need for a loading dose is not related to the drug's kinetics but rather its long half-life, which delays the attainment of therapeutic levels.

explanation_text:
Labetalol is first-line for pregnancy-induced hypertension

The correct answer is

labetalol

. Labetalol is considered first-line treatment for hypertension in pregnancy according to NICE guidelines, particularly in cases of pre-eclampsia. It is both safe and effective during pregnancy, working through combined alpha and beta blockade to lower blood pressure. It can be given orally or intravenously if rapid blood pressure control is needed.

Nifedipine

is also used in pregnancy-induced hypertension but is generally considered second-line after labetalol. While it is safe in pregnancy, there are some concerns about rapid blood pressure lowering with short-acting preparations.

Atenolol

is not recommended in pregnancy as it has been associated with intrauterine growth restriction. While other beta-blockers may be used in pregnancy, atenolol specifically should be avoided.

Losartan

and other angiotensin receptor blockers are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as they can cause severe fetal abnormalities, particularly in the second and third trimesters. They should never be used in pregnant women.

Methyldopa

was historically used as first-line treatment for hypertension in pregnancy but has largely been superseded by labetalol due to its side effect profile, which includes sedation and depression. While still safe in pregnancy, it is now generally considered third-line therapy.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man is admitted with palpitations. He has no chest pain, physical examination is normal apart from tachycardia and he is haemodynamically stable. Cardiac monitoring shows a regular, monomorphic, broad complex tachycardia. A 12-lead electrocardiogram does not show any features of myocardial ischaemia.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and previous percutaneous coronary intervention to his left anterior descending, right coronary and circumflex arteries.

Which of the following management options is contraindicated in this scenario?
options_json: ["Adenosine", "Amiodarone", "Magnesium sulphate", "Vagal manoeuvres", "Verapamil"]
explanation_text:
Ventricular tachycardia - verapamil is contraindicated

The correct answer is verapamil.

The most likely diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia (VT). Verapamil is contraindicated in VT as intravenous administration of a calcium channel blocker can precipitate cardiac arrest.

Adenosine is used to treat regular narrow complex tachycardias. If this patient was known to have supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with bundle branch block then his broad complex tachycardia could be treated with adenosine, and adenosine is not contraindicated in broad complex tachycardias.

Amiodarone is the recommended treatment for regular broad complex tachycardia (300mg IV over 20-60 minutes then 900mg over 24 hours).

Magnesium sulphate 2g intravenously over 10 minutes is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Whilst magnesium sulphate is not the first-choice treatment for monomorphic VT, it is unlikely to be harmful in this patient and is not contraindicated.

Vagal manoeuvres are used to treat regular narrow complex tachycardias. If this patient was known to have an SVT with bundle branch block then his broad complex tachycardia could be treated with vagal manoeuvres.

On examination, she appears dyspnoeic and a D-dimer test is positive. A subsequent CT pulmonary angiogram confirms a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism. There is no clear cause that could have provoked this. Accordingly, she is commenced on anticoagulation.

For how long should this treatment continue?
options_json: ["3 months", "4 months", "6 months", "12 months", "Lifelong"]
explanation_text:
'Unprovoked' pulmonary embolisms are typically treated for 6 months

The correct answer is 6 months. As of 2020, first-line treatment is now with direct oral anticoagulants. Patients are usually reviewed after 3 months, and for those in whom no cause was found (unprovoked), it is usually continued for a further 3 months, to a total of 6 months.

3 months would be appropriate if the embolism was provoked - for instance, recent major surgery with associated extended bed rest and immobility. However, as there was no clear cause here, 6 months is more appropriate.

4 months is not a standard length of time that anticoagulation is given for.

12 months is not a standard length of time to continue anticoagulation. After review, the doctor may well decide to extend it for this period of time, but 6 months is the usual duration.

In some cases, anticoagulation may be recommended lifelong, for example, if an underlying prothrombotic condition is found. For this patient, however, 6 months is appropriate.

question_text: Which part of the jugular venous waveform may be exaggerated in tricuspid regurgitation?
options_json: ["x descent", "v wave", "y descent", "a wave", "c wave"]
explanation_text:
JVP: giant v waves in tricuspid regurgitation

The correct answer is the

v wave

. In tricuspid regurgitation, blood flows back into the right atrium during systole which leads to an increased volume of blood in the atrium. This results in a higher pressure during atrial filling and therefore an exaggerated v wave on the jugular venous waveform.

Discussing the incorrect options:

x descent

- The x descent represents atrial relaxation and ventricular contraction. It is not directly affected by tricuspid regurgitation because it doesn't reflect changes in right atrial pressure that occur with this condition.

y descent

- The y descent occurs after the v wave and represents rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle following the opening of the tricuspid valve. While this may be affected in some cases of tricuspid regurgitation, it is not typically exaggerated as a result of this condition.

a wave

- The a wave represents right atrial contraction. Tricuspid regurgitation does not typically cause an exaggerated a wave because it does not affect atrial contraction.

c wave

- The c wave follows the a wave and reflects closure of the tricuspid valve and bulging of it into the right atrium during early ventricular systole. It is not typically exaggerated in tricuspid regurgitation because this condition affects valve function during diastole rather than systole.

question_text: Each one of the following is associated with left axis deviation on ECG, except:
options_json: ["Left anterior hemiblock", "Ostium primum ASD", "Left posterior hemiblock", "Obesity", "Left bundle branch block"]
explanation_text:
Right axis deviation - left posterior hemiblock

The correct answer is

Left posterior hemiblock

. Left axis deviation on ECG is associated with conditions that cause left ventricular hypertrophy or an increased leftward electrical activity. These include Left anterior hemiblock, Ostium primum ASD, Obesity and Left bundle branch block. However, Left posterior hemiblock does not cause a left axis deviation.

Left anterior hemiblock

is characterised by a leftward shift of the QRS axis between -45 to -90 degrees. This is because the depolarisation wavefront moves from right to left in the frontal plane, causing a left axis deviation.

Ostium primum ASD

, a type of atrial septal defect (ASD), is associated with left axis deviation due to the anomalous location of the AV node and His bundle which results in abnormal activation of the ventricles.

In

Obesity

, there can be an increased load on the heart leading to cardiac remodelling and subsequent changes in ventricular depolarisation. This may result in a shift of the electrical axis towards the left.

A

Left bundle branch block

(LBBB) also causes left axis deviation as it involves delayed activation of the left ventricle due to blockage in the bundle branch. The initial vector of depolarisation is directed towards right and anteriorly (due to septal activation) and then finally ends up moving towards left and posteriorly (due to delayed LV free wall activation), hence causing a net overall shift towards left resulting in LAD.

In contrast,

Left posterior hemiblock

, causes right axis deviation rather than left. This occurs because it involves failure of impulse conduction through the posterior fascicle of the Left Bundle Branch which supplies the inferior-posterior part of LV resulting in delayed activation of this region. The initial vector remains unchanged but the late vector shifts rightwards and inferiorly leading to RAD instead of LAD.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a longstanding history of leg swellings is now also complaining of becoming short of breath when walking. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischaemic heart disease and diabetes mellitus. He recently stopped smoking after doing so for the last 40 years and is now retired at home living with his wife in a two-bedroom house. Upon examination, he had a pansystolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge with peripheral pitting oedema to the shins and a clear chest when auscultated. He appeared comfortable at rest and was not in any distress.

What is the most likely cause for his murmur?
options_json: ["Connective tissue disorder", "Hyperdynamic circulation", "Patent ductus arteriosus", "Pulmonary hypertension", "Ventricular septal rupture"]
explanation_text:
Functional tricuspid regurgitation often occurs secondary to pulmonary hypertension

Functional tricuspid regurgitation often occurs secondary to pulmonary hypertension as a result of chronic lung disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) producing a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, raised jugular venous pressure and a pansystolic murmur in the left lower sternal edge.

Other secondary causes of tricuspid regurgitation involve mitral valve stenosis and regurgitation as well as pulmonary thromboembolism.

Ventricular septal rupture is a rare but serious complication of myocardial infarction which can occurs 2-8 days after an infarction and often precipitates cardiogenic shock. It can give rise to a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) produces a continuous 'machine-like' murmur which is commonly seen in newborns.

Connective tissue disorders can give rise to various murmurs. Aortic regurgitation can occur in Marfan's syndrome. Mitral valve prolapse can occur in Marfan's syndrome and Ehler's Danlos Syndrome.

Hyperdynamic circulation of the blood can produce a functional murmur in cases of anaemic or thyrotoxic states.

explanation_text:
Labetalol is first-line for pregnancy-induced hypertension

Labetalol is the correct answer. This woman has gestational hypertension as evidenced by the development of new-onset stage I hypertension after 20 weeks gestation. There is no proteinuria to suggest pre-eclampsia. NICE guidelines in 2019 suggest medical treatment if the blood pressure remains elevated >140/90 mmHg.
