question_text:
A 72-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath and leg swelling.

An echocardiogram is performed:


Echocardiogram	Left ventricular systolic dysfunction; Ejection fraction 22%

Blood results are as follows:


BNP	1248 pmol/L	(47 - 236)

How does the measured hormone help the body adapt to heart failure?
options_json: ["Decreases cardiac afterload", "Increases cardiac afterload", "Increases sympathetic tone", "Reduces myocardial contractility", "Stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system"]
explanation_text:
BNP - actions:

The clinical history and raised BNP are suggestive of heart failure. It is important to note that while BNP has many protective physiological effects in heart failure, its levels can become chronically elevated in advanced heart failure, which can be a sign of worsening disease. In such cases, healthcare providers may use medications like angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and beta-blockers to help manage heart failure and improve outcomes.

Decreases cardiac afterload

is correct. BNP is elevated in patients with chronic heart failure. It has natriuretic effects and is a potent vasodilator. Vasodilation results in a reduction in cardiac afterload. These may have some protective roles.

Increases cardiac afterload

is incorrect. BNP is a potent vasodilator resulting in a reduction in cardiac afterload.

Increases sympathetic tone

is incorrect. BNP suppresses sympathetic tone.

Reduces myocardial contractility

is incorrect. BNP has no direct effect on myocardial contractility. However, it can reduce the cardiac afterload due to its vasodilation effect.

Stimulates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

is incorrect. BNP suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

question_text:
An 80-year-old man presents to accident and emergency with leg swelling. He has been more fatigued recently. His past medical history includes diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has been on metformin and inhalers for many years.

On examination, you note a barrel chest, elevated jugular venous pressure, and a systolic murmur over the 4th intercostal left parasternal region. You ask him to take a deep breath in and the murmur becomes louder. You listen over the carotids but hear no murmurs. Lungs are vesicular with no wheezes or crackles. You examine his legs which show bilateral pitting oedema. Heart rate 85 and blood pressure 130/80mmHg.

What valvular pathology is present in this patient's heart?
options_json: ["Aortic stenosis", "Mitral regurgitation", "Mitral stenosis", "Tricuspid regurgitation", "Tricuspid stenosis"]
explanation_text:
Tricuspid regurgitation becomes louder during inspiration, unlike mitral regurgitation

This patient has tricuspid regurgitation as evidenced by the following:

1- Systolic murmur.

2- Loudest in the 4th intercostal left parasternal region.

3- Louder on inspiration.

4- The patient has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is developing signs of core pulmonale.

Aortic stenosis presents as an ejection systolic murmur loudest in the right parasternal 2nd intercostal space. The murmur becomes louder on expiration due to increased left ventricular preload and softer on inspiration as left ventricular preload decreases due to reduced intra-thoracic pressure. Aortic stenosis commonly radiates to the carotids which was not the case in this patient.

Mitral regurgitation presents as a pan-systolic murmur loudest in the left mid-clavicular 4th intercostal space. It is louder on expiration due to higher left ventricular preload, and softer on inspiration due to pooling of the blood in the lungs. Mitral regurgitation often occurs in patients with hypertension, which is not present in this patient and is not a consequence of COPD and cor pulmonale.

Mitral stenosis presents with an end-diastolic murmur loudest in the left mid-clavicular fourth intercostal space. It often leads to left heart failure with pulmonary oedema and breathlessness. This patient did not have crackles in the chest. Furthermore, the anatomical location and the timing of the murmur in the cardiac cycle were not suggestive of mitral stenosis.

Tricuspid stenosis is rare and usually presents in neonates as an end-diastolic murmur loudest in the left parasternal 4th intercostal space. Both tricuspid stenosis and regurgitation increase on inspiration as the intrathoracic pressure decreases leading to right heart filling and increased preload. Despite being in the same anatomical location as in this patient, it is a diastolic rather than a systolic murmur.

options_json: ["An opening snap", "Longer murmur", "Loud S1", "Loud S2", "Louder murmur"]
explanation_text:
In mitral stenosis, an opening snap indicates the leaflets still have some mobility

This is a two-part question. The first step is getting the diagnosis resulting in the patient's symptoms. He has presented with haemoptysis, dyspnoea, an irregularly irregular pulse - likely secondary to atrial fibrillation, and a mid-diastolic murmur. These symptoms are all suggestive of mitral stenosis.

An opening snap

indicates the leaflets are still mobile. This is due to the forceful opening of the mitral valve when the pressure in the left atrium is greater than the pressure in the left ventricle.

A longer murmur

is an indication of the severity of mitral stenosis. This is due to the fact that factors reducing the left ventricular volume including decreased venous return, tachycardia, increased myocardial contractility or reduced afterload will cause the mitral valve leaflets to prolapse earlier in systole. This will result in the systolic click and murmur moving further towards the first sound, resulting in the murmur becoming longer.

Loud S2

is not a feature of mitral stenosis.  S2 occurs due to the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. A loud S2 can be a loud A2 or a loud P2. Loud A2 can occur in systemic hypertension due to dilated proximal aorta. A loud P2 is heard in pulmonary hypertension.

Loud S1

is a feature of mitral stenosis but does not indicate the leaflets still have some mobility. Loud S1 occurs due to greater excursion of leaflets during the closure as elevated left atrial pressure has kept the leaflets wide apart.

A louder murmur

again may indicate the severity but does not reflect on the mobility of the leaflets. The duration of the murmur is directly proportional to the severity of mitral stenosis, the intensity is not.  Advanced mitral stenosis can present with signs of heart failure.

A 46-year-old woman presents to the medical assessment unit with a four-month history of shortness of breath and lightheadedness on exertion. On examination, she has a systolic murmur. When palpating her radial artery, a double pulse is felt during systole.

What condition is most likely to produce this pulse?
options_json: ["Aortic stenosis", "Asthma", "Cardiac tamponade", "Left ventricular failure", "Mixed aortic valve disease"]
explanation_text:
Bisferiens pulse - mixed aortic valve disease

Mixed aortic valve disease

is the correct answer. A double pulse felt in systole is called a bisferiens pulse or pulsus bisferiens. The first pulse is caused by the pressure increase related to left ventricular ejection - the second pulse is caused by a reflected wave from the periphery due to an artery's recoil effect (Goudar, R. B., & ElBebawy, B. (2023). Pulsus Bisferiens. In StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing.). The most common causes of a bisferiens pulse are mixed aortic valve disease (i.e. aortic regurgitation and stenosis) and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

Aortic stenosis

is the incorrect answer. Aortic stenosis can cause a slow-rising pulse (a delayed upstroke in the pulse, often noted in the central pulse), but does not cause a bisferiens pulse unless accompanied by aortic regurgitation.

Asthma

is the incorrect answer. Severe asthma does not cause a bisferiens pulse. However, severe asthma can cause pulsus paradoxus (a >10mmHg fall in blood pressure during inspiration).

Cardiac tamponade

is the incorrect answer. Cardiac tamponade can also cause pulsus paradoxus but does not cause a bisferiens pulse.

Left ventricular failure

is the incorrect answer. Severe left ventricular failure can cause pulsus alternates (regular alternation of the force of the arterial pulse) but does not cause a bisferiens pulse.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic for the management of chronic heart failure. He has been established on bisoprolol, ramipril and eplerenone for over a year.

The patient reports ongoing symptoms of breathlessness and swelling of the legs.

His observations are as follows:

Heart rate: 66 beats per minute
Blood pressure: 130/80 mmHg
Oxygen sats: 94% on room air & at rest
Temperature: 36.5 oC

An ECG shows sinus rhythm and an echocardiogram performed in the clinic showed an LVEF of 30% with no evidence of valvular disease.

What alteration to the patient's medication is most appropriate?
options_json: ["Add hydralazine", "Add spironolactone", "Stop bisoprolol and start carvedilol", "Stop ramipril and start ivabradine", "Stop ramipril and start sacubitril-valsartan"]
explanation_text:
Sacubitril-valsartan is considered in heart failure patients with a LVEF < 35% who are still symptomatic on ACE-inhibitors & beta-blockers

This patient has a significant reduction in cardiac function with ongoing symptomatic heart failure despite second-line treatment. His heart rate is <75 beats per minute and he is in a sinus rhythm.

Sacubitril-valsartan

would therefore be the most appropriate agent to commence as the patient has an LVEF <35%, is symptomatic and already established on an ACE-inhibitor (ACE-i) and beta-blocker. This drug combines the neprilysin-inhibitor sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan and is recommended for third-line use in the 2018 NICE heart failure management guidelines. As sacubitril-valsartan contains an ARB it should only be commenced following a wash-out period of any ACEi or ARB a patient is already established on (in this case the patient's ramipril should be stopped).

Hydralazine

may be considered as an alternative third agent in the management of chronic heart failure. However, it must be used in combination with nitrates. Hydralazine alone has not demonstrated significant improvement in symptoms or a reduction in mortality and therefore is only recommended if used with a nitrate.

Spironolactone

is an aldosterone antagonist used as a second-line agent in chronic heart failure management. This patient has already been established on eplerenone, which is an aldosterone antagonist, and remains symptomatic therefore another class of drug must be commenced.

Carvedilol

can be used in the management of chronic heart failure as a non-selective beta blocker and alpha-1 blocker however this patient has already been established on a beta-blocker and remains symptomatic. Carvedilol is therefore very unlikely to improve his symptoms and is not recommended as an alternative agent.

Ivabradine

is another third-line agent that can be used in the management of chronic heart failure. However, the patient must have a resting heart rate of at least 75/min to be commenced on this drug. Ivabradine's mechanism of action is to block channels responsible for cardiac pacing and therefore patients with a lower resting heart rate are potentially more prone to adverse events.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man attends for a follow-up appointment after starting on rate control treatment for their atrial fibrillation. They have had no episodes of palpitations, light-headedness, or syncope.

On examination, they have an irregularly, irregular pulse with a heart rate of 82 beats per minute. Overall, he feels his atrial fibrillation is well-controlled but he has noticed that his bowel habit has altered since starting this treatment, and has had problems moving his bowels.

What rate-control medication is he most likely to be on?
options_json: ["Diltiazem", "Bisoprolol", "Verapamil", "Metoprolol", "Digoxin"]
explanation_text:
Verapamil can cause constipation

Calcium channel blockers commonly cause constipation. Of the two calcium channel blockers commonly used as rate control for atrial fibrillation, verapamil is most commonly associated with constipation and NICE guidance recommends people starting on verapamil eat more fibre and increase their water consumption to counteract this. The reason that calcium channel blockers cause constipation is that their mechanism of action is to relax smooth muscle which inadvertently relaxes the muscles of the gut thereby reducing motility.

Diltiazem may also cause constipation but this side-effect is less common than with verapamil.

Digoxin is more likely to cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Bisoprolol and metoprolol are examples of beta-blockers. They are associated with diarrhoea rather than constipation as a side-effect.

A 45-year-old female is due to undergo a dental extraction for relief of neuralgic pain. Additionally, she is having a hysterectomy in 4 weeks for a fibroid uterus with menorrhagia. She mentions to you that she has previously been diagnosed with a heart murmur and wants to know if this will affect her operation.

In regard to her valvular heart disease and associated risk, what is the most appropriate thing to advise her?
options_json: ["She should have antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of hysterectomy only", "She should have antibiotic prophylaxis for both procedures", "She is not at risk of infective endocarditis so should not worry", "She is at theoretical risk of infective endocarditis but antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer advised routinely for either procedure", "She should be offered chlorhexidine mouthwash as prophylaxis when undergoing the dental extraction"]
answer_text: She is at theoretical risk of infective endocarditis but antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer advised routinely for either procedure
explanation_text:
Antibiotic prohylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis is not routinely recommended in the UK for dental and other procedures

The answer to this question is based on NICE Guidance (CG64 - March 2008).

According to this guidance, as neither procedure requires prophylaxis (either antibiotics or mouthwash) the only appropriate answer here is 4: that the patient is at theoretical risk of infective endocarditis but that antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended.

question_text:
An 89-year-old man attends your clinic, complaining of bright spots in his vision that come and go. He has a past medical history of asthma, triple vessel coronary artery disease opting for medical management of his anginal symptoms, and has just completed a course of itraconazole for a fungal infection. His heart rate is 60bpm and blood pressure 120/70mmHg.

Which of his regular medications is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
options_json: ["Amlodipine", "Bezafibrate", "Ivabradine", "Ranolazine", "Ventolin"]
explanation_text:
Ivabradine use may be associated with visual disturbances including phosphenes and green luminescence

Ivabradine is indicated for the symptomatic relief of angina in patients with a heart rate >70, as an alternative to first line therapies. It is also indicated for the treatment of chronic heart failure (NYHA II-IV) in addition to standard therapy, in patients with a heart rate of >75.

The mode of action of ivabradine is by inhibition of If channels (known as funny channels), I = current, f =funny. These funny channels are so called because of their unusual features compared to other ion channels. They are mixed sodium and potassium channels found in spontaneously active regions of the heart such as the sinoatrial node and are triggered by hyperpolarisation. Activated funny channels allow an influx of positive ions, triggering depolarisation and are therefore responsible for the spontaneous activity of cardiac myocytes.

By inhibiting If channels ivabradine delays depolarisation in the sinoatrial node and therefore selectively slows heart rate.

The commonest side effect caused by ivabradine is transient luminous phenomenon (reported by up to 15% of patients), such as bright spots appearing in their field of vision. Less commonly blurred vision is reported. Patients should be informed of this common side effect before starting the medication. The visual side effects of ivabradine are likely to be mediated by inhibition of a channel similar to the If channel found in the retina called the Ih channel. The h = hyperpolarisation-activated, these channels were formerly called IQ channels, Q = queer, again for their unusual characteristics.

Ivabradine is metabolised by oxidation through cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) only. Therefore drugs that induce (e.g rifampicin) or inhibit (e.g erythromycin, itraconazole) CYP3A4, will decrease or increase the plasma concentration of ivabradine respectively. In this case the patient has been taking the potent CYP3A4 inhibitor Itraconazole, this would have increased the plasma concentration of ivabradine, resulting in the visual side effects experienced.

question_text:
A 60-year-old woman presents to her GP experiencing intermittent palpitations for several weeks. She is in good overall health and has not reported any episodes of chest pain.

She has hypertension, which is effectively managed with a single antihypertensive medication. Otherwise, she is well and has no other previous medical history.

Upon conducting an ECG, it was discovered that she was in atrial fibrillation. All other observations are within normal range.

What anticoagulation strategy would you recommend?
options_json: ["Commencing aspirin", "Commencing clopidogrel & aspirin", "Commencing dabigatran", "Commencing warfarin", "No anticoagulation treatment is required currently"]
explanation_text:
DOACs should be offered first-line for reducing stroke risk in AF

This patient has presented with atrial fibrillation (AF) and a CHA

2

DS

2

-VAS

c

score of 2 (+1 as she is female and +1 as she has hypertension). According to the 2021 NICE guideline updates, she should be recommended an anticoagulant as a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC).

Dabigatran

is currently a NICE-approved DOAC for reducing the risk of stroke. It is a direct thrombin inhibitor, blocking the enzyme in the blood clotting process. Unlike older anticoagulants like warfarin, it is administered orally and doesn't require frequent blood monitoring, offering both effectiveness and convenience for patients who need anticoagulation therapy.

Aspirin

is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in AF patients, as it is less effective than newer anticoagulants like DOACs. DOACs specifically target the clotting process, whereas aspirin primarily inhibits platelet aggregation, offering inferior prophylaxis. With the risk of bleeding complications comparable between aspirin and DOACs, DOACs are now recommended as the first-line treatment.

Clopidogrel & aspirin

are generally only used in combination for cardiac diseases such as coronary atherothrombosis. Antiplatelet therapy is no longer recommended for stroke prevention, with newer DOACs advised instead.

Warfarin

is no longer the first-line treatment for stroke prevention in AF, primarily because of its requirement for frequent blood testing and its potential for increased medication interactions. NICE now recommends using DOACs as the first-line choice due to their convenience, effectiveness, and fewer interactions. In certain conditions, like uncontrolled hypertension and severe renal impairment, warfarin might be considered instead of DOACs, but this patient does not have any of these conditions.

question_text:
You are performing a skin biopsy on a 65-year-old woman with possible skin cancer. Shortly after infiltration of the skin with xylocaine with adrenaline, you note that her fingers start to turn blue and cold.

What treatment is indicated?
options_json: ["Lipid emulsion", "Phenoxybenzamine", "Phentolamine", "Physostigmine", "Propranolol"]
explanation_text:
Adrenaline induced ischaemia - phentolamine

Adrenaline is often added to a local anaesthetic to prolong its effect. Caution is recommended when adrenaline is used in body parts with end arteries (e.g. fingers and toes). Adrenaline may constrict the arteries and reduce blood supply to those organs, resulting in complications. Adrenaline acts on α-1 adrenoceptors to cause vascular smooth muscle constriction.

Phentolamine

is correct. This drug is a competitive α-adrenoreceptor antagonist which can be injected to reverse the effects of adrenaline on the vasculature.

Lipid emulsion

is incorrect. This can be used for local anaesthetic toxicity which presents with peri-oral numbness, paraesthesia, tinnitus and confusion, leading to coma, seizure and cardiac toxicity.

Phenoxybenzamine

is incorrect. This drug is a non-selective α-adrenergic antagonist. Although this would result in vasodilation it is not licensed for use in this context.

Physostigmine

is incorrect. This drug is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor which can be used to treat anti-cholinergic toxicity. Features of anti-cholinergic toxicity includes fever, confusion, dry mouth, and urinary retention.

Propranolol

is incorrect. Propranolol is a β-adrenoreceptor antagonist and thus would not reverse the effects of adrenaline on the smooth muscle of the vasculature.

A 25-year-old primigravida woman presents to the hospital with a headache, fever, vomiting, and three episodes of convulsions. They were tonic-clonic movements lasting one to two minutes. She has no history of hypertension or epilepsy. Her blood pressure was 186/136 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats per minute, and temperature 36.9ºC on admission. Given the suspected diagnosis, she is commenced on intravenous magnesium sulfate. The evening senior house officer is handed over to perform a neurological examination in order to monitor her reflexes.

What else would be important to monitor with this treatment?
options_json: ["Blood ketones", "Blood sugar", "Heart rate", "Pupil size", "Respiratory rate"]
explanation_text:
Magnesium sulphate - monitor reflexes + respiratory rate

Respiratory rate

is monitored to ensure there is no evidence of respiratory depression as the breath rate should not be under 16 breaths per minute, which may indicate toxicity.

Heart rate

would be routinely monitored but is not specific with this treatment of intravenous magnesium sulphate.

Blood ketones

would not be routinely monitored and is not specific with this treatment of intravenous magnesium sulphate to assess for toxicity.

Blood glucose

would only be routinely monitored if needed and is not specific to this treatment of intravenous magnesium sulphate to assess for toxicity.

Pupil size

is not required to be specifically monitored but the patient's consciousness level is to assess for any magnesium toxicity.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man presents to his general practitioner for a review of his anti-hypertensive treatment. He has a past medical history of essential hypertension and his regular medications are ramipril and amlodipine.

His ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is reviewed and demonstrates an average blood pressure of 161/94 mmHg.

The examination is unremarkable.

His general practitioner decides to add a medication to better control his blood pressure.

What is the mechanism of action of the likely medication?
options_json: ["Aldosterone inhibition", "Angiotensin receptor blocker", "Inhibition of Na+-Clˆ’ symporter at the distal convoluted tubule", "Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme", "Beta-1-adrenergic antagonists"]
answer_text: Inhibition of Na+-Clˆ’ symporter at the distal convoluted tubule
explanation_text:
Thiazides/thiazide-like drugs (e.g. indapamide) - inhibits sodium reabsorption by blocking the  Na

Inhibition of Na+-Clˆ’ symporter at the distal convoluted tubule is the correct answer. This man with essential hypertension has inadequately controlled blood pressure on a combination of amlodipine and ramipril. NICE guidelines suggest a thiazide diuretic is the next appropriate step in management in this situation. The mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics is inhibition of Na+-Clˆ’ symporter at the distal convoluted tubule causing inhibition of sodium reabsorption.

Aldosterone inhibition is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of spironolactone, which would be indicated if the addition of a thiazide diuretic was insufficient (and the initial potassium level was <4.5 mmol/L).

Angiotensin receptor blocker is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of losartan. The patient is already on an ACE inhibitor. These medications are not typically used in combination for hypertension as they have a similar mechanism of action.

Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of ramipril, which he is already taking.

A beta-1-adrenergic antagonist is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of atenolol. If the blood pressure is not well controlled on four drugs (or spironolactone is unsuitable) then this would be an option for better blood pressure control.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction 5 years ago presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations and mild dizziness for the past hour. He is haemodynamically stable. An ECG shows a broad complex tachycardia at a rate of 150 beats per minute. On closer examination, P waves can be seen that are dissociated from the QRS complexes, with more QRS complexes than P waves. The QRS duration is 170 ms with a northwest axis. There is positive concordance across the precordial leads.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block", "Atrial flutter with aberrant conduction", "Sinus tachycardia with pre-existing bundle branch block", "Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction", "Ventricular tachycardia"]
explanation_text:
Atrioventricular dissociation suggests VT rather than SVT with aberrant conduction

Ventricular tachycardia

is the correct diagnosis based on several key features in this case. The ECG shows atrioventricular (AV) dissociation, which is one of the most specific findings for ventricular tachycardia (VT). This is evidenced by P waves that are clearly dissociated from the QRS complexes, with more QRS complexes than P waves. The patient also has multiple other features strongly suggestive of VT: a very broad QRS complex (170 ms, which exceeds the 160 ms threshold that favours VT), positive concordance across the precordial leads (where all QRS complexes in the chest leads point in the same direction), and a northwest axis (marked left axis deviation). Additionally, the patient's history of previous myocardial infarction significantly increases the pre-test probability of VT, as scarred myocardium provides an ideal substrate for ventricular arrhythmias. The combination of these features makes VT the most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

Atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block

would present with an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves, rather than the regular rhythm with dissociated P waves described in this case. While bundle branch block would cause QRS widening, the other features such as the positive concordance and extreme axis deviation would not be typical. Additionally, the rate in atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block is often more variable than the stable 150 bpm described here.

Atrial flutter with aberrant conduction

would typically present with a regular rhythm, but the ventricular rate would usually be a fraction of the atrial rate (commonly 2:1 or 3:1 conduction), creating a consistent relationship between atrial and ventricular activity. In this case, the P waves are completely dissociated from the QRS complexes, ruling out this diagnosis. Atrial flutter waves would also have a characteristic sawtooth pattern, which is not described in this scenario.

Sinus tachycardia with pre-existing bundle branch block

would show a 1:1 relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, with each P wave followed by a QRS complex at a consistent PR interval. The AV dissociation described in this case excludes this diagnosis. Additionally, sinus tachycardia rarely reaches 150 bpm in adults unless there is significant physiological stress.

Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction

would maintain AV synchrony, with each QRS complex being preceded by a P wave (though P waves may be hidden within the preceding T wave in some forms of SVT). The presence of AV dissociation, extremely wide QRS complexes, positive concordance, and marked left axis deviation all strongly favour VT over SVT with aberrancy.

question_text: A 62-year-old female with a known history of a sigmoid adenocarcinoma is admitted to hospital with shortness of breath and pyrexia. On examination a murmur is heard and an echo reveals a vegetation on the aortic valve. Which one of the following organisms is most characteristically associated with causing infective endocarditis in patients with colorectal cancer?
options_json: ["Escherichia coli", "Enterococcus faecalis", "Salmonella", "Campylobacter", "Streptococcus bovis"]
explanation_text:
Streptococcus bovis

The correct answer is

Streptococcus bovis

.

Streptococcus bovis

is characteristically associated with causing infective endocarditis in patients with colorectal cancer. This association is well-documented, and it has been found that up to 25% of patients with

S. bovis

endocarditis have underlying colorectal neoplasms. It is thought that the bacteria may translocate from the gut to the bloodstream due to disruptions in the mucosal barrier caused by the malignancy.

The first incorrect option is

Escherichia coli

. Although

E. coli

is a common cause of urinary tract infections and can occasionally cause bacteremia, it is not typically associated with infective endocarditis or colorectal cancer.

The second incorrect option is

Enterococcus faecalis

. While

E. faecalis

can be a cause of infective endocarditis, particularly in healthcare-associated cases or those related to genitourinary procedures, it does not have a specific association with colorectal cancer like

S. bovis

.

The third incorrect option is

Salmonella

. Although some rare cases of infective endocarditis due to non-typhoidal Salmonella have been reported, this organism is not characteristically associated with either infective endocarditis or colorectal cancer.

Finally, the fourth incorrect option is

Campylobacter

. While Campylobacter species are a common cause of gastroenteritis, they are not typically associated with infective endocarditis or colorectal cancer.

question_text:
A 79-year-old female, newly diagnosed as hypertensive is taken to the emergency department with collapse. She recalls feeling 'giddy' moments before. She had just started a new medication from her GP.

Her past medical history includes: type II diabetes mellitus, glaucoma, diverticular disease.

Which of the following medications is she most likely to have just started?
options_json: ["Ramipril", "Prochlorperazine", "Fludrocortisone", "Metformin", "Timolol eye drops"]
explanation_text:
ACE inhibitors can cause first dose hypotension

The prodrome of feeling 'giddy' should raise suspicions of syncope.

ACE inhibitors (eg ramipril) can characteristically cause first-dose hypotension. It is also the first line anti-hypertensive in diabetics.

Prochlorperazine is a medication used to treat vertigo, amongst other indications. It is not used in the treatment of any of this lady's medical problems. Additionally, it is unlikely to result in syncope.

Fludrocortisone acts to increase blood pressure and therefore would not lead to syncope.

Metformin rarely causes hypoglycaemia and is therefore unlikely to cause collapse.

While beta-blockers could cause syncope this is very unlikely after application of eye drops.

question_text:
An 88-year-old woman presents with palpitations for three days. Her medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), symptomatic postural hypotension, wheelchair-bound, and recurrent falls. Her ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate of 126 bpm. A decision to rate control is decided. With the risk of worsening postural hypotension with other rate-control agents, she is given an oral rate-control medication that does not induce hypotension and is a weakly positive inotrope.

What is the mechanism of action of this rate-controlling medication?
options_json: ["Blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels", "Inhibiting the Na+/Cl- symporter", "Inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump", "Inhibits the Na+/K+/Cl2- cotransporter", "Muscarinic receptor antagonist"]
explanation_text:
Digoxin - inhibits the Na

It is recommended to start beta blockers in patients with HFrEF, and atrial fibrillation. However, the patient would be at increased risk of postural hypotension, if beta-blockers were started. Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are contraindicated in patients with HFrEF and would increase the risk of postural hypotension. The palpitations started more than 48 hours. Therefore, a chemical or electrical cardioversion is not recommended unless a transoesophageal echocardiogram shows no left atrial appendage thrombus. Digoxin would be an appropriate medication in this scenario given its lack of effect on blood pressure, and the patient's history of HFrEF and her immobility. Digoxin

inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump

causing increased intracellular sodium and calcium levels leading to a decrease in conduction through the AV node. This inhibition can lead to hyperkalaemia in acute digoxin toxicity.

Thiazide diuretics decrease intravascular volume by

inhibiting the Na+/Cl- symporter

in the distal convoluted tubule. Thiazide diuretics would not be first-line diuretics if this woman is clinically overloaded. Side effects of thiazides include hypercalcemia, hypokalaemia, and hyperglycaemia.

Class I antiarrhythmics, such as lidocaine, work by

blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels

in phase 0 of the cardiac action potential. Class I antiarrhythmics such as flecainide are used for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. Flecainide is contraindicated in this woman as she has heart failure. These class I antiarrhythmics are not used in rate control management of atrial fibrillation.

Loop diuretics, such as furosemide,

inhibit the Na+/K+/Cl2- cotransporter

in the thick ascending loop of Henle. The woman has presented with palpitations and no overt signs of heart failure so furosemide will not be beneficial in this scenario. Side effects of loop diuretics include hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, and hyperglycaemia.

Muscarinic receptor antagonism

medications are not used to treat tachyarrhythmias. Atropine's mechanism of action to increase the heart rate is through cardiac

muscarinic receptor antagonism

. Atropine is a first-line treatment for hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. Its use is limited in hemodynamically unstable bradycardia caused by infra-nodal heart blocks.

question_text:
A 69-year-old man has been brought to the emergency department by ambulance with sudden onset tearing chest pain.

Cross-sectional imaging has confirmed a thoracic aortic dissection, involving the descending aorta only. There is no evidence of malperfusion.

He is currently alert and orientated. His pulse rate is 100bpm and his blood pressure is 156/98mmHg.

What is the most appropriate treatment strategy for this patient?
options_json: ["Intravenous labetalol", "Intravenous sodium nitroprusside", "Observation and optimise analgesia", "Referral for urgent surgery", "Sublingual nifedipine"]
explanation_text:
Aortic dissection

Acute aortic dissection involves the splitting of the tunica media of the aorta, resulting in the creation of a true lumen and a false lumen. Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta, while type B dissections do not.

As this man has a type B aortic dissection (involving the descending aorta only), the general principle of treatment is medical, rather than surgical, management. This is because the sparing of the ascending aorta means that risks of cardiac tamponade, aortic valve insufficiency and myocardial infarction do not occur.

Treatment with intravenous labetalol should be commenced to reduce the heart rate and maintain a systolic blood pressure target of 100-120 mmHg, which allows end-organ perfusion to be maintained while limiting further damage.

Intravenous sodium nitroprusside and sublingual nifedipine are not first-line antihypertensives used for the treatment of aortic dissection.

Observation and analgesia alone is also an inappropriate strategy as his blood pressure requires lowering.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the respiratory clinic with shortness of breath. She gives a history of breathing difficulties and fatigue which is preventing her from going to the gym. She is a non-smoker. After further investigations, she is diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension. Acute vasodilator testing shows a negative response.

What is the first-line treatment for this patient?
options_json: ["Beta-blockers", "Calcium channel blockers", "Diuretics", "Endothelin receptor agonists", "Endothelin receptor antagonists"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with negative response to vasodilator testing should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. Often combination therapy is required

Endothelin receptor antagonist

is the correct answer. Endothelin receptor antagonist, prostacyclin analogues, or phosphodiesterase inhibitors are the first-line treatment for patients with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH) who have a negative response to acute vasodilator testing. Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that is activated in IPAH. Hence, endothelin receptor antagonists are a mainstay of treatment in IPAH.

Calcium channel blockers

are the first-line treatment in IPAH with a positive response to acute vasodilator testing, this is not the case in the question.

Endothelin receptor agonist

is not the correct answer as endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that plays a major role in the pathogenesis of IPAH.

Beta-blockers

are not currently indicated in IPAH due to potential systemic hypotension. Unlike left ventricular failure where beta-blockers are a cornerstone of treatment, the use of beta-blockers for IPAH and subsequent right-sided heart failure is unclear.

Diuretics

are used as an adjunct in the treatment of IPAH to relieve fluid retention if needed, not as a first-line. Hence, not the correct option here.

question_text: A 63-year-old female on long-term warfarin for atrial fibrillation attends the anticoagulation clinic. Despite having a stable INR for the past 4 years on the same dose of warfarin her INR is measured at 5.4. Which one of the following is most likely to be responsible?

options_json: ["Blockage of sodium channels", "Opening of potassium channels", "Blockage of potassium channels", "Opening of calcium channels", "Opening of sodium channels"]
explanation_text:
Long QT syndrome - usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels

This patient is likely to have developed torsades de pointes secondary to a prolonged QT interval.

question_text: Which one of the following electrolyte disturbances is most associated with the development of a prolonged QT interval on ECG?
options_json: ["Hyponatraemia", "Hypocalcaemia", "Hyperkalaemia", "Hypercalcaemia", "Hypophosphataemia"]
explanation_text:
Hypocalcemia is associated with QT interval prolongation; Hypercalcemia is associated with QT interval shortening

The correct answer is

Hypocalcaemia

. Hypocalcaemia, or low serum calcium levels, can lead to a prolonged QT interval on an ECG. The QT interval represents the time from the start of the Q wave to the end of the T wave and corresponds to ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. Calcium plays a crucial role in cardiac muscle contraction and relaxation; therefore, lower levels can affect these processes, leading to prolonged repolarisation and hence a longer QT interval.

Hyponatraemia

, or low sodium levels, does not typically cause a prolonged QT interval. Sodium is primarily responsible for initiating action potentials in cardiac cells by allowing rapid influx of sodium ions during phase 0 of the action potential. However, hyponatraemia might cause bradycardia, hypotension or nonspecific ST-T changes but not prolongation of QT interval.

Similarly,

Hyperkalaemia

, or high potassium levels, does not usually result in a prolonged QT interval either. Potassium is vital for repolarising cardiac cells after an action potential. Hyperkalaemia may cause various ECG changes including peaked T waves, widened QRS complexes and eventually sine wave pattern or asystole if severe but it doesn't typically prolong the QT interval.

Hypercalcaemia

, or high calcium levels, shortens rather than lengthens the QT interval. This is because calcium contributes to phase 2 (plateau phase) and phase 3 (rapid repolarisation) of the cardiac action potential. Increased serum calcium leads to faster movement through these phases hence shortening of the QT duration.

Finally,

Hypophosphataemia

, or low phosphate levels do not directly impact on ECG findings including QT intervals as they are not directly involved in cellular depolarisation or repolarisation processes within myocardial cells.

In conclusion, while all these electrolytes play roles in cardiac function and their disturbances can lead to various cardiovascular manifestations including arrhythmias , it's only hypocalcaemia among them that specifically causes prolongation of QT intervals on ECG.

question_text:
A 55-year-old previously fit and well man presents with chest pain, this is heavy in nature and radiating to the left arm. Associated symptoms included nausea and vomiting as well as diaphoresis. There were no ST-segment changes on the ECG. His troponin level at six hours post-onset of pain is outlined below:


Troponin T	350 ng/L	(<14)

The patient was diagnosed with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction and you decide to prescribe aspirin 300mg.

What is the mechanism of action of the treatment that has been prescribed?
options_json: ["Decreases the formation of thromboxane A1 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation", "Decreases the formation of thromboxane A2", "Inhibits phospholipase A2 thereby reducing production of inflammatory mediators", "Selectively inhibits binding of ADP to the P2Y12 receptor thereby inhibiting platelet aggregation", "Undergoes isolated cyclooxygenase (COX) 2 inhibition"]
answer_text: Decreases the formation of thromboxane A2
explanation_text:
Aspirin decreases the formation of thromboxane A2 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation

The answer requires you to outline the mechanism of action of aspirin. Aspirin decreases the formation of thromboxane A2 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation. It can both inhibit cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1) and 2 and therefore inhibit thromboxane A2 formation and therefore results in decreased platelet aggregation.

Aspirin acts on thromboxane A2 and not thromboxane A1.

Steroids work upstream of arachidonic acid by inhibiting phospholipase A2, aspirin works downstream of this intermediate metabolite.

Clopidogrel is a selective inhibitor of ADP to the P2Y12 receptor, this is not the mechanism of action of aspirin.

NSAIDs such as celecoxib inhibit COX-2 in isolation whereas aspirin acts on both COX-1 and 2 and therefore this answer is incorrect.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man attends the clinic with hypertension. He was previously started on amlodipine which has been titrated to maximal dose. His blood pressure is currently 175/95 mmHg. You start the patient on indapamide.

He attends clinic 4-weeks later with the following blood tests:


Na+	134 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	2.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	28 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	6.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	84 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the mechanism of hypokalemia?
options_json: ["Increased ADH secretion", "Increased aldosterone secretion", "Increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule", "Increased delivery of sodium to the proximal part of the distal convoluted tubule", "Reduced aldosterone secretion"]
answer_text: Increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule
explanation_text:
Mechanism of hypokalaemia due to thiazides: increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule

Increased delivery of sodium to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule

is correct. Thiazide diuretics cause inhibition of sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule. This results in the delivery of a high sodium load to the distal part of the distal convoluted tubule with a resulting physiological secretion of potassium.

Increased ADH secretion

is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of hyponatraemia in causes such as the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, and liver disease.

Increased aldosterone secretion

is incorrect. Hyperaldosteronism is associated with hypernatraemia rather than hyponatraemia.

Increased delivery of sodium to the proximal part of the distal convoluted tubule

is incorrect. It is the distal part, rather than the proximal part, of the distal convoluted tubule which is implicated in thiazide-related hypokalemia.

Reduced aldosterone secretion

is incorrect. Although hypoaldosteronism is associated with hyponatraemia, the effects of aldosterone secretion by thiazide diuretics are minimal.

question_text:
A 28-year-old male presents with to the emergency department with his wife. She explains how her husband has become more confused. As well as this, he has been experiencing palpitations and has been going to the toilet more frequently during the day.

A blood test revealed the following:


Calcium	4.08 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	0.9 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.88 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)
Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)	5.2 mU/L	(0.5-5.5)
Free thyroxine (T4)	9.0 pmol/L	(9.0 - 18)

An ECG is performed.

Which of the following changes would you expect to see?
options_json: ["Delta waves", "ST depression", "Shortening of the QT interval", "Widening of the QT interval", "U waves in leads v4 to v6"]
explanation_text:
The main ECG abnormality seen with hypercalcaemia is shortening of the QT interval

Multiple ECG changes are associated with hypercalcaemia. The main finding being shortening of the QT interval. Other findings include prolonged PR, widened QRS and ST elevation.

Hypercalcaemia causes certain calcium ion channels to be opened for shorter amounts of time which in turn reduce phase 2 (the plateau phase) of the cardiomyocyte. This shortens the QT interval.

The characteristic U waves are associated with hypokalaemia due to the reduced efflux of potassium resulting in delayed ventricular repolarisation.

A widened QT interval is associated with low potassium, calcium and magnesium.

ST depression is commonly seen in ischaemia such as post-myocardial infarct. Other causes include hypokalaemia, ventricular hypertrophy and an adverse effect of digoxin.

Delta waves are slurred upstrokes (in the QRS) showing early ventricular activation present in Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man with chronic heart failure is reviewed in clinic. His symptoms are controlled with ramipril, bisoprolol, and furosemide but he experiences persistent hypokalaemia.

He cannot tolerate potassium supplements due to gastrointestinal side effects. Spironolactone was also trialled but discontinued due to gynaecomastia. To conserve potassium, he is started on amiloride.

Which option is the site of action of this drug?
options_json: ["Aquaporins in the collecting ducts", "Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule", "Na+-Cl- symporters in the distal convoluted tubule", "Na+-K+-Cl- cotransporters in the ascending limb", "Specific receptors in the cortical collecting ducts"]
answer_text: Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule
explanation_text:
Amiloride selectively blocks the epithelial sodium transport channels

Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule

is correct. This patient’s hypokalaemia is caused by furosemide, a loop diuretic that increases potassium excretion. Amiloride conserves potassium by blocking epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts, reducing sodium reabsorption and subsequent potassium secretion. However, discontinuing furosemide may risk worsening their heart failure, precipitating pulmonary congestion and peripheral oedema as less fluid is excreted. Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that can be used as an adjunct for potassium conservation in people taking diuretics for heart failure.

Aquaporins in the collecting ducts

is incorrect. No drugs directly block aquaporins, though tolvaptan indirectly affects them by inhibiting ADH. Blocking aquaporins would increase free water excretion, which could worsen hypovolaemia in a patient already on diuretics. Due to amiloride's relatively weak diuretic effect, it is more appropriate here as an adjunct. Tolvaptan is only licensed for use in polycystic kidney disease and syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion under specialist supervision.

Na+-Cl- symporters in the distal convoluted tubule

is incorrect as this describes the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics, like bendroflumethiazide. Thiazides would be harmful, as they increase potassium excretion similarly to furosemide.

Na+-K+-Cl- cotransporters in the ascending limb

is incorrect. This describes the mechanism of action of loop diuretics like furosemide, the cause of this patient’s hypokalaemia. Discontinuing this patient's furosemide may worsen their heart failure, as less water excretion causes pulmonary congestion, peripheral oedema, and increased dyspnoea.

Specific receptors in the cortical collecting ducts

is incorrect. This describes the target of aldosterone antagonists, such as spironolactone. While they are potassium-sparing, the patient discontinued spironolactone due to gynaecomastia. While eplerenone is less commonly linked with this, this patient is being started on amiloride. If amiloride is ineffective or not tolerated, then this could be considered.

question_text:
A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department following a collapse. He states that he became lightheaded whilst on a jog. This has happened on two occasions previously. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal supplements).

Blood results are as follows:


Na+	136 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Calcium	2.4 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	0.9 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.75 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)

An ECG is performed in the department:


ECG	Sinus rhythm with a rate of 74 beats per minute; markedly prolonged QTc 540ms

What is the most likely abnormality?
options_json: ["Gain-of-function of K+ channels", "Gain-of-function of Na+ channels", "Loss-of-function of Ca2+ channels", "Loss-of-function of K+ channels", "Loss-of-function of Na+ channels"]
explanation_text:
Long QT syndrome - usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels

Syncope on exercise is a red flag for a serious cardiac disorder necessitating the need for further investigations and management.

The severely prolonged QTc (> 500ms) with the absence of any obvious cause (e.g. drugs and electrolyte derangement) favours a diagnosis of a hereditary long QT syndrome (LQTS).

It is important to recognise this condition as it may lead to ventricular tachycardia/torsade de pointes and can therefore cause collapse/sudden death.

The most common variants of LQTS (LQT1 & LQT2) are caused by defects in the alpha subunit of the slow delayed rectifier K+ channel resulting in

loss-of-function of K+ channels

.

question_text: A 54-year-old man is admitted with suspected pulmonary embolism. He has no past medical history of note. Blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg with a pulse of 90/min. The 2003 British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines, however, recommended that CTPA is now used as the initial lung imaging modality of choice. question_text:
A 78-year-old man presents with several weeks of palpitations and light-headedness. He has a past medical history of hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and congestive cardiac failure. On examination, his pulse feels irregular. This is confirmed on ECG, which shows atrial fibrillation. He is commenced on digoxin by the cardiology team - initially, a loading dose, followed by a maintenance dose.

What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options_json: ["If channel inhibitor", "Non-selective beta blocker", "Sodium-potassium ATPase pump inhibitor", "Voltage-gated potassium channel blocker", "Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker"]
explanation_text:
Digoxin - inhibits the Na

Digoxin is sometimes used to manage atrial fibrillation in the context of heart failure. It is positively inotropic and so can improve symptoms of heart failure in these patients - although it does not improve mortality. It

inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase pump

. In doing so, it increases the force of cardiac muscle contraction.

The most common example of an

If channel inhibitor

is the drug ivabradine. This is an anti-anginal drug, not an anti-arrhythmic drug.

Non-selective beta blockers

are also used in the management of arrhythmias. The most common example in this context is sotalol. Digoxin, however, is a sodium-potassium ATPase pump inhibitor.

Voltage-gated potassium channel blockers

include drugs such as amiodarone (although this is a fairly non-specific drug with several targets) and ibutilide. Digoxin does not fall into this category.

Voltage-gated sodium channel blockers

include flecainide and quinidine. Digoxin does not primarily act through this mechanism.

Despite 4000ml of IV 0.9% saline in the emergency department she remained hypotensive and was commenced on noradrenaline and a fixed dose vasopressin infusion. Unfortunately, despite escalating doses of noradrenaline, her mean arterial pressure (MAP) remains 50mmHg (target >=65 mmHg). She has a rising serum lactate and she has produced only 25ml urine since admission 2h ago. question_text:
An 87-year-old man with mild dementia presents to your GP practice.

He has a documented drug allergy to calcium channel blockers and has hypertension confirmed on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. He has developed an intolerable cough whilst trialling ramipril.

He is otherwise fit and well and takes only donepezil. He is interested in taking anti-hypertensives and you have a discussion with him regarding the anti-hypertensive most commonly used in this scenario.

What is the mechanism of action of the next-line antihypertensive for this patient?
options_json: ["It prevents angiotensinogen being converted to angiotensin 1", "It acts on the adrenal cortex to reduce the amount of aldosterone released", "It is a diuretic that acts on the loop of Henle to increase the amount of sodium excreted in the urine", "It prevents angiotensin 1 being converted to angiotensin 2", "It prevents angiotensin 2 acting on AT1 receptors"]
answer_text: It prevents angiotensin 2 acting on AT1 receptors
explanation_text:
Angiotensin II receptor blockers block the effects of angiotensin 2 at the AT1 receptor

As this patient is allergic to calcium channel blockers and has not tolerated an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor due to cough, an angiotensin 2 receptor blocker such as candesartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker would be the next most appropriate therapy; these block the effects of angiotensin 2 at the AT1 receptor.

ACE inhibitors prevent angiotensin 1 being converted to angiotensin 2.

AT2 receptors full role is still under investigation but it is thought to relate to apoptosis and cellular growth.

question_text:
A neonate female born at 37 weeks gestation develops severe cyanosis 1 hour after birth. She develops worsening respiratory distress and becomes highly tachypnoeic with difficulty feeding. She is soon transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit for supportive treatment. Her mother did not seek any antenatal care and the baby was born via an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery.

On physical examination, the neonate is cyanosed and lethargic. Her vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate 62/min, oxygen saturation 84% (on 60% oxygen), heart rate 160/min, blood pressure 96/66 mmHg. Cardiac auscultation reveals a loud S2 heart sound.

Chest x-ray shows the cardiac silhouette with an 'eggs on a string' appearance. Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows a right ventricular dominance. Further diagnostic workup with echocardiography confirms a congenital heart defect.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying embryological pathology in this neonate's congenital heart defect?
options_json: ["Absent tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle", "Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum", "Defect in interatrial septum", "Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral", "Aortic narrowing near insertion of ductus arteriosus"]
answer_text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
explanation_text:
Transposition of great vessels is due to the failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral

The clinical stem here is significant for a cyanotic heart disease. The clinical findings as well as the classic X-ray description point towards a diagnosis of transposition of great vessels which is caused by the failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral during early life.

Absent tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle are seen in tricuspid atresia (cyanotic heart defect).

Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum is seen in Tetralogy of Fallot (cyanotic heart defect). The x-ray in this condition would show a 'boot-shaped' heart.

A defect in the interatrial septum is present in the atrial septal defect (non-cyanotic).

Aortic narrowing near the insertion of ductus arteriosus occurs in aortic coarctation.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man with a history of chronic heart failure secondary to ischaemic cardiomyopathy is reviewed. He was discharged two weeks ago from hospital following a myocardial infarction. An echocardiogram done during his admission showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% but did not demonstrate any valvular problems.

Despite his current treatment with furosemide, ramipril, carvedilol, aspirin and simvastatin he remains short of breath on minimal exertion such as walking 30 metres. On examination his chest is clear and there is minimal peripheral oedema. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Stop aspirin", "Refer for cardiac resynchronisation therapy", "Switch carvedilol to bisoprolol", "Add angiotensin-2 receptor blocker", "Add an aldosterone antagonist"]

question_text:
A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute swelling of his face, lips, and tongue. He has no pruritus or rash. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and he has no known allergies.

His pulse is 70 bpm, blood pressure is 135/95 mmHg, oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air, and respiratory rate is 14 /min. Auscultation of the chest reveals equal air entry bilaterally, with no added sounds and no observable rash.

Which option is the most likely underlying cause?
options_json: ["Amlodipine", "Atorvastatin", "Bendroflumethiazide", "Candesartan", "Lisinopril"]
explanation_text:
Drug-induced angioedema without urticaria is most frequently associated with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or, less frequently, angiotensin II receptor blockers

Lisinopril

is correct. This patient’s acute facial, lip, and tongue swelling without pruritus or rash is characteristic of angioedema without urticaria, most commonly caused by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors like lisinopril. ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin levels by preventing its breakdown, leading to increased vascular permeability and tissue swelling, particularly in the face, lips, and tongue. The absence of wheezing, hypotension, or skin rash makes an allergic reaction less likely. ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema can occur at any time, even after years of use, requiring immediate discontinuation of the drug to prevent recurrence.

Amlodipine

is incorrect as calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are not known to cause angioedema affecting the face and airways. Amlodipine instead works by inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, leading to vasodilation. This can cause peripheral oedema which is thought to be due to arteriolar dilation, increasing capillary pressure, leading to fluid extravasation. However, this tends to affect the feet and legs rather than the face.

Atorvastatin

is incorrect. Angioedema is not commonly associated with atorvastatin, and its incidence is significantly low compared to ACE inhibitors, as it does not share the same mechanisms leading to bradykinin accumulation. Instead, it can cause myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, presenting with muscle pain, weakness, and elevated creatine kinase rather than the angioedema seen in this patient.

Bendroflumethiazide

is incorrect as thiazide diuretics like bendroflumethiazide are not known to cause angioedema affecting the face. Bendroflumethiazide works by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, leading to increased urine output and decreased blood volume. This would be more likely to cause dehydration rather than the accumulation of fluid. It is also more likely to cause electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalaemia, which can lead to muscle weakness, palpitations, or arrhythmias, which are not seen here.

Candesartan

is incorrect. Candesartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), can rarely cause angioedema, but this is much less common than with ACE inhibitors. ARBs minimally affect bradykinin compared to ACE inhibitors, but rare angioedema can still occur via alternative pathways. Since patients who develop ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema may still be at risk with ARBs, caution is required when switching medications.

question_text:
A 53-year-old woman presents for review.

Her blood pressure is poorly controlled at 152/92 mmHg despite treatment with ramipril 10mg OD. She also takes lansoprazole 30mg OD. She has no known drug allergies.

Her blood tests from 3 weeks ago reveal:


Na+	141 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.7 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	115 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the best next step in management?
options_json: ["Add atenolol", "Add indapamide", "Add spironolactone", "Increase dose of ramipril", "Lifestyle advice"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor - add a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

Given her blood pressure is poorly controlled with an ACE inhibitor, adding a thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) or alternatively a calcium channel blocker would be the most appropriate option.

She is already taking the maximum dose of ramipril so it would not be safe to increase the dose of the ACE inhibitor further.

Lifestyle advice would not be appropriate as her blood pressure remains poorly controlled despite a high dose of one antihypertensive.

Low-dose spironolactone is likely to cause hyperkalaemia, given her current potassium level, and it is not indicated at this stage.

Beta blockers are no longer used in the early steps of treating hypertension. For resistant hypertension with K

+

>4.5, atenolol could be considered.

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with increasing shortness-of-breath on exertion. During the examination a third heart sound is heard. Examination of the respiratory system is unremarkable. Which one of the following is most consistent with this finding?

question_text: What is the usual target INR for a patient with a mechanical mitral valve?
explanation_text:
Mechanical valves - target INR:

For a patient with a mechanical mitral valve, the correct target INR is

3.5

. This higher target INR is necessary because mechanical mitral valves carry a greater risk of thromboembolism compared to mechanical aortic valves. The mitral position experiences lower pressure and flow conditions which increases the risk of thrombus formation. Current guidelines recommend maintaining an INR between 3.0-4.0 for mechanical mitral valves, with a target of 3.5.

2.0

is too low for any mechanical valve and would place the patient at significant risk of valve thrombosis and systemic embolism. This target would be more appropriate for conditions like atrial fibrillation.

2.5

is also insufficient for a mechanical mitral valve. While this might be an appropriate target for a mechanical aortic valve (target range 2.0-3.0), it provides inadequate anticoagulation for the mitral position.

3.0

represents the lower end of the acceptable range for a mechanical mitral valve but would not be the optimal target. Aiming for this level could result in periods of inadequate anticoagulation.

4.0

represents the upper end of the therapeutic range. While this level of anticoagulation would protect against thrombosis, maintaining an INR this high increases the risk of bleeding complications unnecessarily. The optimal balance between preventing thrombosis and avoiding bleeding is achieved with a target of 3.5.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fall after tripping over a step outside his house. There were no preceding presyncopal symptoms. He sustained a head injury but did not lose consciousness. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He takes dabigatran, amlodipine and metformin.

His observations on arrival were heart rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/77 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/minute, oxygen saturations 96% on air and temperature 36.4ºC. He was alert with a Glasgow coma scale of 15/15. A neurological examination was normal. There was evidence of an external head injury with some bruising.

A CT head demonstrates a small subdural haematoma. There is no midline shift or mass effect.

What is the most appropriate medication to administer at this point?
options_json: ["Tranexamic acid", "Idarucizumab", "Protamine sulphate", "Prothrombin complex", "Phytomenadione"]
explanation_text:
Bleeding on dabigatran? Can use idarucizumab to reverse

Tranexamic acid is incorrect. Given that the patient has sustained a subdural haematoma as a consequence of trauma and anticoagulant treatment with dabigatran, we need to reverse the effect of dabigatran. While tranexamic acid is an anti-fibrinolytic medication that reduces bleeding in a variety of situations, it is not the specific reversal agent in this circumstance.

Idarucizumab is the correct answer. This is a monoclonal antibody used as a reversal agent for dabigatran. As this patient has suffered a potentially life-threatening complication of anticoagulant treatment, the anticoagulant effect of the medication should be reversed.

Protamine sulphate is incorrect. This medication is used to reverse the effects of heparin.

Prothrombin complex is incorrect. This is used to treat major bleeding on warfarin despite treatment with phytomenadione.

Phytomenadione (vitamin K) is incorrect. This is used to reverse the effects of warfarin.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset, severe chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic and hypertensive with a blood pressure of 210/120 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray reveals a widened mediastinum. CT angiography confirms a Stanford type A aortic dissection.

What is the most appropriate initial management?
options_json: ["Immediate surgical repair", "Intravenous labetalol followed by surgical repair", "Intravenous labetalol and conservative management", "Intravenous thrombolysis", "Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion"]
answer_text: Intravenous labetalol followed by surgical repair
explanation_text:
Aortic dissection

Intravenous labetalol followed by surgical repair

is the correct management for this patient with a Stanford type A aortic dissection. Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and are surgical emergencies with high mortality rates if left untreated. However, before proceeding to surgery, it is essential to control the patient's severely elevated blood pressure (210/120 mmHg) to reduce shear forces on the aortic wall and prevent extension of the dissection. Intravenous labetalol is particularly useful in this scenario as it provides both alpha and beta blockade, effectively reducing blood pressure and heart rate, which decreases the force of cardiac contraction (dP/dt). The target systolic blood pressure should be 100-120 mmHg. Once the blood pressure is controlled, the patient should proceed to emergency surgical repair, which is the definitive management for type A dissections.

Immediate surgical repair

without prior blood pressure control would be dangerous in this hypertensive patient. Taking a patient with uncontrolled severe hypertension directly to surgery could lead to extension of the dissection, rupture, or other catastrophic complications during induction of anaesthesia or the procedure itself. Blood pressure control is a critical first step before surgical intervention.

Intravenous labetalol and conservative management

would be appropriate for a Stanford type B dissection (involving only the descending aorta), but not for a type A dissection. Type A dissections have a high mortality rate without surgical intervention and require definitive repair after initial medical stabilisation.

Intravenous thrombolysis

is absolutely contraindicated in aortic dissection. Thrombolytic therapy would worsen the dissection by dissolving any protective clots that may have formed and could lead to catastrophic bleeding or rupture. This highlights the importance of ruling out aortic dissection before administering thrombolytics for suspected myocardial infarction.

Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion

alone would be inadequate for managing this patient. While nitrates can reduce blood pressure, they primarily cause venodilation rather than the arterial dilation needed to reduce shear forces on the aortic wall. Additionally, reflex tachycardia from nitrates could worsen the dissection. Beta-blockers like labetalol are preferred as they reduce both blood pressure and heart rate.
