question_text:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of tertiary syphilis and severe rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppressants was referred to the respiratory clinic following her complaint of dyspnoea. On physical examination, a new soft high-pitched diastolic murmur was auscultated. She was discussed with cardiology who advised the team to perform a routine echocardiogram.

What condition is the echocardiogram most likely to show?
options_json: ["Aortic regurgitation", "Aortic stenosis", "Mitral prolapse", "Mitral regurgitation", "Mitral stenosis"]
explanation_text:
Aortic regurgitation typically causes an early diastolic murmur

Aortic regurgitation

typically causes an early diastolic murmur and is seen in tertiary cardiovascular syphilis and rheumatoid arthritis. Aortic regurgitation is the most frequent complication of syphilitic aortitis, occurring in 60% of those with cardiovascular syphilis. Aortic incompetence secondary to connective tissue diseases including rheumatoid arthritis has a relatively accelerated course rapidly leading to severe left ventricular failure.

Aortic stenosis

produces a loud systolic ejection murmur which is commonly due to old-age-related valvular degeneration and calcification. This is therefore unlikely the case here.

Mitral valve prolapse

is caused by valve tissue weakness. This condition is known as myxomatous degeneration. It is described as a mid-systolic click usually accompanied by a late systolic murmur. It is more common in people with connective tissue disorders, such as Marfan syndrome.

Mitral regurgitation

is a high-pitched pan-systolic murmur that is heard best at the apex of the diaphragm. It can be caused due to left-ventricular dilatation from cardiomyopathy, ischaemic heart disease or dysfunction of the mitral valve apparatus.

Mitral stenosis

is associated with a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur heard loudest over the apex. The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic fever which is a complication of strep throat, making the answer incorrect here.

question_text:
A 45-year-old is reviewed in the respiratory clinic after presenting with progressive shortness of breath on exertion and evidence of right-sided heart failure. She was previously well with no comorbidities and no smoking or drug use history and therefore a diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension was considered.

Further investigation in the form of imaging and pulmonary artery pressure testing confirms the diagnosis. An acute vasodilator test is carried out and demonstrates a significant fall in pulmonary arterial pressure.

What medication should this patient be commenced on?
options_json: ["Antifibrotic", "Calcium channel blockers", "Endothelin receptor antagonists", "Phosphodiesterase inhibitors", "Prostacyclin analogue"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with positive response to vasodilator testing should be treated with calcium channel blockers

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is due to narrowing and thickening of the pulmonary vascular resulting in increased pressure within the vessels and right heart strain. The cause is normally unknown although several risk factors have been identified including family history, pulmonary emboli, cocaine use, COPD and sleep apnoea. Management of PAH, once secondary underlying conditions have been optimised, is based on acute vasodilator testing. This testing demonstrates if a patient shows a significant fall in pulmonary arterial pressure following the administration of a vasodilator (e.g. IV epoprostenol). Only a small percentage of patients have a positive response however if a patient does they can be considered 'vasoreactive' and may benefit/respond to

calcium channel blockers

. A calcium channel blocker should be initiated, and the patient's condition monitored. Unfortunately, only approximately half of vasoreactive patients improve with calcium channel blockers.

Although vessel fibrosis does eventually occur in PAH this is a result of long-standing increased pressure within the vascular and not the driving mechanism of the condition. As such

antifibrotics

are not effective in PAH and these agents are mainly used in the condition of pulmonary fibrosis instead.

If patients with PAH have a negative acute vasodilator test, then several different agents can be trialled. Endothelin is thought to play a major role in the pathogenesis of PAH and so

endothelin receptor antagonists

have been studied and have moderate evidence of improving exercise capacity and decreasing symptom severity. Examples of endothelin receptor antagonists approved for use in certain countries include bosentan and ambrisentan.

Phosphodiesterase inhibitors

, such as sildenafil, are another group of agents used in patients who do not respond to acute vasodilator testing. These agents are thought to increase vasodilation within the pulmonary arteries and inhibit vascular remodelling, therefore, reducing pressure and vascular resistance.

Prostacyclin analogues

are commonly considered the most effective form of treatment in patients with negative acute vasodilator testing. Prostacyclin results in pulmonary artery vasodilation as well as having anti-thrombotic, anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory effects. Until recently these agents could only be given via IV. Newer inhaled forms including treprostinil and iloprost are now available but research is still required to establish their effectiveness. As such they are currently used as an adjunct to calcium channel blockers which remain the first-line treatment .

question_text:
A 28-year-old female who is known to be 16 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of leg pain. She reports a progressive aching and swelling of her right calf. The patient is otherwise well and denies any other symptoms

General examination is normal, and observations are all within normal range. On examination of the affected leg the right calf is swollen >3cm compared to the left which localised tenderness along on deep palpation of the calf. There are collateral superficial veins as well as pitting oedema also noted on the affected leg.

What is the mechanism of action of the treatment most appropriate to commence in this patient?
options_json: ["Activated antithrombin I which inhibits of factor Xa, IXa, Xia and XIIa", "Activated antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa", "Directly inhibits factor Xa", "Inhibits cyclooxygenases (COX) reducing platelets aggregation", "Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase which inhibits vitamin K1"]
answer_text: Activated antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa
explanation_text:
Low-molecular weight heparin activates antithrombin III. Forms a complex that inhibits factor Xa

This patient has presented with typical signs and symptoms in keeping with a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Pregnancy can result in an increased hypercoagulable state and therefore patients are more at risk of forming these DVTs. In standard cases, there are a variety of treatment options available to manage DVTs long term including warfarin, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin. Only low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) has been recommended for use in pregnancy due to the potential or confirmed teratogenic properties of the other treatment options. LMWH actives antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa only, bringing about a breakdown in clot formation.

Standard heparin is useful for thrombosis management in situations where there is a high risk of bleeding or in renal impairment due to its short half-life. It works by activating antithrombin III (not antithrombin I) which inhibits a number of factors including Xa, IXa, Xia and XIIa. Heparin must be given intravenously and therefore is less appropriate than LMWH, which can be given subcutaneously.

DOACs which can be used in DVT management directly inhibit factor Xa, breaking down clot formation. The teratogenic profile of DOACs are unknown and therefore, to date are not advised in pregnancy, with LMWH being the preferred option.

One of aspirin's main mechanisms of action is the inhibition of COX 1 and 2 which inhibits platelet aggregation. Although used to reduce the risk of some thrombosis conditions including acute coronary syndrome and stroke aspirin has no role in the management of DVTs.

Warfarin causes the breakdown of clot formation by blocking vitamin K epoxide reductase which is required to reactivate vitamin K1. Without active vitamin K1 several clotting factors including II, VII, IX and X have reduced function. Warfarin can be used in the management of a DVT however it is teratogenic causing foetal warfarin syndrome with characteristic abnormalities including, birth weight issues, central nervous system issues and malformation of bones, cartilage and joints.

A 24-year-old man presents with recurrent palpitations and presyncope. Following an echocardiogram and ECG he is diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

You start the patient on flecainide.

How does this agent reduce the occurrence of tachyarrhythmia?
options_json: ["Acts indirectly via increased vagal influences and decreased sympathetic influences due to blockade of Na/K-ATPase", "Binds to the alpha-1 subunit, Cav1.2, which is highly expressed on L-type calcium channels", "Increases the duration of the cardiac action potential by delaying repolarisation", "Increasing action potential duration and the effective refractory period by antagonism of the beta 1 receptors", "Slows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential by blocking Nav1.5 sodium channels"]
answer_text: Slows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential by blocking Nav1.5 sodium channels
explanation_text:
Flecainide blocks the Nav1.5 sodium channels in the heart

Slows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential by blocking Nav1.5 sodium channels

is correct. Flecainide is a Class I antiarrhythmic drug and a potent inhibitor of the cardiac (Nav1.5) sodium channel. This results in slowing of the upstroke of the cardiac action potential thereby 'reducing excitability'.

Acts indirectly via increased vagal influences and decreased sympathetic influences due to blockade of Na/K-ATPase

is incorrect. Digoxin is a selective inhibitor of the plasma membrane Na/K-ATPase. It results in a positive inotropic and a negative chronotropic effect.

Binds to the alpha-1 subunit, Cav1.2, which is highly expressed on L-type calcium channels

is incorrect. Calcium channel blockers include verapamil, amlodipine and nifedipine.

Increases the duration of the cardiac action potential by delaying repolarisation

is incorrect. Potassium channel blockers block potassium currents that cause repolarization during the third phase of the cardiac action potential. Drugs in this class include sotalol and amiodarone.

Increasing action potential duration and the effective refractory period by antagonism of the beta 1 receptors

is incorrect. Drugs in this class include metoprolol and bisoprolol.

question_text:
A 69-year-old man is reviewed on the Coronary Care Unit. He experienced an inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) two days previously, for which he underwent successful percutaneous coronary intervention. A post-procedure echocardiogram showed normal valvular function, with no obvious septal defects and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%.

His ECG report is as follows:


ECG	1mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Heart rate 48 beats per minute. Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes

Given these findings, which of the following is most likely to be heard on auscultation?
options_json: ["Ejection systolic murmur", "Pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur", "Variable intensity S1", "Variable intensity S2", "Fixed split S2"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block causes a variable intensity of S1

This patient has developed complete heart block (CHB) after an inferior myocardial infarction (MI). In the majority of patients, the atrioventricular node receives its blood supply from a branch of the right coronary artery, which also supplies the posterior and inferior walls of the left ventricle (LV). As such, an occlusion of the right coronary artery in this patient has caused ischaemic damage to the atrioventricular node (resulting in impaired conduction between the atria and ventricles, and hence, atrioventricular dissociation), as well as the mild impairment in LV ejection fraction. As we are told that no valvular or septal defects have arisen as a result of the MI, the only plausible causes for an abnormal auscultation finding are the CHB or left ventricular failure. None of the options listed are seen in the context of left ventricular failure, leaving a variable intensity S1 due to CHB as the best answer. The mechanism for this is that S1 intensity decreases with PR interval prolongation, as diastolic filling pressures in the left ventricle increase and cause the mitral valve leaflets to drift together. Hence, the variation in PR interval seen in CHB causes variation in S1 intensity.

An ejection systolic murmur may be heard in aortic or pulmonary stenosis, for which there was no evidence on this patient's post-PCI echocardiogram.

A pansystolic murmur may be heard in the setting of a ventricular septal defect or tricuspid or mitral regurgitation, all of which were excluded on echocardiogram.

The intensity of the second heart sound is determined primarily by the pressure gradient across the aortic valve as it closes. The intensity of the second heart sound can be altered in aortic valvular pathology such as aortic stenosis, but does not tend to fluctuate in complete heart block.

A fixed split second heart sound is heard in the context of atrial septal defects.

question_text: A 53-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic with a history of chest pain and syncope. On examination he has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid area. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options_json: ["Bicuspid aortic valve", "Aortic root abscess", "Post rheumatic fever", "Posterior myocardial infarction", "Calcification of the aortic valve"]
explanation_text:
Aortic stenosis - most common cause:

The correct answer is

Bicuspid aortic valve

. This is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms based on the clinical presentation. The patient presents with chest pain and syncope, which are classic symptoms of aortic stenosis. The ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid area is characteristic of aortic stenosis. Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly, affecting 1-2% of the population, and is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients under 65 years of age. A bicuspid aortic valve has two leaflets instead of the normal three, which predisposes to early calcification and stenosis. Patients with bicuspid aortic valves typically develop symptoms in their 50s or 60s, which aligns with this 53-year-old patient's presentation. The classic triad of symptoms in aortic stenosis includes angina (chest pain), syncope, and heart failure, though not all patients will exhibit all three symptoms.

Aortic root abscess

is incorrect. An aortic root abscess is a serious complication of infective endocarditis, particularly involving the aortic valve. Patients typically present with fever, new or changing heart murmurs, and signs of systemic infection. The absence of fever or other signs of infection in this case makes an aortic root abscess unlikely. Additionally, aortic root abscesses often cause conduction abnormalities due to their proximity to the conduction system, which was not mentioned in this case.

Post rheumatic fever

is incorrect. While rheumatic fever can lead to valvular heart disease, including aortic stenosis, it typically affects the mitral valve more commonly than the aortic valve. Rheumatic aortic stenosis usually presents later in life than bicuspid aortic valve disease and is becoming increasingly rare in developed countries due to the effective treatment of streptococcal infections. Additionally, patients with rheumatic heart disease often have a history of rheumatic fever in childhood, which was not mentioned in this case.

Posterior myocardial infarction

is incorrect. While a posterior myocardial infarction can cause chest pain, it would not typically cause a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Posterior myocardial infarctions may be associated with mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle dysfunction, which would produce a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Additionally, syncope is not a typical presenting symptom of myocardial infarction unless there are significant conduction abnormalities or cardiogenic shock.

Calcification of the aortic valve

is incorrect as a standalone diagnosis, although it is part of the pathophysiology. Calcific aortic stenosis is indeed a common cause of aortic stenosis in older patients (typically over 65 years), but it is usually degenerative in nature and affects a previously normal trileaflet valve. In younger patients like this 53-year-old man, aortic stenosis is more commonly due to a congenital bicuspid aortic valve that has undergone accelerated calcification. While calcification is the process that leads to stenosis, the underlying anatomical abnormality (bicuspid valve) is the primary cause in this age group.

His blood tests from 2 weeks ago show:

K+	3.9 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	4.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	109 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the best next step in management?
options_json: ["Add atenolol", "Add furosemide", "Add ramipril", "Add spironolactone", "Increase dose of amlodipine"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking a calcium channel blocker - add an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

Adding ACE inhibitor (ramipril) or angiotensin receptor blocker would be the most appropriate step given his blood pressure is still poorly controlled despite treatment with amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker.

Increasing the dose of the calcium channel blocker would not be appropriate as he is already taking the maximum dose of amlodipine.

Adding low-dose spironolactone is not indicated, although it could be considered at a later stage if his potassium remains below 4.5 mmol/L.

Adding a beta blocker, such as atenolol, could be considered later for resistant hypertension if his blood pressure remains poorly controlled.

question_text: Where is the site of action of bendroflumethiazide?
options_json: ["Proximal convoluted tubules", "Ascending loop of Henle", "Descending loop of Henle", "Proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules", "Distal part of the distal convoluted tubules"]
answer_text: Proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules
explanation_text:
Thiazides/thiazide-like drugs (e.g. indapamide) - inhibits sodium reabsorption by blocking the  Na

The correct answer is that bendroflumethiazide acts at the

proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules

. Thiazide diuretics, including bendroflumethiazide, work by inhibiting the sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the early portion of the distal convoluted tubule. This results in decreased sodium and chloride reabsorption, leading to increased sodium and water excretion. Additionally, thiazides increase calcium reabsorption, making them useful in treating conditions like hypercalciuria and osteoporosis.

Proximal convoluted tubules

is incorrect. While this segment is responsible for reabsorbing approximately 65% of filtered sodium, it is not the site of action for thiazide diuretics. Loop diuretics and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (like acetazolamide) act here, but not thiazides.

Ascending loop of Henle

is incorrect. This is the site of action for loop diuretics such as furosemide, which inhibit the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter (NKCC2). Loop diuretics are more potent than thiazides because of their location and mechanism of action.

Descending loop of Henle

is incorrect. This segment is primarily involved in water reabsorption through aquaporin channels and is not a target for any major diuretic medications.

Distal part of the distal convoluted tubules

is incorrect. While this segment is involved in sodium reabsorption through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), it is the target for potassium-sparing diuretics like amiloride and triamterene, not thiazides.

Bisoprolol is the correct answer given that this patient is already taking an ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blockers and thiazide-like diuretic, and has a potassium >4.5 mmol/L.

Furosemide is not used for the management of hypertension alone and therefore is an incorrect answer.

question_text:
A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (PE) following a total knee replacement 2 weeks ago. She is haemodynamically stable with no significant comorbidities. She is started on rivaroxaban. She asks how long she will need to continue anticoagulation.

What is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
options_json: ["1 month", "3 months", "6 months", "12 months", "Lifelong"]
explanation_text:
'Provoked' pulmonary embolisms are typically treated for 3 months

3 months

is the correct answer. This patient has a provoked pulmonary embolism following recent knee surgery, which is a clear precipitating factor. According to NICE guidelines, provoked VTEs (venous thromboembolisms) should be treated with anticoagulation for at least 3 months. Since the precipitating factor (surgery) is transient and no longer present, the risk of recurrence after 3 months of adequate anticoagulation is relatively low. The use of rivaroxaban, a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC), is appropriate first-line treatment as per current UK guidelines.

1 month

is incorrect. This duration is insufficient for treating any pulmonary embolism, regardless of whether it is provoked or unprovoked. NICE guidelines recommend a minimum of 3 months of anticoagulation for all patients with VTE to ensure adequate treatment and reduce the risk of recurrence. One month of treatment would leave the patient at significant risk of recurrent VTE.

6 months

is incorrect for this specific case. While 6 months of anticoagulation is often recommended for unprovoked VTEs, this patient has a clearly provoked PE following knee surgery. For provoked VTEs where the risk factor is transient and no longer present (as in this case), 3 months of anticoagulation is generally sufficient. Extending treatment to 6 months would unnecessarily increase the bleeding risk without providing significant additional benefit.

12 months

is incorrect. This duration would be excessive for a provoked PE with a clear transient risk factor. Prolonged anticoagulation beyond the recommended 3 months would expose the patient to unnecessary bleeding risks without providing proportional benefits in terms of preventing recurrence. This duration might be considered in specific cases with ongoing risk factors or recurrent VTEs, which is not the case here.

Lifelong

anticoagulation is incorrect and would be inappropriate for this patient. Lifelong anticoagulation is typically reserved for patients with recurrent unprovoked VTEs, certain thrombophilias, or ongoing significant risk factors. This patient has a single provoked PE with a clear transient risk factor (recent surgery) that is no longer present. The bleeding risks associated with lifelong anticoagulation would far outweigh any potential benefits in preventing recurrence in this scenario.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the hypertension clinic. He has been taking ramipril 10 mg once daily for 6 months. His blood pressure today is 158/96 mmHg. He has no other medical conditions. His blood tests are normal. He has been advised about lifestyle modifications including salt reduction and regular exercise.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Add amlodipine", "Add bendroflumethiazide", "Add indapamide", "Change ramipril to losartan", "Increase ramipril dose"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor - add a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

This patient has poorly controlled hypertension despite being on maximum dose ramipril (an ACE inhibitor). According to NICE guidelines for hypertension management, the next step would be to add a second antihypertensive agent.

Add amlodipine

is the correct answer. For step 2 treatment in hypertension, NICE guidelines recommend that if a patient is already taking an ACE inhibitor (like ramipril) or an ARB, the next step is to add either a calcium channel blocker (like amlodipine) or a thiazide-like diuretic. Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that works by relaxing blood vessels, making it easier for the heart to pump blood. It has good evidence for efficacy and is generally well-tolerated. The combination of an ACE inhibitor and a calcium channel blocker provides complementary mechanisms of action for blood pressure control.

Add bendroflumethiazide

is not the most appropriate choice. While adding a diuretic is a reasonable step, bendroflumethiazide is a thiazide diuretic rather than a thiazide-like diuretic. NICE guidelines specifically recommend thiazide-like diuretics (such as indapamide or chlortalidone) rather than conventional thiazide diuretics like bendroflumethiazide, as they have better evidence for cardiovascular outcomes.

Add indapamide

would be a reasonable alternative to amlodipine. Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic that is recommended by NICE as a step 2 agent when a patient is already on an ACE inhibitor. However, calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are typically preferred as the first choice for step 2 treatment unless there are specific indications for a diuretic.

Change ramipril to losartan

is not appropriate. Switching from one ACE inhibitor to an ARB is generally only recommended if the patient is experiencing side effects from the ACE inhibitor (such as cough). There's no indication in this scenario that the patient is experiencing side effects, and this switch would not be expected to significantly improve blood pressure control.

Increase ramipril dose

is not appropriate as the patient is already on the maximum recommended dose of ramipril (10 mg). Increasing beyond this would not provide additional benefit but would increase the risk of side effects.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man is under regular review in the respiratory clinic after a recent diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension.

A summary of investigations is below:


CT thorax	No evidence of acute or chronic lung disease


Acute vasodilator testing	Negative response

He was initially prescribed iloprost but has only seen a small improvement in his symptoms.

What medication could be used in addition to iloprost?
options_json: ["Bosentan", "Diltiazem", "Epoprostenol", "Nifedipine", "Treprostinil"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with negative response to vasodilator testing should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. Often combination therapy is required

Once pulmonary hypertension is diagnosed, vasodilator testing is now the initial investigation to initiate appropriate treatment. Vasodilator testing involves the administration of either intravenous epoprostenol or inhaled nitric oxide.

A negative response to vasodilator testing, much more common than a positive response, can be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. Patients often require combination therapy.

Bosentan

is the correct answer and is an endothelin receptor antagonist. It is an option for pulmonary hypertension management if there is a negative response to vasodilator testing and is commonly used alongside prostacyclin analogues.

Diltiazem

is a calcium channel blocker that can be used if there is a positive response to acute vasodilator testing.

Epoprostenol

, as with iloprost, is a prostacyclin analogue and so shouldn't be used in combination with other prostacyclin analogues.

Nifedipine

is a long-acting calcium channel blocker that, as with diltiazem, can be used if there is a positive response to acute vasodilator testing.

Treprostinil

is also a prostacyclin analogue and therefore could be used instead of iloprost but not in combination.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. He has a history of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. He is on furosemide, bisoprolol, ramipril, and digoxin.

On examination, he has bilateral crackles to the midzones.

He is treated with intravenous furosemide.


Na+	128 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	2.7 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	10.1 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	111 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Calcium	2.05 mmol/L	(2.20-2.60)
Troponin	3 ng//L	(0-14)
TSH	2.1 mIU/L	(0.4-4.0)

He reports feeling unwell. He begins to vomit and reports yellow-green discoloration of his vision.

What is the likely mechanism of drug toxicity in this case?
options_json: ["Decreased binding to ATPase pump", "Increased binding to ATPase pump", "Increased calcium influx", "Reduce volume and distribution of clearance", "Reduced calcium influx"]
explanation_text:
Digoxin normally binds to the ATPase pump on the same site as potassium. Hypokalaemia → digoxin more easily bind to the ATPase pump → increased inhibitory effects

Increased binding to ATPase pump

is correct. The patient presents with nausea, vomiting, and yellow-green discoloration of vision. This suggests digoxin toxicity, which has likely been precipitated by hypokalemia secondary to furosemide treatment. Digoxin normally binds to the ATPase pump on the same site as potassium. Hypokalaemia results in digoxin more easily binding to the ATPase pump and increased inhibitory effects,

Decreased binding to ATPase pump

is incorrect. If digoxin is inhibited from binding to the ATPase pump, there will be fewer inhibitory effects and less toxicity risk.

Increased calcium influx

is incorrect. This can cause digoxin toxicity given that calcium and digoxin have additive inotropic effects. However, in this case, the calcium is low rather than high, so this is unlikely.

Reduce volume and distribution of clearance

is incorrect. This is the mechanism by which hypothyroidism predisposes to digoxin toxicity. However, this patient's TSH level is normal, so this is incorrect.

Reduced calcium influx

is incorrect. It is hypercalcaemia rather than hypocalcaemia that predisposes to digoxin toxicity. This patient is hypocalcaemic so this is not the likely cause of toxicity.

question_text:
A 62-year-old known chronic alcohol use is brought to the emergency department with acute onset of abdominal pain and vomiting large volumes of dark blood. He has known chronic liver disease and is established on warfarin for atrial fibrillation.

On examination he appears pale and sweaty with epigastric tenderness. His observation and blood tests are:

Observation

Heart rate 108/min
BP 100/60 mmHg
Resp rate 28/min
Oxygen sats 98%
Temperature 36.7 oC

Bloods:

Haemoglobin	90 g/L	(130-180)
Platelet count	200 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
INR	5.6	(0.8-1.2)



Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options_json: ["IV vitamin K 1-3mg & restart when INR <5.0", "IV vitamin K 5mg & fresh frozen plasma (FFP)", "IV vitamin K 5mg & prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)", "IV vitamin K 5mg & repeat the dose if INR still raised after 24hours", "Oral vitamin K 5mg & repeat the dose if INR still raised after 24hours"]
answer_text: IV vitamin K 5mg & prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
explanation_text:
Major bleeding - stop warfarin, give intravenous vitamin K 5mg, prothrombin complex concentrate

This patient has evidence of a major bleed most likely to a gastrointestinal bleed, with a haemoglobin drop (below normal range) and evidence of shock, in the context of oral anticoagulant warfarin use. These patients should be managed as an emergency and receive 5mg of vitamin K IV as well as prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) regardless of how high their INR is if it is raised (above normal range). These agents replace the clotting factors inhibited/reduced by warfarin. The use of vitamin K and PCC is often incorporated into major haemorrhage protocols.

Patients presenting with raised INR between 5.0-8.0 and minor bleeding (i.e. any bleeding not categorised as major) should receive a single dose of IV vitamin K 1-3mg and have their warfarin restarted when bleeding has stopped and the INR is under 5.0. As this patient has major bleeding this is not an appropriate management plan.

Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can be given for major bleeding in warfarin use but only if PCC is unavailable. Studies have show PCC is superior to FFP in normalising INR levels and therefore it should be used first-line if available. FFP can also take time to defrost, causing further delays when compared to PCC.

If a warfarin patient's INR is found to be over 8.0 and there is evidence of minor bleeding (i.e. any bleeding not categorised as major) then 1-3mg of IV vitamin K should be given initial and a repeat dose provided if the INR is still raised after 24hours.

Oral vitamin K should be given at a dose of 1-5mg to patients presenting with an INR above 8.0 so long as there is no evidence of bleeding. These patient's INR can then be checked, and a further dose provided in 24hours if the INR is still raised. This patient has evidence of a major bleed and therefore required further management.

question_text:
A 59-year-old woman is seen in clinic, with a history of chest pain upon exertion, relieved by rest. Her pain never occurs at rest. She takes aspirin, atorvastatin and the maximum dose of atenolol, but she is still persistently experiencing exertional chest pain. She has tolerated all medicines since commencement.

What would be the best recommendation for the next step in her management?
options_json: ["Commence diltiazem", "Commence amlodipine", "Commence ranolazine", "Commence verapamil", "Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)"]
explanation_text:
If angina is not controlled with a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker should be added

Commencing amlodipine is the correct answer. This patient is experiencing stable angina and is accordingly already taking a beta-blocker for this reason. The next step in management is the addition of a calcium-channel blocker; when being added in addition to a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine is recommended.

Commencing diltiazem is incorrect. If being used as

monotherapy

for angina, a rate-limiting non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is appropriate; a dihydropyridine such as amlodipine should be used for

dual therapy

.

Commencing ranolazine is incorrect. Ranolazine is only indicated if one of a calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker is not tolerated for dual therapy.

Commence verapamil is incorrect. A rate-limiting calcium channel blocker such as verapamil would be appropriate as

monotherapy

for angina, but there is a risk of complete heart block if verapamil is used in addition to a beta-blocker.

question_text:
A 67-year-old man attends his GP for a check-up. He has a background of hypertension, and his current medications include ramipril 5mg, amlodipine 10mg, and indapamide 2.5 mg. His blood pressure for the last few appointments has been raised. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring reveals an average blood pressure of 152/78 mmHg despite good compliance with medications. His most recent blood results are as follows:


Na+	134 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.9 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	125 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the most appropriate next step in controlling his hypertension?
options_json: ["Add doxazosin", "Add fludrocortisone", "Add spironolactone", "Increase dose of indapamide", "Repeat blood pressure at a later date"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blocker and a standard-dose thiazide diuretic. K+ > 4.5mmol/l - add an alpha- or beta-blocker

This man is already on an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, calcium-channel blocker (CCB) and thiazide diuretic. NICE advises adding an alpha-blocker such as doxazosin or beta-blocker at this stage if potassium is >4.5 mmol/l. NICE also suggests seeking specialist advice and discussing adherence with patients in these cases. Patients should also be assessed for postural hypotension (this can be done by measuring lying to standing blood pressure).

Fludrocortisone is a corticosteroid used to treat postural hypotension. It is not normally used to treat hypertension. It may increase his blood pressure further so is an incorrect option.

Spironolactone would be the appropriate next step if his potassium had been less than 4.5 mmol/l.

His indapamide dose cannot be increased any further as he is already on the maximum dose.

His persistently high blood pressure has been observed on multiple dates and been confirmed with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). His hypertension needs to be treated, and repeating blood pressure would only delay this further.

question_text:
An 82-year-old man attends the cardiology clinic. He has a past medical history of heart failure. He has had worsening shortness of breath over the last month and is now symptomatic at rest. His regular medications include ramipril, bisoprolol, furosemide and eplerenone. On examination, you note pitting oedema to the mid calves and bilateral coarse crepitations. His pulse rate is 65 beats per minute.

An echocardiogram and ECG is performed:


Echo	Left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%


ECG	Sinus rhythm; QRS 115 msec

What treatment is most likely to be beneficial to long-term survival?
options_json: ["Bendroflumethiazide", "Bumetanide", "Cardiac resynchronisation therapy", "Ivabradine", "Sacubitril-valsartan"]
explanation_text:
Sacubitril-valsartan is considered in heart failure patients with a LVEF < 35% who are still symptomatic on ACE-inhibitors & beta-blockers

The patient has symptomatic (NYHA class IV) cardiac failure requiring escalation of treatment.  He is already on an ACE-I, beta blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and loop diuretic. He has severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) with an ejection fraction of 30%.

Sacubitril-valsartan

is correct. Sacubitril-valsartan is considered the next line in patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 35% who are still symptomatic on an ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker.

Bendroflumethiazide

is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide can be used for mild or moderate heart failure. Although diuretics can have major benefits for patient symptomatology, they have no benefit to long-term survival.

Bumetanide

is incorrect. Bumetanide is a type of loop diuretic which has been shown to have greater bioavailability compared to furosemide due to increased absorption in patients who have oedematous bowels. Although diuretics can have major benefits for patient symptomatology, they have no benefit to long-term survival.

Cardiac resynchronisation therapy

is incorrect. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) is recommended as a treatment option for people with heart failure who have left ventricular dysfunction with an LVEF of 35% or less, and LBBB with a QRS duration > 130 msec. The patient in this clinical case has a QRS of 115 msec and therefore does not fulfil this criterion. Furthermore, the PROVE-HF trial (as well as case reports and observational studies) have shown that sacubitril/valsartan is able to induce reverse cardiac remodelling, which has the potential to avoid ICD or CRT implantation.

Ivabradine

is incorrect. Ivabradine is recommended as an option for treating chronic heart failure for patients who are in sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 75 beats per minute or more and who are already on standard therapy with ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists. The patient in this clinical case has a heart rate of 65 beats per minute and ivabradine is therefore not indicated.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis is admitted for an elective total hip replacement. She experiences hip pain but is otherwise well.

Examination reveals a reduced range of motion in her right hip. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are normal.

The operation is successful, but she collapses on the ward two days post-operatively. She shows no signs of life, and CPR is initiated. The rhythm is pulseless electrical activity (PEA). An echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilatation.

What medication should be administered alongside standard adult life support measures?
options_json: ["Alteplase", "Isoprenaline", "Lidocaine", "Naloxone", "Sodium bicarbonate"]
explanation_text:
Thrombolytic drugs should be considered during CPR if a PE is suspected

This patient's sudden collapse postoperatively, combined with ultrasound findings of right ventricular dilatation, suggests a massive pulmonary embolism (PE), which is a known complication following orthopaedic surgery. Therefore, the correct treatment option is

alteplase

, a thrombolytic agent.

Isoprenaline

can be used as a second-line drug for life-threatening bradyarrhythmias. However, isoprenaline has no role in the management of PE and is not recommended during cardiac arrest.

Lidocaine

is indicated during cardiac arrest when the underlying rhythm is pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. Since the patient’s rhythm is PEA, lidocaine is not appropriate in this case.

Naloxone

is an opiate reversal agent and would not be effective for treating PE-induced cardiac arrest. There is no history suggesting opiate toxicity, which would typically present with drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, and respiratory depression leading to type 2 respiratory failure.

Sodium bicarbonate

, administered as a high-concentration bolus (50 ml of 8.4%), can be used as an adjunct in treating cardiac arrest caused by hyperkalemia. It helps reverse acidosis by shifting potassium intracellularly, thus lowering serum potassium levels. However, there is no history indicating hyperkalemia; the clinical presentation points to PE.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman with a background history of ischaemic cardiomyopathy with moderate left ventricular impairment and atrial fibrillation is admitted due to vomiting from norovirus.

Her bloods from 3 months ago were:


Na+	135 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	8.9 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	131 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

Her bloods today show:


Na+	132 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	2.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	9.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	145 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Digoxin level	2.9 ng/ml	(0.8-2.0)

Which of her regular medications likely contributed to her digoxin toxicity?
options_json: ["Ramipril", "Bendroflumethiazide", "Aspirin", "Amlodipine", "Bisoprolol"]
explanation_text:
Digoxin normally binds to the ATPase pump on the same site as potassium. Hypokalaemia → digoxin more easily bind to the ATPase pump → increased inhibitory effects

Hypokalaemia is one of the most common precipitants of digoxin toxicity. Digoxin functions by biding to the sodium-potassium ATPase pump on cardiac myocytes to slow down conduction and therefore slow heart rate. It binds to the same site as the potassium usually would on the ATPase pump. In periods of hypokalaemia, there is less competition for the binding site, resulting in an increased effect of digoxin.

Bendroflumethiazide has caused hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia coupled with vomiting. The renal function is not significantly affected, so is unlikely to be acute kidney injury-related. This hypokalemia has precipitated digoxin toxicity.

Looking at the other options:

Ramipril would cause hyperkalemia. Hyperkalaemia is usually seen as a consequence of digoxin toxicity, not as a cause of it. In addition, a stage 1 acute kidney injury is usually defined as a creatinine increase of >26umol/l, 1.5-1.9x increase in reference creatinine or reduced urine output (<0.5ml/kg/hr for 6 consecutive hours).

Aspirin would not influence the metabolism of digoxin.

Amlodipine would not typically influence digoxin levels. However, other calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem are known to reduce digoxin excretion via the kidneys.

Bisoprolol is not known to directly influence digoxin levels. It can sometimes be associated with hyperkalemia, but as described before, this is often a consequence rather than a precipitant of digoxin toxicity.

Most common cause of endocarditis:

is the most common cause of endocarditis within 2 months of prosthetic valve surgery.

accounts for 20% of endocarditis cases making it a less likely culprit than

question_text:
You are reviewing a 75-year-old male patient with hypertension. He takes 10mg once a day of ramipril and 10mg once a day of amlodipine. His blood pressure remains uncontrolled and you want to start a third agent. His K+is 4.3 mmol/l.

According to the NICE guidelines, what would be the most appropriate third-line agent for this man?
options_json: ["Bendroflumethiazide", "Candesartan", "Hydrochlorothiazide", "Spironolactone", "Indapamide"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor and a calcium channel blocker - add a thiazide-like diuretic

This patient is >55 years old and is already on an ACE-inhibitor (ramipril) at the maximum dose and a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) at the maximum dose.

According to the NICE guidelines, thiazide-like diuretics are the next line therapy eg chlortalidone (12.5-25.0 mg once daily) or indapamide (1.5 mg modified-release once daily or 2.5 mg once daily). Therefore, the correct answer here is 5, indapamide.

NICE state that a thiazide-like diuretic should be used in preference to a conventional thiazide diuretic such as bendroflumethiazide or hydrochlorothiazide. Therefore, these two answers are wrong. Candesartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) and should not be used in conjunction with an ACE-inhibitor. Spironolactone is used as a fourth agent in resistant hypertension if the K+ is <4.5 mmol/l.

question_text:
A 50-year-old man with a history of hypertension and recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus is being followed up in the clinic. He was initially prescribed a thiazide diuretic for his hypertension while living abroad. In light of his new diagnosis, it has been decided to switch him to an antihypertensive medication that targets angiotensin-converting enzyme for long-term renoprotection.

What best explains the renoprotective mechanism of his new medication?
options_json: ["Constriction of the afferent arteriole, reducing glomerular pressure", "Dilation of the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure", "Enhancement of sodium excretion via inhibition of sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporters", "Inhibition of sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule", "Reduction of sympathetic outflow, decreasing systemic vascular resistance"]
answer_text: Dilation of the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure
explanation_text:
The renoprotective effects of ACE inhibitors are mediated through dilation of the glomerular efferent arteriole

Dilation of the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure

is correct because this patient has hypertension and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus. In diabetic nephropathy, chronic hyperglycemia leads to glomerular hyperfiltration, where angiotensin II causes preferential constriction of the efferent arteriole, increasing intraglomerular pressure and promoting albuminuria. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors counteract this process by dilating the efferent arteriole, reducing glomerular hypertension, and slowing disease progression.

Constriction of the afferent arteriole, reducing glomerular pressure

is incorrect because while lowering glomerular pressure is beneficial, afferent constriction would also reduce renal perfusion and glomerular filtration rate, potentially worsening kidney function. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which inhibit vasodilatory prostaglandins, have this effect and are known to exacerbate chronic kidney disease, particularly in patients with diabetes. In contrast, ACE inhibitors selectively target efferent arteriolar tone without compromising overall renal perfusion.

Enhancement of sodium excretion via inhibition of sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporters

is incorrect because this describes the action of loop diuretics, such as furosemide, which reduce extracellular volume and lower blood pressure but do not have specific renoprotective effects. While loop diuretics are useful in managing fluid overload, this patient does not have clinical signs of volume excess, making this mechanism irrelevant to his current treatment needs.

Inhibition of sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule

is incorrect because this describes thiazide diuretics, which the patient was previously prescribed. While effective for blood pressure control, thiazides do not specifically reduce intraglomerular pressure or slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy. An ACE inhibitor is preferred for blood pressure control and renal protection.

Reduction of sympathetic outflow, decreasing systemic vascular resistance

is incorrect because this describes centrally acting antihypertensives like clonidine or methyldopa, which are not first-line choices for hypertension, especially in diabetes. While these agents lower blood pressure, they do not have specific effects on glomerular hemodynamics or albuminuria, making them unsuitable for patients with early diabetic kidney disease.

He has a history of angina, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His regular medications include ramipril, metformin, sitagliptin, verapamil and atorvastatin.

On abdominal examination, he is tender in the left lower quadrant. An abdominal X-ray shows faecal loading.

Verapamil can cause constipation

The correct answer is verapamil. Verapamil, like other calcium channel blockers, is a common pharmacological cause of constipation.

Of the other options, ramipril and atorvastatin are not frequently associated with altered bowel habit, whilst sitagliptin and particularly metformin are associated with diarrhoea.

question_text: A 71-year-old man who is known to have atrial fibrillation comes for review. He had a transient ischaemic attack two weeks ago and takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension but is otherwise well. His latest blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg. You are discussing management options to try and reduce his future risk of having a stroke. What is his CHA2DS2-VASc score?

You are part of the cardiac arrest team and are called to see a 72-year-old man who was admitted to the care of the elderly ward. He presented with shortness of breath, productive cough and hypoxia. He was being treated for community-acquired pneumonia with IV antibiotics. His early warning score has continued to worsen throughout the day and then he became unresponsive. There were no signs of life, therefore, chest compressions were commenced by the ward staff and the crash call was put out. The first rhythm check shows the patient is in ventricular fibrillation.

Apart from restarting chest compressions, what should be the next step taken as part of the advance life support algorithm?
options_json: ["Adrenaline", "Atropine", "Amiodarone", "1 shock", "3 successive shocks"]
explanation_text:
VF/pulseless VT should be treated with 1 shock as soon as identified

This man has had a cardiac arrest and at the first rhythm check is in a shockable rhythm. Therefore the next step is to give 1 shock.

Adrenaline is given after the 3rd shock if following the 'shockable rhythm' pathway (AF/pulseless VT) or immediately if on the 'non-shockable rhythm' pathway (asystole or pulseless electrical activity).

Atropine is not used in cardiac arrest. It can be used for the management of bradycardia with adverse features.

Amiodarone is given after the 3rd shock in the algorithm.

3 successive shocks are used where the cardiac arrest is witnessed and in a monitored are such as post-myocardial infarction in a coronary care unit.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man presents to you with intermittent left-sided crushing chest pain which is brought on by walking his dog on an incline. The pain settles within a couple of minutes of rest and glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray. The pain is not associated with shortness of breath or lightheadedness.

He first presented to you with these same symptoms six months ago, at this time you gave him lifestyle advice and prescribed bisoprolol, aspirin, GTN and atorvastatin. He has noted only minimal improvement of his symptoms over the last six months.

On examination he is comfortable at rest, with blood pressure 124/73 mmHg, heart rate 63 beats/minute, oxygen saturation 99%, respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute and he is afebrile. His chest is clear, and heart sounds are normal. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm, with no ischaemic changes. He is also awaiting a CT coronary angiography.

What would be the next stage of treatment for this patient?

explanation_text:
If angina is not controlled with a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker should be added

If monotherapy with bisoprolol has not been successful, the next step in treating stable angina is to add a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, such as amlodipine.

Bisoprolol should not be given concurrently with a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, like verapamil, as both reduce conduction at the AV node and this could lead to complete heart block.

A long-acting nitrate or nicorandil might be considered if an additional calcium channel blocker was not tolerated. But this would not be a second-line treatment plan.

As a side note, the maximum dose of bisoprolol within 24 hours is typically 10mg, and although higher doses are sometimes prescribed by cardiologists, this would not be the most appropriate next step, especially considering his low-normal heart rate of 63 beats per minute.

Amlodipine may cause gingival hyperplasia

amlodipine

Pulsus alternans is when the upstroke of the pulse alternatives between strong and weak. It indicates systolic dysfunction and is seen in patients with heart failure.

A collapsing pulse has a forceful rapid upstroke AND descent.

A jerky pulse is characterised by a rapid forceful upstroke.

A slow-rising pulse has a slow upstroke.

Dipyridamole is an antiplatelet agent that acts via phosphodiesterase inhibition. It can be used in combination with aspirin for secondary prevention following transient ischaemic attack if clopidogrel is not tolerated.

The platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor binds to collagen and is inhibited by tirofiban.

Glycoprotein VI is the platelet receptor that interacts with subendothelial collagen.

Glycoprotein 1b is the platelet receptor for von Willebrand Factor. There is no specific drug that targets this interaction but autoantibodies to glycoprotein Ib are the basis of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

A 50-year-old man presents with increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He has a past history of rheumatic fever but is otherwise normally fit and well. He has a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur best heard on expiration. Echocardiogram demonstrates severe mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area <1.5 cm².

options_json: ["Mitral valve repair", "Mitral valve replacement with a mechanical valve", "Mitral valve replacement with a tissue valve", "Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy", "Transcatheter mitral valve replacement"]
explanation_text:
Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is the intervention of choice for severe mitral stenosis

The correct answer is percutaneous mitral commissurotomy (PMC). Patients with severe mitral stenosis who are symptomatic should be considered for percutaneous mitral commissurotomy. The atrial septum is punctured and a balloon is deployed across the valve. The balloon is inflated to split the mitral valve commissures, the area where the anterior and posterior leaflets meet at their insertion in the annulus.

Mitral valve repair is mostly used for mitral regurgitation or prolapse.

Surgical valve replacement, such as mitral valve replacement with a mechanical or tissue valve, is considered where PMC is unsuccessful.

Transcatheter mitral valve replacement was approved as a treatment in 2020 for patients unsuitable for open surgery.

question_text: A 37-year-old woman who was investigated for progressive shortness-of-breath is diagnosed with primary pulmonary hypertension and started on bosentan. What is the mechanism of action of bosentan?
options_json: ["Activator of soluble guanylate cyclase", "Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors", "Endothelin receptor antagonist", "Prostanoid", "Slow calcium channel blocker"]
explanation_text:
Bosentan - endothelin-1 receptor antagonist

The correct answer is

Endothelin receptor antagonist

. Bosentan works by blocking the action of endothelin, a substance produced by the body that causes blood vessels to narrow and prevents normal blood flow in individuals with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). By inhibiting the receptors for endothelin, bosentan helps to decrease pulmonary vascular resistance and increase cardiac output, thereby improving symptoms associated with PAH.

The first incorrect option is

Activator of soluble guanylate cyclase

. This mechanism of action refers to drugs like riociguat. These drugs work by stimulating soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), an enzyme in the cardiopulmonary system. This leads to increased levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which causes vasodilation and thus improves symptoms in conditions such as PAH. However, this is not how bosentan works.

The second incorrect option is

Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors

. These are drugs like sildenafil and tadalafil which inhibit the phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) enzyme, leading to an increase in cGMP levels and resulting in pulmonary vasodilation. Again, this is not the mechanism of action of bosentan.

The third incorrect option is

Prostanoid

. Prostanoids such as epoprostenol and iloprost are potent vasodilators that also inhibit platelet aggregation. They have been used in the treatment of PAH but their mechanism differs from that of bosentan.

Lastly,

Slow calcium channel blocker

also represents an incorrect answer. While some calcium channel blockers like nifedipine or diltiazem can be used in patients with PAH who respond to acute vasoreactivity testing, they act by blocking calcium channels on heart cells and blood vessels rather than acting via endothelin antagonism like bosentan.

question_text:
A 35-year-old man presents after a syncopal episode while at rest. He denies chest pain or palpitations before the event. There is no significant past medical history. His father died suddenly at the age of 40. An ECG performed in the emergency department shows a coved-type ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V2 with a partial right bundle branch block pattern.

What is the underlying cause of this condition?
options_json: ["Abnormal calcium ion channel protein", "Abnormal potassium ion channel protein", "Abnormal sodium ion channel protein", "Myocardial fibrosis", "Structural right ventricular outflow tract abnormality"]
explanation_text:
Brugada syndrome is due to a mutation of the myocardial sodium ion channel protein

Abnormal sodium ion channel protein

is correct. Brugada syndrome is a genetic condition; the most common mutations are in the SCN5A gene, identified in approximately 20% to 30% of affected individuals. The SCN5A gene encodes the alpha-subunit of the cardiac sodium ion channel protein and this mutation results in impaired sodium channel function, leading to altered depolarisation and repolarisation in the right ventricular myocardium. These alterations are associated with fatal ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Typical ECG findings are coved-type ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V2 with a partial right bundle branch block pattern.

Abnormal calcium ion channel protein

is incorrect. Mutations in calcium ion channel proteins (e.g., CACNA1C) are associated with long QT syndrome (LQTS) type 8 (Timothy syndrome), not Brugada syndrome. Calcium channel dysfunction does not explain the coved ST-segment elevation or susceptibility to arrhythmias seen in Brugada syndrome.

Abnormal potassium ion channel protein

is incorrect. Potassium ion channel abnormalities are associated with LQTS types 1 and 2, not Brugada syndrome. These mutations lead to delayed repolarisation and prolonged QT intervals, which predispose to torsades de pointes rather than the specific ECG findings of Brugada syndrome.

Myocardial fibrosis

is incorrect. Myocardial fibrosis is seen in structural heart diseases, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or post-myocardial infarction scarring. Brugada syndrome typically occurs in structurally normal hearts and is unrelated to fibrosis.

Structural right ventricular outflow tract abnormality

is incorrect. This is associated with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), which can present with arrhythmias and right ventricular dysfunction. Unlike Brugada syndrome, ARVC is characterised by structural abnormalities and fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium. ECG may show T-wave inversion in V1-V3 or an Epsilon wave.

question_text:
Mr Brown is a 62-year-old man with colon cancer. He is undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy, however in the past six months has suffered four deep vein thrombotic (DVT) events, despite being optimally anti-coagulated with the maximum dose of dabigatran. On one occasion he suffered a DVT during treatment with dalteparin (a low molecular weight heparin) . He has been admitted with symptoms of another DVT.

How should his DVT be treated?
options_json: ["Add apixaban to his prescription", "Initiate end of life drugs and prepare the family", "Increase the dose of dabigatran off-licence", "Prescribe Thrombo-Embolic Deterrent (TED) stockings", "Insert an inferior vena caval filter"]
answer_text: Insert an inferior vena caval filter
explanation_text:
Patients with recurrent venous thromboembolic disease may be considered for an inferior vena cava filter

This patient has cancer and suffered multiple DVTs in a short space of time, despite being fully anti-coagulated. NICE have produced guidelines on such patients:

'Consider inferior vena caval filters for patients with recurrent proximal DVT or PE despite adequate anticoagulation treatment only after considering alternative treatments such as:

increasing target INR to 3-4 for long term high-intensity oral anticoagulant therapy or
switching treatment to LMWH.'

[NICE (2015) Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing. CG144]

Add apixaban to his prescription - This is not the most appropriate answer. This patient has already been trailed on a LMWH. An inferior vena caval filter is the most appropriate next step.

Initiate end of life drugs and prepare the family - This is not the most appropriate answer. This clinical description does not give any indication to initiate an end of life pathway. This would be something to discuss with their oncologist.

Increase the dose of dabigatran off-licence - This is not the most appropriate answer. The patient is already on maximum dose and increasing it further, beyond recommended levels, could cause harm.

Prescribe Thrombo-Embolic Deterrent (TED) stockings - This is not the most appropriate answer. A medical or surgical patient will likely be prescribed these on admission as prophylaxis. However, they are of limited use in treating a DVT.

Insert an inferior vena caval filter - This is the correct answer. As per NICE guidelines above, this patient should be considered for an IVC filter.

question_text:
A 22-year-old male presents to the cardiology clinic with exertional dyspnoea and two episodes of syncope while playing football. His father died suddenly at age 40. On examination, he has a jerky pulse and a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva manoeuvre. Echocardiogram shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.

What is the most likely genetic mutation responsible for his condition?
options_json: ["Myosin-binding protein C gene", "Dystrophin gene", "Lamin A/C gene", "Troponin T gene", "Titin gene"]
explanation_text:
HOCM is usually due to a mutation in the gene encoding β-myosin heavy chain protein or myosin binding protein C

Myosin-binding protein C gene

is the correct answer. This patient presents with classic features of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), including exertional dyspnoea, exercise-induced syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, and characteristic examination findings (jerky pulse and systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva). The echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. HOCM is most commonly caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, with myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3) and β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) accounting for approximately 70-80% of genotyped cases. MYBPC3 mutations are the most common, found in about 40-50% of genotype-positive patients. These mutations lead to disorganized myocardial architecture and fibrosis, resulting in the pathophysiological features of HOCM.

Dystrophin gene

mutations are responsible for Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies. While these conditions can have cardiac involvement (typically dilated cardiomyopathy), they primarily present with skeletal muscle weakness and elevated creatine kinase levels. The patient's presentation with isolated cardiac symptoms without skeletal muscle involvement makes dystrophin gene mutations unlikely.

Lamin A/C gene

mutations cause laminopathies, including Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy and familial dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defects. These typically present with early conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and dilated cardiomyopathy rather than hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The echocardiographic findings in this case are inconsistent with laminopathies.

Troponin T gene

mutations can cause HOCM, but they account for only about 5% of genotyped cases, making them less likely than myosin-binding protein C mutations. Troponin T mutations are associated with milder hypertrophy but a higher risk of sudden cardiac death. While this could fit with the family history, the prevalence makes it less likely than MYBPC3.

Titin gene

mutations are primarily associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and some cases of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. They are not typically associated with HOCM. The echocardiographic findings of asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve are inconsistent with titin gene mutations.

question_text:
A 70-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden onset chest pain that is radiating to his left shoulder. He had a past medical history of a previous transient ischaemic attack two years ago for which he is taking aspirin 75mg OD.

An initial ECG was performed.


ECG	ST-segment elevation in V1-V3

He was managed with percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent and was haemodynamically stable after the procedure. He is given ramipril, ticagrelor, simvastatin and atenolol as part of further management.

Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the newly prescribed antiplatelet medication?
options_json: ["Inhibit the binding of ADP to platelets", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor inhibition", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist", "Inhibit phosphodiesterase", "Inhibition of adenosine reuptake"]
answer_text: Inhibit the binding of ADP to platelets
explanation_text:
Ticagrelor has a similar mechanism of action to clopidogrel - inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors

This patient presents with STEMI based on his classic symptoms and ECG finding and gets managed with a percutaneous coronary intervention using a drug-eluting stent. As part of secondary management, these patients get dual antiplatelet therapy, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and anti-hyperlipidemic drugs.

There are several antiplatelets available with different mechanisms of action.

When ADP binds to its platelet receptor, it leads to activation of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex and eventually results in platelet aggregation. Clopidogrel first gets metabolized by CYP450 enzymes to the active form which then selectively inhibits the binding of ADP to its platelet receptor, thereby preventing platelet aggregation. Newer medications like ticagrelor have a similar mechanism of action as clopidogrel.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa are fibrinogen receptors found on the platelet. When activated, they bind fibrinogen, facilitating the adhesion of platelets to the extracellular matrix and cross-linking of adjacent platelets. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors bind to this receptor, creating a conformational change that prevents access of ligands to their binding site.  Abciximab is an example of a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists compete with the receptor ligands such as fibrinogen for its binding site on the receptor. It blocks the binding site and prevents the formation of thrombi. Eptifibatide is an example of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonist.

Dipyridamole acts in multiple ways, one being inhibition of platelet cAMP-phosphodiesterase. It then increases intra-platelet cAMP, which leads to reduced arachidonic acid release. It finally results in decreased thromboxane A2 formation.

Dipyridamole also acts by inhibiting the reuptake of adenosine by vascular endothelial cells and erythrocytes. An increased concentration of adenosine leads to activation of adenyl cyclase and increased production of cAMP.

question_text:
A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of feeling faint. He has no significant medical history, nor does he take any medications.

Among other investigations, an ECG is performed which shows convex ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V3 followed by a negative T-wave. A partial right bundle branch block is also identified. The cardiologist on-call is asked to review the patient, and administers flecainide, before repeating an ECG - the changes become more apparent.

explanation_text:
Mutations in the SCN5A gene (which encode the myocardial sodium ion channel protein are the most common gene abnormality seen in Brugada syndrome

The correct answer is SCN5A. The description that has been given here is highly suggestive of Brugada syndrome, which usually is picked up incidentally, but may also cause fainting (and sudden death). The ECG changes are typical of Brugada syndrome. Most commonly, it is associated with mutations in the SCN5A gene, which encodes the Na

v

1.5 sodium channel.

KCNQ1 encodes part of the K

v

7.1 slow delayed rectifier potassium channel. Mutations in this are implicated in Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, not Brugada. This is a rare form of long QT syndrome.

CACNB2 encodes part of the Ca

v

β2B voltage-gated calcium channel. It is also implicated in Brugada syndrome, but not as commonly as SCN5A mutations.

PRKAG2 encodes for a protein kinase enzyme that is implicated in Wolff-Parkinson White syndrome. This would have different ECG findings - namely, a short PR interval and a delta wave.

KCNE3 encodes for MiRP2, a subunit of voltage-gated potassium channels. Mutations in this gene are also involved in the pathogenesis of Brugada syndrome, but not as commonly as SCN5A.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman is referred to cardiology outpatients with palpitations. She has no significant past medical history. On examination, she has a fixed, widely split second heart sound and a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur heard loudest at the upper left sternal edge. The murmur increases in intensity during inspiration. Her ECG shows right bundle branch block.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Atrial septal defect", "Mitral regurgitation", "Patent ductus arteriosus", "Pulmonary stenosis", "Ventricular septal defect"]
explanation_text:
Atrial septal defect - ejection systolic murmur louder on inspiration

Atrial septal defect

is the correct diagnosis based on the clinical findings. The patient presents with a fixed, widely split second heart sound, which is characteristic of atrial septal defect (ASD). This occurs because the right ventricular volume overload leads to delayed right ventricular emptying, causing persistent splitting of S2 that doesn't vary with respiration. The ejection systolic murmur heard at the upper left sternal edge that increases with inspiration is due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve (relative pulmonary stenosis). This is a right-sided murmur, and right-sided murmurs classically increase during inspiration due to increased venous return to the right heart. The right bundle branch block on ECG is also consistent with ASD, as the increased right ventricular volume leads to right ventricular conduction delay. The young age of the patient and presentation with palpitations are also typical for ASD.

Mitral regurgitation

is incorrect. Mitral regurgitation produces a pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla. Being a left-sided murmur, it would typically decrease in intensity during inspiration rather than increase. Additionally, mitral regurgitation would not cause a fixed, widely split second heart sound or right bundle branch block on ECG.

Patent ductus arteriosus

is incorrect. PDA typically produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur that persists throughout systole and diastole, best heard in the left infraclavicular area. It would not cause a fixed, widely split second heart sound, and the murmur would not characteristically increase with inspiration as it is primarily a left-sided lesion.

Pulmonary stenosis

can produce an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge that increases with inspiration, similar to ASD. However, pulmonary stenosis typically causes an ejection click followed by the murmur, and the second heart sound would be widely split but not fixed (it would still vary with respiration). The absence of an ejection click and the presence of fixed splitting of S2 make pulmonary stenosis less likely than ASD.

Ventricular septal defect

produces a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal edge. The murmur is typically harsh in character and does not vary significantly with respiration as it is primarily a left-to-right shunt. VSD does not cause fixed splitting of S2, and small VSDs (more common in adults) typically cause a louder murmur than larger ones due to the greater pressure gradient across a smaller defect.
