question_text: A 1-year-old girl is noted to have a continuous murmur, loudest at the left sternal edge. She is not cyanosed. A diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus is suspected. What pulse abnormality is most associated with this condition?
options_json: ["Collapsing pulse", "Bisferiens pulse", "Pulsus parodoxus", "'Jerky' pulse", "Pulsus alternans"]
explanation_text:
Patent ductus arteriosus - large volume, bounding, collapsing pulse

The correct answer is

Collapsing pulse

. In patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), the ductus arteriosus, which normally closes shortly after birth, remains open. This results in a left-to-right shunt from the aorta to the pulmonary artery, leading to increased stroke volume and subsequently a rapid rise and fall of arterial pressure - hence a collapsing pulse. The collapsing pulse is characterised by a forceful upstroke followed by a rapid drop in systolic pressure, giving it a 'water-hammer' feel.

Bisferiens pulse

is incorrect. Bisferiens pulse is characterised by two peaks in systole and can be felt as a double beat for each cardiac cycle. This type of pulse is typically associated with conditions like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe aortic regurgitation, not PDA.

Pulsus paradoxus

is also incorrect. Pulsus paradoxus refers to an exaggerated decrease in pulse amplitude during inspiration and can be seen in conditions such as cardiac tamponade or severe asthma - again not typically associated with PDA.

The

'Jerky' pulse

option is incorrect too. A 'jerky' pulse, also known as pulsus bisferiens, describes a double-peaked (or 'jerky') sensation when palpating the radial artery. It's most commonly associated with combined stenosis and regurgitation of the aortic valve.

Lastly,

Pulsus alternans

is incorrect as well. Pulsus alternans refers to alternating strong and weak pulses which may indicate left ventricular failure or other serious cardiac disease but it's not specifically associated with patent ductus arteriosus.

question_text: Which part of the jugular venous waveform is associated with the opening of the tricuspid valve?
options_json: ["x descent", "v wave", "a wave", "c wave", "y descent"]
explanation_text:
JVP: y descent = opening of tricuspid valve

The correct answer is

y descent

. The y descent of the jugular venous waveform corresponds to the early diastolic rapid filling phase of the right ventricle, which occurs immediately after the tricuspid valve opens. As the tricuspid valve opens, blood rapidly flows from the right atrium into the right ventricle, causing a decrease in right atrial pressure. This decrease in pressure is reflected as the y descent on the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform. The y descent follows the v wave and represents the transition from atrial filling to ventricular filling.

x descent

is incorrect. The x descent occurs during ventricular systole and represents atrial relaxation while the tricuspid valve is closed. It follows the c wave and precedes the v wave in the cardiac cycle. During this phase, the right atrium relaxes and expands, creating a decrease in pressure that is visible as the x descent on the JVP waveform. This occurs while the tricuspid valve remains closed, not when it opens.

v wave

is incorrect. The v wave represents passive filling of the right atrium during late ventricular systole when the tricuspid valve is still closed. It occurs due to continued venous return to the right atrium while the tricuspid valve remains closed during ventricular contraction. The v wave precedes the opening of the tricuspid valve rather than corresponding to it.

a wave

is incorrect. The a wave represents right atrial contraction (atrial systole) and occurs at the end of ventricular diastole, just before ventricular systole begins. This wave is produced by the increase in right atrial pressure as the atrium contracts to push the final volume of blood into the right ventricle before the tricuspid valve closes. The a wave occurs well before the opening of the tricuspid valve in the next cardiac cycle.

c wave

is incorrect. The c wave is a small positive deflection that follows the a wave and represents bulging of the closed tricuspid valve into the right atrium during the initial phase of right ventricular contraction (isovolumetric contraction). This occurs at the beginning of ventricular systole when the tricuspid valve has just closed, not when it opens. The c wave is often difficult to distinguish from the a wave in clinical practice.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of sudden-onset weakness in his face and arm. His past medical history includes hypertension for which he is treated with amlodipine. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. He is independent and lives alone.

His observations are heart rate 89 beats per minute, blood pressure 145/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/minute, oxygen saturation 97% on room air and temperature 37.1ºC.

Clinical examination reveals a right sided facial droop and a weak right upper limb (3/5) with preserved power in the right lower limb. Sensation is normal. The cranial nerve examination is otherwise unremarkable. Chest auscultation reveals equal air entry bilaterally. His heart sounds are normal and there are no murmurs but his pulse is irregular.

An ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation.

A CT head excludes haemorrhage and CT angiography does not demonstrate a specific site of occlusion.

What is the mechanism of action of the appropriate pharmacological treatment?
options_json: ["Activation of tissue plasminogen", "Inhibition of activated factor Xa", "Inhibition of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa", "Inhibition of formation of thromboxane A2", "P2Y12 Receptor Antagonist"]
answer_text: Inhibition of formation of thromboxane A2
explanation_text:
Aspirin decreases the formation of thromboxane A2 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation

Inhibition of the formation of thromboxane A2 is the correct answer. The patient presents with a right-sided facial and upper limb weakness, indicating a likely stroke. A CT head excludes a haemorrhage and CT angiography does not demonstrate evidence of a specific site of occlusion. The patient is outside the thrombolysis window. Therefore, the patient is not suitable for either thrombolysis or thrombectomy. He will therefore be administered with 300mg aspirin for the treatment of probable ischaemic stroke. Aspirin inhibits the formation of thromboxane A2 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation.

Inhibition of activated factor Xa is incorrect. This is the mechanism of apixaban. The patient will be anti-coagulated for new-onset atrial fibrillation in due course but this is usually delayed until 14 days after the acute stroke due to risk of haemorrhagic transformation.

Inhibition of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of tirofiban. This is an antiplatelet medication used occasionally in the management of acute coronary syndromes. It is not indicated in the management of stroke.

Activation of tissue plasminogen is incorrect. Alteplase is a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator which catalyzes the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, the major enzyme responsible for clot breakdown. This medication is used for thrombolysis. However, the patient presents outside the thrombolysis window and therefore this medication is not indicated.

P2Y12 receptor antagonist is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel, which works by antagonism of P2Y12 platelet receptors and subsequent prevention of binding of ADP to the P2Y12 receptor leading to decreased platelet aggregation. This is the antiplatelet of choice in secondary prevention of stroke. However, it is not used in the treatment of acute stroke. High dose aspirin is administered in the first 14 days post-event.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man is admitted to the cardiology ward following an episode of syncope. He reports a 6-month history of angina and dyspnoea. An echocardiogram reveals severe aortic stenosis, and he is scheduled for an angiogram prior to aortic valve replacement surgery, which demonstrates significant right coronary artery disease.

He subsequently undergoes successful coronary artery bypass grafting and mechanical aortic valve replacement without complications.

What is the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy for this patient?
options_json: ["Apixaban", "Aspirin", "Low molecular weight heparin", "Warfarin", "Warfarin and aspirin"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy:

Warfarin and aspirin

is the correct answer here. This patient has two indications for antithrombotic therapy. Firstly, he has a mechanical aortic valve replacement which requires long-term anticoagulation to prevent thrombosis of the valve. Warfarin is the only licensed anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves, and so this patient should be on it. Secondly, he has had coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) for significant right coronary artery disease, which would usually require antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, according to the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines. Therefore, the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy for this patient is both warfarin and aspirin.

Apixaban

is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) utilised in the management of venous thromboembolism and atrial fibrillation. However, DOACs have not received approval for use with mechanical heart valves, whereas warfarin has. In addition to anticoagulation, this patient should be prescribed aspirin due to the presence of ischaemic heart disease.

Aspirin

monotherapy would be inappropriate for this patient. Although he exhibits signs of ischaemic heart disease on angiography, necessitating aspirin therapy, his mechanical heart valve significantly increases his risk of thrombotic events, thus requiring effective anticoagulation with warfarin.

Low molecular weight heparin

is typically used for short-term anticoagulation (e.g., perioperative period), but does not have an indication for long-term management of ischaemic heart disease or in those with mechanical heart valves.

Warfarin

is the appropriate choice for patients with mechanical heart valves as it stands as the only endorsed anticoagulant for this indication. Furthermore, given this patient's evidence of ischaemic heart disease, he should also receive aspirin as per the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.

question_text:
A 78-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with nausea, abdominal pain, constipation and low mood with generalised musculoskeletal pain and weakness. On examination she appears dehydrated.

Blood tests demonstrate a marked electrolyte abnormality.

Which of the following is most likely to be seen on her ECG?
options_json: ["Lengthening of the PR interval", "Shortening of the QT interval", "T wave inversion", "Torsades de pointes", "U waves"]
explanation_text:
The main ECG abnormality seen with hypercalcaemia is shortening of the QT interval

The correct answer is 'shortening of the QT interval'. The cluster of signs and symptoms being described here is typical of hypercalcaemia - 'stones, bones, groans and psychiatric moans'. This patient will most likely have been commenced on intravenous fluids and, depending on severity, a bisphosphonate. The most commonly seen ECG change in hypercalcaemia is shortening of the QT interval.

Lengthening of the PR interval may be seen in abnormalities with potassium levels. Higher levels of potassium lead to progressive paralysis of the atria, lengthening the PR interval. Severe hypokalaemia may also cause this change. This is not usually seen with hypercalcaemia.

T wave inversion is seen in a number of problems, including hypokalaemia. It is not, however, typically associated with hypercalcaemia.

Torsades de pointes may rarely be seen in hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia. It is more commonly associated with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.

U waves are small deflections immediately following the T wave and usually in the same direction. They are most commonly seen with bradycardia and severe hypokalaemia. There is a rarer association with hypocalcaemia - not hypercalcaemia.

question_text: A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago is reviewed. What long term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
options_json: ["Nothing", "Direct acting oral anticoagulants", "Aspirin", "Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months", "Warfarin"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy:

Following the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines, aspirin is only normally given in addition if there is an additional indication, e.g. ischaemic heart disease.

Direct acting oral anticoagulants are not used in patients with a mechanical heart valve.

question_text: You are asked to review a 79-year-old man who reports new onset yellow tinting of his vision. He reports he is on numerous medications but cannot remember their names. His past medical history is significant for heart failure, benign prostatic hyperplasia and COPD. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this side effect?
options_json: ["Furosemide", "Ramipril", "Digoxin", "Sildenafil", "Salbutamol"]
explanation_text:
Digoxin may cause yellow-green vision

Due to its narrow therapeutic range, digoxin has a high risk of causing toxicity in patients. A characteristic feature of toxicity is xanthopsia or yellow-tinted vision.

Sildenafil can cause blue-tinted vision or cyanopsia.

question_text:
A 42-year-old woman has 8 months of dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, and intermittent haemoptysis. She also has occasional orthopnoea and lower limb swelling.

She has a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur. Her radial pulse is irregular, and an ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P-waves. On echocardiography, the affected valve’s area is reduced, but still mobile, and the left atrium is enlarged.

Which option is the best definitive step in her management?
options_json: ["Monitor with regular echocardiograms", "Monitor with regular echocardiograms and start anticoagulation", "Refer for percutaneous valve commissurotomy", "Refer for surgical valve replacement", "Refer for transcatheter valve replacement"]
explanation_text:
Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is the intervention of choice for severe mitral stenosis

The

referral for percutaneous valve commissurotomy

is correct. A low-pitched, rumbling, diastolic murmur is characteristic of mitral stenosis (MS). The dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, palpitations, and intermittent haemoptysis suggest pulmonary congestion due to elevated left atrial pressure. The ECG findings are also in keeping with atrial fibrillation (AF), which is commonly associated with MS due to left atrial enlargement. Since this patient has symptomatic MS, definitive treatment is indicated. Since they still have mitral valve mobility, they are a candidate for percutaneous valve commissurotomy. This is the most appropriate treatment as it is less invasive than open surgery and is associated with quicker recovery times.

Monitoring with regular echocardiograms

is incorrect as this patient is symptomatic, due to the presence of dyspnoea, haemoptysis, orthopnoea, and palpitations. This indicates the need for definitive intervention, which would likely be via percutaneous valve commissurotomy due to their retained valve mobility. If this patient were to have no or very mild symptoms, then echocardiography would be appropriate. However, since she has AF, this would warrant anticoagulation as well to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.

Monitoring with regular echocardiograms and starting anticoagulation

is incorrect as this patient’s dyspnoea, orthopnoea, palpitations, and haemoptysis indicate symptomatic mitral stenosis, which warrants definitive treatment. If this patient had no or minimal symptoms that do not significantly impair daily activities, then this option could be considered to monitor progression. However, doing so at this stage would risk further deterioration in this patient.

The

referral for surgical valve replacement

is incorrect. Surgery would be appropriate if percutaneous valve commissurotomy were not feasible, such as heavily calcified valves with very little motility, or if percutaneous valve commissurotomy had failed. This patient’s mitral valve is still mobile, suggesting it is amenable to percutaneous valve commissurotomy. Surgery is also more invasive and carries higher risks of complications, such as infection and bleeding, along with longer recovery times. Hence, this step may be premature at this stage.

The

referral for transcatheter valve replacement

is incorrect as this is not routinely performed first-line in people with symptomatic mitral stenosis. Instead, it is more likely to be used in aortic stenosis, which presents with an ejection systolic murmur and features like exertional chest pain and pre-syncope or syncope, which are not seen here. For mitral valve pathology, transcatheter valve replacements may instead be performed for mitral valve regurgitation or its associated disorders, such as mitral valve annular calcification or mixed valve disease.

question_text:
You get bleeped in the middle of your night shift to talk to a worried father whose daughter has been admitted with cyanosis. He tells you that they were aware she has had a murmur since birth, but it has only been the last few days in which she has had symptoms. You believe that this is a case of Eisenmenger's syndrome.

What is the medical definition of Eisenmenger's syndrome?
options_json: ["The reversal of a right-to-left shunt", "An audible ventricular septal defect", "Presence of a ventricular septal defect alongside an atrial septal defect", "The reversal of a left-to-right shunt", "All four of the following: overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect"]
answer_text: The reversal of a left-to-right shunt
explanation_text:
Eisenmenger's syndrome - the reversal of a left-to-right shunt

Eisenmenger's syndrome is the reversal of left-to-right shunt associated with ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus.

question_text: A 74-year-old man with symptomatic aortic stenosis is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. He is otherwise fit and well and keen for intervention if possible. What type of intervention is he most likely to be offered?
options_json: ["Annual echocardiography, intervention when valve gradient > 75 mmHg", "Aortic bypass graft", "Bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement", "Balloon valvuloplasty", "Mechanical aortic valve replacement"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - mechanical valves last longer and tend to be given to younger patients

The correct answer is

Bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement

. This patient with symptomatic aortic stenosis who is fit for surgery would most likely be offered a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. According to UK guidelines, this intervention is recommended for patients aged >65 years or younger patients not wishing to take lifelong anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic valves have the advantage of not requiring long-term anticoagulation, unlike mechanical valves, and are generally preferred in older patients due to their better hemodynamic properties and lower risk of thromboembolic complications.

The option

Annual echocardiography, intervention when valve gradient > 75 mmHg

is incorrect as it represents watchful waiting rather than an actual intervention. While regular monitoring via echocardiography may be appropriate in asymptomatic patients or those unfit for surgery, this patient has symptomatic aortic stenosis and is keen for intervention.

Aortic bypass graft

is also incorrect. This procedure involves bypassing the obstructed section of the aorta but does not address the issue at its source - the stenotic valve. It's used primarily in cases of aortic coarctation or dissection, not aortic stenosis.

The option

Balloon valvuloplasty

is incorrect because while it can provide temporary relief from symptoms in some cases, it's generally reserved for patients who are too high-risk for surgical intervention or as a bridge to definitive treatment such as valve replacement. Balloon valvuloplasty has been largely replaced by transcatheter methods due to higher rates of restenosis and complication.

Finally,

Mechanical aortic valve replacement

is less likely to be offered in this case because it requires lifelong anticoagulation which can increase bleeding risks and necessitate regular monitoring. Mechanical valves are typically offered to younger patients (<65 years) who have longer life expectancy and therefore more at risk of bioprosthetic valve degeneration.

question_text: A 67-year-old diabetic gentleman who recently underwent aortic valve replacement presented with a fever, raised inflammatory markers and deranged renal function. Which one of the following organisms contribute to the highest rate of mortality in patients with his condition?
options_json: ["Enterococci", "Streptococci", "Staphylococci", "Pseudomonas", "HACEK Organisms"]
explanation_text:
Staphylococci is the leading organism contributing to mortality in infective endocarditis

Staph aureus followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci are two of the most common organisms causing infective endocarditis.

Enterococci - Belongs to the bowel organisms group and contributes to only 15% of mortality.

Streptococci - Only contribute to around 5% of mortality.

Pseudomonas - Rare cause of endocarditis, occurs when infected water enters the bloodstream.

HACEK Organisms - Lives on dental gums and are more common in intravenous drug users.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department after collapsing while playing football. Witnesses report that he suddenly collapsed without any preceding symptoms. There was no seizure activity, and he regained consciousness within minutes. He has no significant medical history but mentions that his father died suddenly at the age of 32.

On examination, his vitals are stable, and no abnormalities are noted. A resting ECG reveals a coved ST-segment elevation in V1-V3 with a right bundle branch block pattern.

What myocardial defect is most likely responsible for this condition?
options_json: ["Connexin gap junction proteins", "Potassium ion channel proteins", "Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase proteins", "Sodium ion channel proteins", "Voltage-gated calcium channels"]
explanation_text:
Brugada syndrome is due to a mutation of the myocardial sodium ion channel protein

This case is consistent with Brugada syndrome due to key clinical features, including a young man collapsing during exercise, a family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age, and characteristic ECG findings showing coved ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V3. Brugada syndrome is caused by mutations in myocardial

sodium ion channel proteins

, particularly the SCN5A gene, which impair sodium ion flow and disrupt cardiac action potentials. SCN5A is the most common gene mutation in Brugada syndrome, accounting for about 20-30% of all cases of Brugada syndrome. These abnormalities predispose to life-threatening arrhythmias, such as polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, which are common triggers of sudden cardiac events in affected individuals. Identifying this genetic defect is crucial for diagnosis and risk stratification.

Connexin proteins

form gap junctions that facilitate electrical coupling between cardiac cells, ensuring coordinated electrical conduction. Defects in connexins play a role in the pathophysiology of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), where disrupted gap junctions contribute to electrical instability and ventricular arrhythmias. However, connexin abnormalities are not implicated in Brugada syndrome. This patient’s family history of sudden cardiac death and specific ECG findings are consistent with Brugada syndrome, which is associated with sodium ion channel dysfunction rather than gap junction abnormalities. Sodium channel mutations, particularly in the SCN5A gene, lead to characteristic changes in cardiac excitability and conduction, distinguishing the condition from connexin-related pathologies like ARVC.

Potassium ion channels

regulate repolarisation during cardiac action potentials and are associated with conditions such as long QT syndrome. Mutations in potassium channels typically lead to delayed repolarisation and prolonged QT intervals, which differ from the coved ST-segment elevation and arrhythmias seen in Brugada syndrome. Potassium ion channel abnormalities do not explain this patient’s sudden collapse or characteristic ECG features.

Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase

(SERCA) proteins regulate calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, critical for cardiac muscle relaxation. Defects in SERCA are associated with heart failure and certain cardiomyopathies rather than Brugada syndrome. This patient’s clinical presentation and ECG findings do not indicate a disorder of calcium handling but are indicative of sodium ion channel protein dysfunction.

Voltage-gated calcium channels

are involved in calcium influx during cardiac action potentials and are critical for myocardial contraction and excitation-contraction coupling. While calcium channel abnormalities can lead to arrhythmias, they are typically implicated in conditions like Timothy syndrome rather than Brugada syndrome. This patient’s presentation and ECG findings align with Brugada syndrome, which is due to sodium channel dysfunction, not calcium channel defects.

question_text: A 24-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant presents with pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. She has noticed some pain in her left calf for the past 3 days and on examination she has clinical signs consistent with a left calf deep vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate investigation?
options_json: ["D-dimer", "Compression duplex Doppler", "Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography", "Venogram", "Ventilation-perfusion scan"]

question_text: A 70-year-old woman is prescribed bumetanide for congestive cardiac failure. Where is the site of action of bumetanide?
options_json: ["Descending loop of Henle", "Macula densa", "Ascending loop of Henle", "Distal collecting duct", "Proximal collecting duct"]
explanation_text:
Furosemide - inhibits the Na-K-Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

Bumetanide, like furosemide, is a loop diuretic.

question_text:
You review a 51-year-old hypertensive patient who you started on 2.5mg of ramipril one month ago. He is complaining of a tickly cough since starting the medication which is keeping him awake at night. However, is blood pressure is now within normal limits.

What should you advise him?
options_json: ["The cough is unlikely to be caused by the ramipril, continue the medication and review in a month", "The cough should settle within the next month, continue the medication and review in a month", "Stop the ramipril and prescribe a different ACE-inhibitor", "Stop the ramipril and prescribe 5mg amlodipine", "Stop the ramipril and prescribe candesartan"]
answer_text: Stop the ramipril and prescribe candesartan
explanation_text:
Angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used where ACE inhibitors are not tolerated

ACE inhibitors are commonly associated with a dry, persistent cough. A cough is unlikely to settle without stopping the ACE-inhibitor and prescribing a different class of drug. For a patient under 55 who is intolerant to an ACE-inhibitor the next step would be to offer an angiotensin 2 receptor blocker (ARB), eg candesartan.

question_text: A 51-year-old man presents four weeks after being discharged from hospital. He had been admitted with chest pain and thrombolysed for a myocardial infarction. This morning he developed marked tongue and facial swelling. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
options_json: ["Atorvastatin", "Isosorbide mononitrate", "Atenolol", "Aspirin", "Ramipril"]

question_text: Which one of the following statements regarding warfarin is correct?
options_json: ["Warfarin can be used when breast-feeding", "Hypothyroidism may develop in a small minority of patients", "Aortic prosthetic valves generally require a higher INR than mitral valves", "The target INR following a pulmonary embolism is 3.5", "All patients with an INR of greater than 6.0 should be given vitamin K"]
answer_text: Warfarin can be used when breast-feeding

question_text:
A 45-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. On arrival, he is minimally responsive with a Glasgow coma score of 4. His partner states that he is usually fit and well but had an aortic valve replacement 8 years ago.

Based on the type of valve replacement this patient likely received, what medication will he be taking?
options_json: ["Aspirin", "Direct acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC)", "Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH)", "No medication indicated", "Warfarin"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - mechanical valves last longer and tend to be given to younger patients

The correct answer is

warfarin.

Given this patient's young age, he likely received a mechanical valve replacement. This is because mechanical heart valves are less prone to structural degradation than biological valves, and so tend to last for a longer period of time. The only anticoagulant treatment currently licensed for mechanical valve replacements is warfarin, hence this is the correct answer.

Aspirin

is incorrect. This may be given as long-term following biological valve replacements but is not used for mechanical valves.

Direct acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC)

is incorrect. DOACs are not licenced for use in patients following mechanical valve replacement. They are generally reserved for stroke prophylaxis in patients with atrial fibrillation, and treatment of venous thromboembolism.

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH)

is incorrect. LMWH is not approved for use following mechanical valve replacements. Due to the increased risk of valve thrombosis, it is felt that LMWH may not provide adequate anticoagulation to prevent clot formation. In addition to this, LMWH requires administration through daily subcutaneous injection. This is less convenient for patients than taking a tablet. It is important to note that patients are often started on LMWH in the post-operative period following mechanical valve replacement whilst they are 'bridged' to warfarin. Once the INR is therapeutic, LMWH is stopped and warfarin is continued long-term.

No medication indicated

is incorrect. Mechanical heart valves have higher thrombogenicity compared to natural or biological valves, and thus require anticoagulation to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.

question_text: Your review a 41-year-old woman. Four months ago she developed a deep vein thrombosis and was warfarinised with a target INR of 2.5. She has presented with a swollen, tender left calf and a Doppler scan confirms a further deep vein thrombosis. Her INR has been above 2.0 for the past three months. You organise some investigations to exclude an underlying prothrombotic condition. What should happen regarding her anticoagulation?
options_json: ["Switch to treatment dose low-molecular weight heparin", "Continue on warfarin, continue with INR target of 2.5", "Add aspirin 75 mg od", "Continue on warfarin, increase INR target to 3.0", "Continue on warfarin, increase INR target to 3.5"]
answer_text: Continue on warfarin, increase INR target to 3.5

question_text:
After sending several invitations, 62-year-old Mr Bentley attends the surgery for his medication review. He has not been into the surgery for nearly two years. He explains he works away during the week so finds it difficult to attend appointments. His medications are allopurinol 200mg, candesartan 8mg, indapamide 2.5mg, omeprazole 20mg and salbutamol inhaler as required.

His blood pressure, which you repeat a couple of times, is 166/95mmHg. He says he does remember to take his medications nearly every day, so you suggest starting him on another medication to lower his blood pressure.

Which class of antihypertensive medication should be added next, according to NICE?
options_json: ["Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor", "Beta-blocker", "Calcium channel blocker", "Loop diuretic", "Spironolactone"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor and a thiazide diuretic - add a calcium channel blocker

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.  Incorrect as the patient is already on candesartan - an angiotensin II receptor blocker - which should not be combined with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

Beta-blocker.  This is a 4th-line option but this patient is on a salbutamol inhaler, suggesting he may have asthma, so it might be contraindicated.

Calcium channel blocker.  Correct, this patient is already on candesartan (an angiotensin II receptor blocker) and indapamide (a thiazide-like diuretic), so the third-line treatment is a calcium channel blocker, such as amlodipine.

Loop diuretic.  Incorrect, loop diuretics (for example furosemide) are not a routine treatment for hypertension.

Spironolactone.  This is a possible 4th-line option, as long as the potassium level is not greater than 4.5mmol/L.

question_text: A middle-aged woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with pleuritic chest pain ten days after having a hysterectomy. There is a clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism. What is the most common chest x-ray finding in patients with pulmonary embolism?
options_json: ["Right heart enlargement", "Normal", "Pleural effusion", "Linear atelectasis", "Dilatation of the pulmonary vessels proximal to the embolism"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary embolism - normal CXR

The vast majority of patients with a pulmonary embolism have a normal chest x-ray.

question_text:
A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a fall. He recently had a hip replacement and regularly takes atorvastatin, metformin, and dabigatran. CT imaging of the brain has revealed a subdural haematoma.

What antidote should be administered?
options_json: ["Andexanet alfa", "Eltrombopag", "Idarucizumab", "Phytomenadione", "Protamine"]
explanation_text:
Bleeding on dabigatran? Can use idarucizumab to reverse

Idarucizumab

is a monoclonal antibody that binds directly to dabigatran molecules with greater affinity than thrombin. Therefore, it is effective at binding and sequestering dabigatran and is the correct answer and is the only licensed option for this indication.

Andexanet alfa

is used for the reversal of apixaban or rivaroxaban. It binds and sequesters direct factor Xa inhibitors. Studies have shown it may also reverse anticoagulation activity from other factor Xa inhibitors, but it has not yet been licensed for these (e.g. edoxaban).

Eltrombopag

is used to treat refractory idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura or acquired severe aplastic anaemia. It stimulates megakaryopoiesis via the JAK/STAT signalling pathway. Dabigatran exerts its activity via thrombin, and so would not be reversed by Eltrombopag.

Phytomenadione

is vitamin K used for the reversal of warfarin, to replenish supplies of coagulation factors.

Protamine

is used to reverse heparin. It is a peptide that binds and sequesters heparin molecules.

question_text:
The arrest team attends a crash call. Cardiac arrest is confirmed and CPR is commenced.

On brief review of the notes, the patient is a 51-year-old man who was admitted with chest pain. He is awaiting CTPA for possible pulmonary embolism. His past medical history is significant for a previous DVT and PE last year, for which he completed a 6-month course of apixaban. Immediately before he arrested, the patient had complained of shortness of breath and observations had shown tachycardia, tachypnoea and hypoxia.

The defibrillator pads are attached and the monitor shows asystole.

How should the team proceed?
options_json: ["Administer 1mg adrenaline and continue chest compressions", "Administer 1mg adrenaline, 300mg amiodarone and continue chest compressions", "Administer 1mg adrenaline, continue chest compressions and administer thrombolysis", "Immediate defibrillation followed by chest compressions", "Stop CPR"]
answer_text: Administer 1mg adrenaline, continue chest compressions and administer thrombolysis
explanation_text:
Thrombolytic drugs should be considered during CPR if a PE is suspected

Administer 1mg adrenaline, continue chest compressions and administer thrombolysis

is correct. This patient's history is highly suggestive of a pulmonary embolism (PE) (previous PE, suggestive signs and symptoms) - this is a reversible cause of cardiac arrest and should be treated with thrombolysis whilst CPR is ongoing. They are in a non-shockable rhythm, so adrenaline should be administered every 3-5 minutes, high-quality chest compressions should continue, and thrombolysis should be given. Resuscitation in a patient having thrombolysis should then be extended. 60-90 minutes is the timeframe suggested by the UK Resuscitation Council. However, specific duration recommendations can vary and are often guided by clinical judgment rather than fixed timeframes. While thrombolysis can be considered in cases of cardiac arrest due to suspected massive PE, it is not universally accepted or routinely recommended without strong clinical suspicion (as in this case).

Administer 1mg adrenaline and continue chest compressions

is incorrect. This patient is in a non-shockable rhythm - adrenaline should be administered, and high-quality chest compression should be continued. The history is very suggestive of a pulmonary embolism as the cause of the cardiac arrest - in addition to the above management thrombolysis should also be administered.

Administer 1mg adrenaline, 300mg amiodarone and continue chest compressions

is incorrect. This patient is in a non-shockable rhythm, and so amiodarone is not indicated. This is only given in shockable rhythms after the 3rd shock. Additionally, the history is very suggestive of a pulmonary embolism as the cause of the cardiac arrest - thrombolysis should be administered.

Immediate defibrillation followed by chest compressions

is incorrect. This patient is in asystole, which is non-shockable. Adrenaline should be administered, chest compressions should be continued and, given the history suggestive of a PE, thrombolysis should be given.

Stop CPR

is incorrect. There is a potentially reversible cause of this cardiac arrest - the history is suggestive of PE as the cause. This cause should be treated with thrombolysis, and CPR should be continued for at least 60-90 minutes before decisions are made about stopping resuscitation.

question_text: A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the resus department after collapsing whilst shopping. The paramedics report she is hypotensive and tachycardia. Initial observations include a heart rate of 160 bpm and a blood pressure of 98 / 60 mmHg. A 12 lead ECG shows a broad complex tachycardia. Which one of the following features on the ECG would suggest a ventricular tachycardia rather than a supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction?
options_json: ["QRS < 160 ms", "A corrected QT interval of 420ms", "Atrioventricular dissociation", "Marked right axis deviation", "Heart rate of 160 bpm"]
explanation_text:
Atrioventricular dissociation suggests VT rather than SVT with aberrant conduction

The correct answer in this case is

Atrioventricular dissociation

. Atrioventricular (AV) dissociation is a key feature that helps differentiate ventricular tachycardia (VT) from supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with aberrant conduction. In AV dissociation, the atria and ventricles are beating independently of each other, which is a characteristic finding in VT. This occurs because the ventricular rate in VT is faster than the sinus rate, causing the atrial impulses to be unable to conduct through the AV node.

QRS < 160 ms

: A QRS duration of less than 160 ms does not necessarily indicate VT or SVT with aberrant conduction. In fact, a broader QRS complex (typically >120 ms) is more suggestive of VT, as it indicates that the electrical impulse is originating from within the ventricles rather than from the atria or AV node.

A corrected QT interval of 420ms

: The corrected QT interval (QTc) represents the time between the start of ventricular depolarization and completion of repolarization, taking into account heart rate variability. A normal QTc interval ranges between 350-450ms for males and 360-460ms for females. A QTc interval of 420ms falls within this normal range and does not provide any specific information about whether the patient has VT or SVT with aberrant conduction.

Marked right axis deviation

: While right axis deviation can be seen in some cases of VT, it is not a definitive feature that differentiates VT from SVT with aberrant conduction. Right axis deviation can occur due to various causes such as right ventricular hypertrophy or chronic lung disease, making it a non-specific finding in this context.

Heart rate of 160 bpm

: A heart rate of 160 bpm is consistent with tachycardia, but it does not provide any information about the origin of the tachycardia (i.e., whether it is ventricular or supraventricular). Both VT and SVT can present with similarly elevated heart rates, so this option does not help differentiate between the two conditions.

In summary,

atrioventricular dissociation

is the most specific ECG feature that suggests ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction in this clinical scenario.

Given her presentation what changes would you expect to see on an ECG?
options_json: ["Q-waves", "Delta waves", "Saddle ST-elevation", "Sinus tachycardia", "J-waves"]
explanation_text:
J-waves are associated with hypothermia

This question is asking about an 82-year-old lady presenting with hypothermia and asking for ECG changes you would expect to see. Therefore the correct answer is J-waves. These are small bumps at the end of the QRS complex.

Q-waves are associated with a previous myocardial infarction
Delta waves are associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome
Saddle ST elevation is associated with pericarditis
Sinus tachycardia would not be expected as patients with hypothermia are often bradycardic

question_text:
A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is admitted to the hospital with a deep vein thrombosis and started on unfractionated heparin. Five days later, he develops new onset pain and pallor in his left leg, and a subsequent ultrasound confirms new arterial thrombosis.

His left leg is cool and mottled, and distal pulses are diminished. Petechiae and purpura are present on his arms and legs.


Hb	150 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	70 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	8.3 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

Which option is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options_json: ["Antibodies against factor Xa", "Antibodies against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa", "Antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complex", "Antibodies against the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor", "Antibodies against β2-glycoprotein I"]
explanation_text:
Heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia - antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin

Antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complex

is the correct answer. This clinical scenario is indicative of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with thrombosis. Characteristic features include the development of new thrombosis following the commencement of unfractionated heparin, which is typical for HIT, pronounced thrombocytopenia, and the appearance of petechiae and purpura that may signify microvascular thrombosis or platelet consumption. Additionally, the onset occurring 5 days post-heparin initiation aligns with the expected timeline for HIT.

HIT arises when antibodies are directed against platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexed with heparin, leading to the formation of immune complexes that subsequently activate platelets. This results in a paradoxical prothrombotic state despite the presence of thrombocytopenia. The immediate discontinuation of heparin and commencement of an alternative anticoagulant therapy (e.g., direct thrombin inhibitors) are critical steps in management.

Antibodies against factor Xa

are an incorrect option as such antibodies are not linked with a recognised clinical syndrome akin to HIT. They do not account for the observed thrombocytopenia or thrombosis in this patient. Furthermore, if present, these antibodies would likely decrease coagulation rather than induce a prothrombotic state as seen in this case.

Antibodies against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

is also incorrect because these antibodies are associated with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), which typically manifests as isolated thrombocytopenia accompanied by bleeding rather than thrombosis. This pathophysiological mechanism does not correlate with the prothrombotic condition observed in HIT.

Antibodies against the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor

are an incorrect choice given there is no clinical syndrome identified with these antibodies. Instead, antiplatelet agents such as clopidogrel act by inhibiting this receptor to mitigate platelet aggregation. Should this be implicated, it would not result in a prothrombotic state as noted in this patient.

Antibodies against β2-glycoprotein I

are not correct either. These antibodies are associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), which can lead to thrombotic events and complications during pregnancy. While APS may precipitate a prothrombotic condition, it does not lead to significant thrombocytopenia nor does it involve immune-mediated activation of platelets characteristic of HIT.

question_text:

Which of the following drugs may reduce the action of adenosine?
options_json: ["Dipyridamole", "Bupivacaine", "Aminophylline", "Amiodarone", "Montelukast"]
explanation_text:
Aminophylline reduces the effect of adenosine

The answer is aminophylline. dipyridamole classically

enhances

the action. This is commonly remembered with the mnemonic DEAR. Bupivicaine (and other -caines) all also enhance the action of adenosine.

Amiodarone and montelukast are distractors, that have no notable effect.

question_text:
A new 60-year-old patient is seen in the anaesthetic outpatient clinic to undergo a pre-operative assessment prior to a surgical procedure. The patient has several co-morbidities, including cardiac issues which have required recent intervention.

As part of the workup, the patient has an ECG performed which shows a clear left bundle branch block. These changes appear new compared to a recent ECG performed by the patient's GP. The patient is asymptomatic, and the examination is normal.

When can these ECG changes be considered normal?
options_json: ["Following electrical cardioversion", "Following initiation of beta blocker", "Following mitral valve replacement", "Following pericardial effusion drainage", "Under no circumstances"]
explanation_text:
New LBBB is always pathological and never normal

Left bundle branch block (LBBB) is a cardiac conduction abnormality due to slow or absent conduction through the left bundle branch resulting in the left ventricle taking longer than normal to fully depolarise. It is seen on ECG as wide QRS complexes in the precordial leads with the complex normal entirely negative (QS morphology) in lead V1 and predominantly positive with a slow upstroke to the R-wave peak in the lateral leads. New LBBB is always pathological and therefore

under no circumstances

can be it considered normal. It may be a result of several conditions including myocardial infarction, hypertension, cardiomyopathy etc and as such the identification of new LBBB warrants further investigation.

Electric cardioversion

is a procedure aimed at converting an abnormally fast cardiac rhythm or cardiac arrhythmia back to a normal sinus rhythm. Synchronised cardioversion can be used in an acute or elective setting where a set amount of electricity is delivered to restore the normal electrical conduction system of the heart. It is commonly used for conditions such as fast atrial fibrillation or ventricular and supraventricular tachycardias. A patient's ECG following electric cardioversion should be sinus rhythm; pathological rhythms can indicate a failure of the procedure or cardiac damage/injury potential sustained as a result of the preceding arrhythmia; new LBBB following electric cardioversion is an indication of pathology and would require further investigation.

Beta blockers

are commenced mainly for blood pressure or arrhythmia control (e.g. in atrial fibrillation). As such, they can result in a slowing of a patient's cardiac rate and potentially the conversion of an arrhythmia to a sinus rhythm. Beta-blockers however should not affect the QRS complexes and therefore do not produce LBBB unless they result in some form of adverse effect.

Mitral valve replacement

(MVR) is the replacement of a diseased mitral valve, either due to regurgitation or stenosis, with a mechanical or tissue valve. Post MVR both significant (e.g. atrial fibrillation) and non-significant (e.g. decrease P wave duration, amplitude and PR interval) cardiac rate and rhythm changes can occur however changes in the QRS duration or axis are not associated with the procedure. LBBB is not associated with the procedure and should not be considered normal.

Pericardial effusion is the collection of fluid within the pericardial sac and can be due to several conditions including infection, inflammation or autoimmune. Although normally diagnosis via imaging (e.g. echo) there are common ECG changes associated with the condition including low QRS voltage, tachycardia and electrical alternans which are consecutive, normally-conducted QRS complexes that alternate in height.

Following pericardial effusion drainage

these ECG changes should improve/resolve. LBBB is not associated with pericardial effusion or its management and therefore should not be considered normal.

Examination of his cardiovascular system is unremarkable with a pulse of 72 bpm and a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanation_text:
If angina is not controlled with a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker should be added

NICE guidelines recommend adding a calcium channel blocker for angina which is not adequately controlled with beta-blocker monotherapy. Verapamil is contraindicated whilst taking a beta-blocker and diltiazem should be used with caution due to the risk of bradycardia.

question_text: A 54-year-old man with atypical chest pain is referred to cardiology. An exercise ECG shows non-specific ST and T wave changes. Following this an coronary angiogram is performed which demonstrates no evidence of atherosclerosis. A diagnosis of Prinzmetal's angina is suspected. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options_json: ["Nicorandil", "Atenolol", "Felodipine", "Fluoxetine", "Isosorbide mononitrate"]
explanation_text:
Prinzmetal angina - treatment = dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker

Start felodipine

is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient with suspected Prinzmetal’s (variant) angina. This condition is caused by transient coronary artery vasospasm, often in the absence of fixed atherosclerotic disease, as confirmed by this patient’s normal coronary angiogram. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as felodipine, amlodipine, or nifedipine, are recommended as first-line agents in UK practice because they directly relax vascular smooth muscle, preventing and relieving vasospasm. They are effective in reducing the frequency and severity of anginal episodes and are usually given as long-acting preparations. NICE guidance for angina and European Society of Cardiology recommendations for vasospastic angina both support the use of calcium channel blockers as initial therapy, with long-acting nitrates reserved as add-on treatment if symptoms persist.

Start nicorandil

is not the most appropriate first-line choice here. Nicorandil has both nitrate-like and potassium channel-opening effects, and can be used for angina, but it is generally reserved for patients whose symptoms are not controlled with first-line agents or who cannot tolerate them. It is not the drug of choice for initial management of vasospastic angina.

Start atenolol

is contraindicated in Prinzmetal’s angina. Beta-blockers, particularly non-selective ones, can exacerbate coronary vasospasm by causing unopposed alpha-adrenergic-mediated vasoconstriction. Even cardioselective agents like atenolol are avoided in this condition.

Start fluoxetine

is not relevant to this presentation. Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used to treat depression and certain anxiety disorders. It has no role in the treatment of angina or coronary vasospasm.

Start isosorbide mononitrate

is a reasonable option for vasospastic angina but is usually used as an adjunct to calcium channel blockers rather than as initial monotherapy. Long-acting nitrates reduce preload and dilate coronary vessels, helping to prevent spasm, but tolerance can develop with continuous use, so they are often introduced later in the treatment pathway if CCB monotherapy is insufficient.

question_text: Which one of the following diuretics works by inhibiting a transmembrane cotransporter protein?
options_json: ["Indapamide", "Eplerenone", "Furosemide", "Amiloride", "Mannitol"]
explanation_text:
Furosemide - inhibits the Na-K-Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

The correct answer is

Furosemide

. Furosemide works by inhibiting the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This results in a decrease in reabsorption of sodium, potassium and chloride ions, which leads to an increase in urine output (diuresis). It's typically used for acute pulmonary oedema and oedematous states associated with heart failure.

Indapamide

is incorrect as it is a thiazide-like diuretic that primarily works by inhibiting the sodium-chloride symporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule. This results in decreased reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions, leading to increased urine output. Indapamide is often used for hypertension and oedema due to mild heart failure.

Eplerenone

is also incorrect because it does not inhibit any transmembrane cotransporter protein. Instead, Eplerenone acts as a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist blocking aldosterone-mediated sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion at the level of collecting ducts. It's mainly used for heart failure after myocardial infarction and hypertension.

Amiloride

is another incorrect option because it doesn't inhibit a transmembrane cotransporter protein either. Amiloride works by blocking epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) on the luminal side of principal cells in collecting ducts, resulting in decreased reabsorption of sodium ions and increased excretion of potassium ions. It's typically used with other diuretics to prevent hypokalemia.

Finally,

Mannitol

is incorrect as well since it doesn't inhibit any transmembrane cotransporter proteins. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that increases osmolarity within renal tubules, preventing water reabsorption and thus increasing urine output. It's mainly used for cerebral oedema or to increase urine production in cases of acute kidney injury.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with palpitations and pre-syncope. He has no past medical history.

Observations:


Heart rate 82 beats per minute
Blood pressure 131/74 mmHg
Respiratory rate 18/minute
Oxygen saturations 97% on room air

The examination is unremarkable.

An ECG demonstrates T wave inversion and an epsilon wave in leads V1-V3.


NT-proBNP	182 pg/ml	(<400)

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the expected pathological finding in this condition?
options_json: ["Apical biventricular ballooning", "Asymmetric hypertrophy of the left ventricle with septal thickening", "No gross anatomic findings", "Non-caseating granulomata", "Right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue"]
answer_text: Right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue
explanation_text:
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is characterised by right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue

Right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue

is correct. The patient presents with palpitations, pre-syncope and ECG findings of T wave inversion and epsilon waves in V1-V3. This suggests arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVD) as the diagnosis. This is characterised by the right ventricular myocardium being replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue.

Apical biventricular ballooning

is incorrect. This suggests a diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Typically, patients with this condition present with chest pain and symptoms suggestive of heart failure and it can mimic myocardial infarction. The NT-proBNP level is often grossly elevated.

Asymmetric hypertrophy of the left ventricle with septal thickening

is incorrect. This is suggestive of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. You can get T wave inversion in the chest leads in HOCM but there will not be epsilon waves, which are more specific for AVRD.

Non-caseating granulomata

is incorrect. This may suggest cardiac sarcoidosis. This can plausibly cause palpitations and pre-syncope. However, this is likely to cause a restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy if present and therefore would likely cause some abnormal examination findings i.e. JVP abnormalities or evidence of heart failure. Additionally, epsilon waves are not characteristic.

No gross anatomic findings

is incorrect. This might be the case if the patient had a channelopathy such as Brugada syndrome. This could also present with pre-syncope. The ECG findings of Brugada syndrome are coved-shaped ST elevation in V1-V2.

question_text:
A 35-year-old woman is referred to cardiology with worsening exertional dyspnoea and occasional haemoptysis. She emigrated from Bangladesh 10 years ago and recalls having 'fever and joint pains' as a child. On examination, she has a malar flush, low-volume pulse, and a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex with presystolic accentuation. Echocardiogram shows mitral valve area of 0.8 cm² with mobile leaflets, moderate left atrial enlargement, and mean gradient of 12 mmHg.

What is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Balloon aortic valvuloplasty", "Medical therapy with diuretics and beta-blockers", "Mitral valve replacement", "Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy", "Surgical mitral commissurotomy"]
explanation_text:
Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is the intervention of choice for severe mitral stenosis

Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy

is the intervention of choice for this patient with severe symptomatic mitral stenosis (MS) who has favorable valve morphology. The echocardiogram shows a mitral valve area of 0.8 cm² (severe MS is defined as <1.0 cm²) with mobile leaflets, which is a key favorable characteristic for percutaneous intervention. The patient's symptoms of exertional dyspnoea and haemoptysis are classic for MS, and her history of childhood fever and joint pains in Bangladesh strongly suggests rheumatic fever, the most common cause of MS worldwide. Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy (PMC) is less invasive than surgery, has lower morbidity, and provides excellent outcomes in appropriately selected patients. The presence of mobile leaflets without significant calcification or subvalvular disease makes her an ideal candidate for PMC according to UK and European guidelines.

Balloon aortic valvuloplasty

is inappropriate as this patient has mitral, not aortic valve disease. The clinical findings (mid-diastolic murmur at the apex with presystolic accentuation) and echocardiographic findings clearly indicate mitral stenosis. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is generally reserved for temporary relief in severe aortic stenosis when definitive treatment must be delayed or as a bridge to more definitive therapy.

Medical therapy with diuretics and beta-blockers

alone is insufficient for severe symptomatic MS. While these medications may temporarily improve symptoms by reducing pulmonary congestion and controlling heart rate, they do not address the mechanical obstruction at the mitral valve. Medical therapy is appropriate for asymptomatic patients or as an adjunct to interventional treatment, but not as sole therapy for symptomatic severe MS with favorable valve morphology.

Mitral valve replacement

would be excessive for this patient who has mobile valve leaflets suitable for commissurotomy. Valve replacement carries higher perioperative risks and long-term complications including anticoagulation requirements (for mechanical valves) or eventual deterioration (for bioprosthetic valves). It is generally reserved for patients with heavily calcified, immobile valves or significant subvalvular disease not amenable to commissurotomy.

Surgical mitral commissurotomy

is a reasonable alternative but is more invasive than percutaneous commissurotomy. In patients with favorable valve morphology (mobile, non-calcified leaflets without significant subvalvular fusion), percutaneous commissurotomy offers similar hemodynamic results with lower morbidity, shorter hospital stay, and quicker recovery. Surgical commissurotomy would be preferred if there were contraindications to percutaneous approach such as left atrial thrombus or significant mitral regurgitation.

question_text: A 43-year-old man who is known to have Wolff-Parkinson White syndrome presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations. He has no other significant history of note. The palpitations started around 4 hours ago and are not associated with chest pain or shortness of breath. On examination blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg and the chest is clear on auscultation. An ECG show atrial fibrillation at a rate of 154 bpm. Of the following options, what is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Adenosine", "Flecainide", "Verapamil", "Digoxin", "Sotalol"]

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of nicorandil?
options_json: ["Fast-sodium channel antagonist", "Nitric oxide reductase inhibitor", "Acts on the If ion current in the sinoatrial node", "Potassium-channel activator", "Glutathione S-transferase inhibitor"]
explanation_text:
Nicorandil is a potassium channel activator

The correct answer is

Potassium-channel activator

. Nicorandil is a vasodilatory drug that acts as both a nitrate and a non-selective potassium channel activator. It opens up ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the smooth muscle of coronary and peripheral blood vessels, leading to hyperpolarisation and relaxation. This results in an increase in blood flow to the myocardium (heart muscle) and a reduction of the heart's workload, thus alleviating angina symptoms.

The option

Fast-sodium channel antagonist

is incorrect. Fast sodium channels are involved in the rapid depolarisation phase of action potentials, particularly in excitable tissues like nerves and muscles. Blocking these channels can have antiarrhythmic effects, but this is not how nicorandil works.

Nitric oxide reductase inhibitor

is also incorrect. Nitric oxide reductase isn't a target for nicorandil. While it does have nitrate-like effects (resulting from its nitro group), this doesn't involve inhibiting nitric oxide reductase - rather it donates nitric oxide which acts on guanylate cyclase to increase levels of cyclic GMP, causing smooth muscle relaxation.

The answer choice

Acts on the If ion current in the sinoatrial node

is not accurate either. The I

f

(funny) current plays a key role in the automaticity of pacemaker cells in the heart, particularly those in the sinoatrial node. Drugs that act on this current can affect heart rate, but nicorandil does not work this way; its primary effect is on vascular smooth muscle cells rather than cardiac pacemaker cells.

Lastly,

Glutathione S-transferase inhibitor

is incorrect as well. Glutathione S-transferases are enzymes involved in detoxification processes within cells by conjugating substances with glutathione. Inhibition of these enzymes isn't related to the mechanism of action of nicorandil.

question_text: A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion. On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78 / min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur. Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?
options_json: ["Atrial septal defect", "Mitral stenosis", "Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy", "Aortic regurgitation", "Mitral regurgitation"]
explanation_text:
Aortic regurgitation - early diastolic murmur, high-pitched and 'blowing' in character

The correct answer is

Aortic regurgitation

. An early diastolic murmur is characteristic of aortic regurgitation, which occurs when the aortic valve does not close properly, allowing blood to flow back into the left ventricle during diastole. This can be due to various causes such as degeneration of the valve, endocarditis, or aortic root dilation. The murmur is best heard at the left sternal edge in the second intercostal space with the patient sitting up and leaning forward.

Atrial septal defect

is incorrect because this condition typically presents with a systolic ejection murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. An atrial septal defect is a congenital heart defect where there is an opening between the atria, leading to the shunting of blood from left to right. This results in increased pulmonary blood flow and volume overload on the right side of the heart.

Mitral stenosis

is also incorrect as it presents with a mid-diastolic murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. Mitral stenosis occurs when the mitral valve narrows and obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole. This can be caused by rheumatic heart disease or other less common etiologies such as congenital abnormalities or infective endocarditis.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

(HOCM) is not associated with an early diastolic murmur either. HOCM presents with a harsh systolic ejection murmur that increases in intensity during the Valsalva manoeuvre or standing up quickly from a squatting position. This condition involves hypertrophy of the interventricular septum, which can obstruct blood flow out of the left ventricle during systole.

Finally,

Mitral regurgitation

is an incorrect option as it presents with a pansystolic murmur rather than an early diastolic murmur. Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve does not close properly during systole, allowing blood to flow back into the left atrium. This can be caused by various factors such as degeneration of the valve, rheumatic heart disease, or mitral valve prolapse.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman presents to a rapid access neurology clinic five days after a self-resolving episode of weakness and sensory disturbance. She is diagnosed as having had a transient ischaemic attack and is started on combined antiplatelets including modified-release dipyridamole.

Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this medication?
options_json: ["A direct and highly selective factor Xa inhibitor", "A non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor that decreases cellular uptake of adenosine", "An irreversible inhibitor of the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes", "A direct-acting P2Y12-receptor antagonist", "A prodrug that selectively inhibits the binding of adenosine diphosphate to its platelet P2Y12 receptor"]
answer_text: A non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor that decreases cellular uptake of adenosine
explanation_text:
Dipyridamole is a non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor and decreases cellular uptake of adenosine

The correct answer is that dipyridamole is a non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor that decreases cellular uptake of adenosine.

Apixaban is a direct and highly selective factor Xa inhibitor.

Dipyridamole has both antiplatelet and vasodilating properties and is thought to inhibit the uptake of adenosine (a potent inhibitor of platelet activation and aggregation) into blood and vascular cells. Dipyridamole may also inhibit the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate.

Aspirin causes irreversible inhibition of the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes which blocks the formation of thromboxane A2 in platelets. This reduces platelet aggregation.

Ticagrelor directly blocks P2Y12-receptors, which are important in the activation of platelets.

Clopidogrel is a prodrug, one of whose metabolites inhibits the binding of ADP to its platelet P2Y12 receptor. Therefore ADP is unable to activate the glycoprotein GPIIb/IIIa complex which inhibits platelet aggregation.

question_text:
A 64-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. He has a history of stable angina, for which he currently takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and isosorbide mononitrate. Despite this, he continues to experience chest pain on exertion.

After further discussion, the cardiologist decides to offer the patient a trial of nicorandil. He explains the side effect profile of the drug to the patient, including its ability to cause ulceration in the gastrointestinal tract.

Where might this ulceration occur?
options_json: ["Anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract", "Lower gastrointestinal tract", "Mouth and oesophagus", "Stomach and duodenum", "Upper gastrointestinal tract"]
explanation_text:
Nicorandil may cause ulceration anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract

The correct answer is anywhere along the tract. Nicorandil is known to cause ulceration of the gastrointestinal tract, although this is not as common as its other side effects - dizziness, nausea, vomiting and headache. This ulceration may occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract.

For this reason, the other options are incorrect, as they all specify specific regions of the tract.

question_text: A 47-year-old lady with a family history of sudden cardiac death developed palpitations while visiting a relative in the emergency department. When attached to a cardiac monitor her heart rate was 164/min and the rhythm strip showed a broad complex tachycardia. Which antiarrhythmic may precipitate ventricular fibrillation (VF) if used in such circumstances?
options_json: ["Verapamil", "Amiodarone", "Procainamide", "Lidocaine", "Flecainide"]
explanation_text:
Patients with VT should not be prescribed verapamil

Verapamil should not be used in patients with Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) as they are class IV antiarrhythmic which only acts on nodal tissue and significantly increase the risk of ventricular fibrillation.

Amiodarone, Procainamide and Lidocaine - All can be used to treat VT.

Flecainide - Has a limited use in certain types of VT.

question_text:
A 38-year-old with no past medical history is referred to the clinic after an abnormal ECG finding is identified as part of a preoperative workup. Long QT syndrome is identified on repeat ECGs.

On further questioning, the patient reports his father had a heart condition identified in his 20s, although he is unsure of the specific diagnosis, and he has experienced previous episodes of syncope following exertion.

The patient is started on a beta-blocker and a plan to insert an implantable cardioverter defibrillator is made.

A loss of what function is associated with this patient's condition?
options_json: ["AV node", "Calcium channels", "Potassium channels", "SA node", "Sodium channels"]
explanation_text:
Long QT syndrome - usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels

A prolonged QT interval can result from certain drugs, electrolyte imbalance and congenital conditions such as long QT syndrome (LQTS). The condition is associated with a delayed repolarisation of the ventricles and can result in fatal dysrhythmias. The commonest variants of LQTS are usually caused by a defect in the alpha subunit of the slow delay rectifier

potassium channels

.

AV node

dysfunctions or blocks can result from several conditions including fibrosis, sclerosis and drugs however they result in PR-interval changes (i.e. prolonged) and do not affect the QT interval.

There are multiple

calcium channels

involved in both the electrical and mechanical functions of the heart. Mutations of these channels can result in cardiac dysrhythmia syndromes such as Brugada and early repolarisation syndrome but they are not associated with LQTS.

Dysfunction of the

SA node

can result from several different conditions but it is not associated with LQTS and is normally identified via abnormalities with the P-waves.

Dysfunction of

sodium channels

can be associated with certain cardiac conditions including those resulting in prolong QT syndromes however a loss of function of these channels is far less likely in LQTS when compared to potassium channels.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man has presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, severe abdominal pain and fresh rectal bleeding. He also reports a number of painful mouth ulcers in the past few weeks.

He has a history of angina pectoris and was recently switched to a new anti-anginal medication due to troublesome side-effects with other drug classes, but cannot remember the name. His other medications include aspirin and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.

His vital signs are as follows: temperature 38.3ºC, pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 112/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

Abdominal examination reveals a markedly tender left iliac fossa with localised peritonism. Subsequent imaging and endoscopy confirm the diagnosis as a perforated ulcer in the sigmoid colon.

Which drug is likely to account for this acute presentation?
options_json: ["Bisoprolol", "Diltiazem", "Isosorbide mononitrate", "Nicorandil", "Ranolazine"]
explanation_text:
Nicorandil may cause ulceration anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract

Nicorandil is a second-line drug treatment for angina pectoris if first-line drugs (beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers) are contraindicated or not tolerated.

However, it has been associated with gastrointestinal ulceration, which can occur in different locations in the same patient, ranging from aphthous ulcers in the mouth down to anal ulcers.

These ulcers can develop at any time after initiating the drug and may be refractory to treatment. If they develop, nicorandil should be rapidly and permanently discontinued.

Ulceration can lead to further complications such as perforation, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, fistula or abscess formation. Patients with existing diverticular disease may be at particular risk of fistula formation or bowel perforation when taking nicorandil.

Bisoprolol (a beta-blocker) can be associated with gastrointestinal disturbances (such as nausea, constipation and diarrhoea), but an acute severe complication as described in this scenario is highly improbable.

Diltiazem (a calcium-channel blocker) tends to cause different gastrointestinal and mucosal side-effects such as dyspepsia, constipation and gingival hyperplasia. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding is not reported in the product literature.

Isosorbide mononitrate is not commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, besides mild nausea.

Erosive duodenitis is listed as a rare side-effect of ranolazine treatment, but this description of gastrointestinal ulceration occurring in both the oral mucosa as well as the colon is much more likely due to nicorandil.
