question_text:
A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left-sided tearing chest pain. He has a past medical history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. He is on regular amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day and drinks 3-4 beers each night. He lives alone and is usually independent of all activities of daily living.

His observations are heart rate 101 beats per minute, blood pressure 182/97 mmHg, respiratory rate 21/minute, oxygen saturations 97% on room air and he is apyrexial.

On clinical examination, chest auscultation demonstrates equal air entry bilaterally. Both heart sounds are audible and there is a diastolic murmur audible at the lower left sternal edge in end-expiration. Abdominal and neurological examinations are normal.

An ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia.

A plain radiograph of the chest is normal.

Blood tests:


Hb	137 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	333 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.1 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.1 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	6 mg/L	(< 5)
Troponin	8ng/L	(<14)


CT angiography of the chest is organized, which demonstrates an intimal flap proximal to the brachiocephalic vessels.

Given the diagnosis, what is the appropriate management?
options_json: ["Control blood pressure (IV glyceryl trinitrate)", "Control blood pressure (IV glyceryl trinitrate) + surgery", "Control blood pressure (IV labetalol)", "Control blood pressure (IV labetalol) + surgery", "Surgery"]
explanation_text:
Aortic dissection

Control blood pressure (IV labetalol) + surgery is correct. This patient has a type A aortic dissection. This is evidenced clinically by the development of the murmur of aortic regurgitation and more definitively by CT evidence of a dissection flap proximal to the brachiocephalic vessels indicating the involvement of the ascending aorta. The patient, therefore, needs surgery in addition to blood pressure control. Furthermore, the first line anti-hypertensive in this scenario is IV labetalol. Beta-blockers should be given first before vasodilators, as the catecholamine release due to vasodilatation can cause an increase in shear forces by increasing ventricular contraction. This can result in the extension of dissection or rupture.

Control blood pressure (IV glyceryl trinitrate) is incorrect. This patient has a type A dissection and therefore needs both surgery and blood pressure control. Vasodilators can be trialled as a second-line option for blood pressure control after beta-blockers have been used. However, as previously mentioned above, the vasodilation associated with this class of medication can increase the risk of extension of the dissection or rupture and they are therefore not the first choice.

Control blood pressure (IV glyceryl trinitrate) + surgery is incorrect. IV glyceryl trinitrate can be used for additional blood pressure control but only after IV labetalol has been trialled.

Control blood pressure (IV labetalol) is incorrect. Type A dissections (i.e. those that involve the ascending aorta) need surgery in addition to blood pressure control. If this was a type B dissection (descending aorta), this would be correct.

Surgery is incorrect. While this patient needs surgery, he also needs tight blood pressure control in the interim.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man is brought into the emergency department after being involved in a road traffic accident. He has reduced consciousness and is intubated by paramedics prior to arrival. A CT head reveals an intracranial bleed.

An arterial line is placed. The waveform shows two systolic peaks and a normal dicrotic notch.

What is the most likely cause for this finding?
options_json: ["Aortic dissection type B", "Cardiac tamponade", "Left ventricular failure", "Mixed aortic valve disease", "Patent ductus arteriosus"]
explanation_text:
Bisferiens pulse - mixed aortic valve disease

The arterial waveform represents the pressure in the artery. Usually, there is a systolic upstroke followed by a downstroke. The dicrotic notch is a small deflection in the downstroke as a result of the closure of the aortic valve. This patient has two systolic peaks to their pulse, known as a bisferiens pulse. This pulse is most associated with

mixed aortic valve disease

.

Aortic dissection if proximal can interfere with the aortic valve, such as causing regurgitation. However, an

aortic dissection type B

affects the distal aorta, so this answer is not correct.

Cardiac tamponade

may cause pulsus paradoxicus, where there is a drop in systolic pressure during inspiration.

Left ventricular failure

may cause pulsus alternans. This is when there is a regular alternation of the force of the arterial pulse.

Patent ductus arteriosus

is typically associated with a collapsing pulse as there is a flow of blood through the defect into the pulmonary vasculature leading to reduced flow through the systemic circulation.

question_text:
You are the ST1 working on cardiology. The nurses have asked you to review a 56-year-old man complaining of dyspnoea which is limiting his mobility.

He presented three days ago with an inferior STEMI. He was loaded with 300mg aspirin and 180mg ticagrelor before being taken to the cath-lab where he underwent primary PCI with a drug eluting stent for a sub-total occlusion of the right coronary artery. He was subsequently commenced on aspirin 100mg od, ticagrelor 90mg bd, atorvastatin 80mg od, bisoprolol 5mg od and perindopril 5mg od. His echo demonstrated only mildly reduced LV systolic function (LVEF 50%).

His vital signs are stable with a blood pressure 125/70mmHg, heart rate 64bpm, oxygen saturations 98% on room air and temperature 36.5ºC. Examination reveals dual heart sounds with no murmurs and his chest is clear on auscultation with no wheeze. JVP is +2cm and there is no peripheral oedema. His calves are soft and non tender. A Chest X-Ray shows mild atelectasis at the bases. His bloods are unremarkable. His ecg shows normal sinus rhythm with inferior q waves.

With respect to his dyspnoea, what would be the next best step in his management?
options_json: ["Cease bisoprolol", "Substitute ticagrelor for clopidogrel", "Order an urgent repeat echo", "Cease ticagrelor and continue aspirin only", "Start antibiotics for a nosocomial pneumonia"]

question_text:
A 56-year-old Caucasian man attends for his annual health check at the GP surgery. He has a past medical history of hypertension and gout. He is well and does not complain of any headache, visual changes or chest symptoms. His clinic blood pressure is 165/95mmHg. He is currently on allopurinol and the maximum dose of perindopril.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step management for his hypertension?
options_json: ["Calcium channel blocker", "Thiazide-like diuretic", "Aldosterone antagonist", "Angiotensin receptor blocker", "Loop diuretic"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor - add a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

The correct answer is 'calcium channel blocker'. This patient's hypertension remains uncontrolled despite the maximum dose of an ACE inhibitor. In this instance, NICE recommends adding a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic. A thiazide-like diuretic is contraindicated due to the history of gout, therefore calcium channel blocker is the more appropriate management for this patient.

Aldosterone antagonist is indicated in the subsequent management steps of hypertension. It may be an option if the patient is intolerant to calcium channel blocker or remains hypertensive despite optimal treatment.

Angiotensin receptor blocker and ACE inhibitor should not be used in combination for the management of hypertension due to the risk of acute kidney injury. Hence the answer 'angiotensin receptor blocker' is incorrect.

Loop diuretics may be indicated in resistant hypertension where blood pressure remains uncontrolled with the optimal or maximum tolerated doses of four drugs. This patient is currently only on one drug. Hence, this answer is incorrect.

question_text: A 61-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease is prescribed simvastatin. What is the most appropriate blood test monitoring?
options_json: ["LFTs + creatinine kinase at baseline, 1-3 months and at intervals of 6 months for 1 year", "LFTs at baseline and every 3 months for first year", "Routine blood tests not recommended", "LFTs at baseline and annually", "LFTs at baseline, 3 months and 12 months"]
answer_text: LFTs at baseline, 3 months and 12 months

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman with no past medical history presents to the cardiology clinic following a fainting episode. She tells you she has had several of these in recent months and has also developed gradually worsening exertional breathlessness, which now limits her from even walking up a flight of stairs. An ECG and 24-hour tape have revealed right axis deviation only.

On examination, she has normal heart and breath sounds, with mild peripheral oedema and a right ventricular heave.

Following confirmatory investigations, what test will be most important in deciding how this patient is managed?
options_json: ["CT coronary angiogram", "CT pulmonary angiogram", "High-resolution CT thorax", "Transthoracic echo", "Vasodilator testing"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with negative response to vasodilator testing should be treated with prostacyclin analogues, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors. Often combination therapy is required

Vasodilator testing

is the cornerstone test in determining the management of pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH), which is the condition demonstrated in this case. It usually affects women between 30-60 years and is characterised by exertional breathlessness and signs of right heart failure (in this case, right axis deviation suggests right ventricular hypertrophy, and peripheral oedema suggests right heart failure). The test involves giving vasodilator agents (e.g. nitric oxide, epoprostenol) and looking for a reduction in pulmonary arterial pressure (usually, a 10mmHg drop is classified as positive). 10-15% of PAH patients will be positive in this test, which suggests a likely benefit from calcium channel blockers in managing the condition. Those with a negative test are treated with prostacyclin analogs, endothelin receptor antagonists or phosphodiesterase inhibitors.

CT coronary angiogram

is recommended in stable chest pain to examine the patency of the coronary arteries and characterise any atheromatous disease, allowing risk stratification. It is not used to guide the management of PAH.

CT pulmonary angiogram

could be used to assess for multiple chronic pulmonary emboli, which could cause the breathlessness and right heart failure seen in this patient. The lack of history or risk factors for VTE and the patient's young age points away from this as a likely diagnosis.

High-resolution CT thorax

is an imaging technique whereby very thin (around 1mm) slices of the lungs can be viewed. This gives excellent detail and is used in the assessment of interstitial lung disease, cystic lung disease, and bronchiectasis. It is of no benefit in the assessment of PAH patients.

Transthoracic echo

this investigation would likely be performed on this patient to assess their degree of right heart failure. However, it will not influence the management of her underlying condition, which is PAH. It is also likely that successful treatment of the PAH will result in a reduction in right heart failure, and thus the findings of a transthoracic echo may not warrant specific management anyway.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week.

Her past medical history is significant for an aortic valve replacement 2 years previously.

What antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended prior to this procedure?
options_json: ["Chlorhexidine mouthwash", "General oral hygiene advice", "Intravenous co-amoxiclav", "Oral amoxicillin", "Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin"]
explanation_text:
Antibiotic prohylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis is not routinely recommended in the UK for dental and other procedures

General oral hygiene advice

is correct. NICE guidance from 2008 recommended that patients undergoing dental procedures are not routinely offered infective endocarditis prophylaxis. This includes those deemed 'at risk' due to cardiac conditions such as valve replacement or structural heart disease.

Chlorhexidine mouthwash

is incorrect. The BNF page 'antibacterials, use for prophylaxis' states that chlorhexidine mouthwash is not recommended for the prevention of infective endocarditis.

Intravenous co-amoxiclav, oral amoxicillin and oral phenoxymethylpenicillin

are all incorrect. NICE does not routinely recommend antibiotics before dental procedures as infective endocarditis prophylaxis. This is because there is no clear association between dental procedures and infective endocarditis. Antibiotic prophylaxis, therefore, exposes patients to side effects without evidence substantiating their use.

question_text: You are called to the obstetric ward to see a woman who is fitting. She is 34-weeks pregnant and currently an inpatient for the treatment of severe pre-eclampsia. The anaesthetist has secured the airway and is giving 100% oxygen. What is the most appropriate next step?
options_json: ["IV calcium gluconate", "IV labetalol", "IV methyldopa", "IV lorazepam", "IV magnesium sulphate"]
explanation_text:
Eclampsia - give magnesium sulphate first-line

The most appropriate next step in this scenario is to administer

IV magnesium sulphate

. Magnesium sulphate is the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures in pregnant women, according to UK guidelines. It has been shown to be effective in preventing recurrent seizures and reducing maternal morbidity. In severe pre-eclampsia, magnesium sulphate can also be used as a prophylactic measure to prevent the development of eclampsia.

IV calcium gluconate

would not be the correct choice in this situation. Calcium gluconate is typically used as an antidote for hypermagnesemia or hypocalcemia, neither of which is indicated in this case. The patient's primary issue is an eclamptic seizure, and calcium gluconate does not have any anticonvulsant properties.

IV labetalol

and

IV methyldopa

are both antihypertensive medications that can be used to manage hypertension in pregnancy. However, they do not address the immediate concern of the patient's ongoing seizure. While controlling blood pressure is important in managing pre-eclampsia, it should not take precedence over treating the active seizure with an appropriate anticonvulsant medication like magnesium sulphate.

IV lorazepam

, a benzodiazepine, might seem like a reasonable choice since it has anticonvulsant properties and is often used to treat status epilepticus. However, it is not the first-line treatment for eclamptic seizures during pregnancy due to its potential adverse effects on both mother and fetus. Magnesium sulphate remains the preferred treatment option because it specifically targets the underlying pathophysiology of eclampsia while providing neuroprotection for both mother and baby.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presented with worsening central chest pain radiating down his left arm associated with difficulty in breathing and nausea. He was diagnosed with an inferior myocardial infarction. Following his recovery in the coronary care unit with serial electrocardiography monitoring, he found to be in a complete heart block. He denies any symptoms from this.

What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options_json: ["Atropine", "Isoprenaline", "Conservative monitoring", "Pacemaker insertion", "Temporary pacing"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block following an inferior MI is NOT an indication for pacing, unlike with an anterior MI

Complete (third-degree atrioventricular) heart blocks are commonly seen with inferior wall myocardial infarctions and usually resolve in hours-to-days after revascularization. Right coronary artery occlusion is usually implicated as it vascularises the AV nodal artery. Bradyarrhythmias and AV block in the context of inferior STEMI are usually transient (lasting hours to days), respond well to atropine and do not require permanent or temporary pacing especially if haemodynamically stable and asymptomatic.

Isoprenaline is used to maintain heart rate temporarily in patients with heart block only until a temporary or permanent pacemaker can be fitted. It is usually given as an intravenous infusion under ECG control but would not be indicated in this case.

Atropine aims to improve conduction through the AVN by reducing vagal tone via receptor blockade. It is often indicated in symptomatic patients and would not be needed in this case.

Permanent pacing is the routine treatment for irreversible third-degree and advanced second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block but in cases such as this where the blockage is transient permanent pacemakers are rarely required.

Temporary pacing may be required if the patient was symptomatic or with haemodynamically unstable bradycardia, not responding to atropine.

question_text: You are an SHO working at district general hospital in Cornwall. A 56-year-old man presents to the emergency department with crushing central chest pain that started 30 minutes ago. His ECG demonstrates ST elevation in the anterior leads and he is treated for an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). So far he has been given aspirin, clopidogrel, low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and his chest pain has significantly improved with sublingual GTN and IV morphine + metoclopramide. There is no cath-lab on site and and the nearest percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) centre in Truro is approximately 2 ½ hours away. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options_json: ["Transfer to PCI centre", "Give bivalirudin", "Start infusion of unfractionated heparin and transfer to PCI centre", "Give alteplase", "Give ticagrelor"]
explanation_text:
STEMI management: fibrinolysis should be offered within 12 hours of onset of symptoms if primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes

In the management of STEMI fibrinolysis with a drug such as alteplase should be offered if primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given.

This problem is most often encountered when a patient initially presents to a district general hospital that lacks a PCI centre. Ambulances are generally directed to PCI centres in cases of chest pain and this has reduced the frequency with which this occurs.

If a repeat ECG at 90 minutes does not show resolution of ST elevation the patient will require transfer to a PCI centre regardless.

1- This is inappropriate. The transfer time is over 120 minutes from when fibrinolysis could be given. This would therefore be an unacceptable delay.

2- This is a direct thrombin inhibitor. It has a role in STEMI management but would not address the main issue which is the need for PCI/fibrinolysis.

3- Though sometimes used in STEMI again, fibrinolysis or PCI are needed. Additionally, the patient has already had LMWH so this would not make a difference

4- Correct! As the time to PCI is more than 120 minutes from the time at which fibrinolysis (with alteplase in this example) could be given, fibrinolysis should be offered.

5. This is an antagonist of the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor like clopidogrel, which has already been given. Adding ticagrelor would therefore confer no benefit in this scenario

question_text:
A 54-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. He has a diagnosis of stable angina and was started on isosorbide mononitrate 20mg twice daily at his last appointment. His other medication includes low dose aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, nifedipine and glyceryl trinitrate sublingual spray as required.

During the consultation he complains that at first his isosorbide mononitrate helped control his angina, however shortly after starting the medication he noticed his anginal symptoms began to recur.

What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's symptoms?
options_json: ["Add ivabradine", "Increase dose of isosorbide mononitrate", "Make no changes to current medication", "Recommend asymmetric dosing regimen of isosorbide mononitrate", "Switch nifedipine to verapamil"]
answer_text: Recommend asymmetric dosing regimen of isosorbide mononitrate
explanation_text:
Asymmetric dosing regimes should be used for standard-release ISMN to prevent nitrate tolerance

Recommend asymmetric dosing regimen of isosorbide mononitrate

is correct. An asymmetric dosing regimen would involve taking the morning dose as normal, then taking the second dose in the early afternoon. This allows a sufficiently long nitrate-free period and helps reduce tolerance.

Add ivabradine

is incorrect. Adding a third anti-anginal medication is recommended if calcium channel blocker therapy and beta-blocker therapy is insufficient. In this instance, however, the patient has already had a third anti-anginal medication added and rather than adding another drug it is more pragmatic to try and increase the benefit obtained from this.

Increase dose of isosorbide mononitrate

is incorrect. Rather than increase dosages and therefore potential side effect burden, it may be possible to try and increase the benefit obtained from the isosorbide mononitrate by reducing the tolerance to this medication using asymmetric dosing.

Make no changes to current medication

is incorrect. The patient is experiencing a recurrence of their anginal symptoms and should not be left in pain.

Switch nifedipine to verapamil

is incorrect. If beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are to be used in combination therapy, NICE recommends using a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Verapamil and beta-blocker combination is not advised due to the risk of heart block.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman suffered from sudden onset central crushing chest pain. Her electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation. Troponin is slightly raised. She was rushed for an emergency invasive angiogram but this revealed slight wall irregularities with no luminal obstruction. Subsequently, cardiovascular MR (CMR) showed an apical ballooning of the myocardium resembling an octopus pot.

She did not have any significant past medical history. There is a family history of premature coronary artery disease. Her partner recently passed away of prostate cancer.

What is the most likely cause of the ST-segment elevation?
options_json: ["Coronary artery disease", "Takotsubo cardiomyopathy", "Left ventricular aneurysm", "Myocardial infarction", "Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy"]
explanation_text:
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a differential for ST-elevation in someone with no obstructive coronary artery disease

The differential diagnosis for ST-elevation:

myocardial infarction
pericarditis/myocarditis
normal variant - 'high take-off'
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Left ventricular aneurysm
Prinzmetal angina
Subarachnoid haemorrhage

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy also known as 'Broken heart syndrome' and 'Takotsubo apical ballooning syndrome' describes a cardiomyopathy induced by severe stressful triggers (e.g. emotional upset). It is commoner in women. In this scenario, we assume that the patient is in bereavement which precipitated the stress cardiomyopathy.

Takotsubo is a Japanese word that describes an octopus trap; this is used to describe the appearance of the heart on left ventriculogram, CMR or echocardiogram. This apical ballooning appearance occurs due to severe hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments with preservation of activity of the basal segments. In simple terms, the bottom of the heart  (the apex) does not contract and therefore appears to balloon out. However, the area closer to the top (the base) continues to contract (creating the neck of the octopus trap).

Myocardial infarction and coronary artery disease are incorrect as it has been ruled out by the invasive coronary angiogram. Besides, CMR would show regional wall motion irregularities in infarcted area.

Left ventricular aneurysm is a possible complication of myocardial infarction (MI). Given that there is no past medical history of MI, this is unlikely. Besides, left ventricular aneurysms would be clearly visible as a discreet dyskinetic area

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy would appear as asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior movement (SAM) of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve.

question_text: A 30-year-old female patient tells you that she is planning to become pregnant over the next year. You note from her records that she has a history of ventricular septal defect. Which one of the following would represent a contraindication to her becoming pregnant?
options_json: ["Aortic regurgitation", "Having a perimembranous rather than a muscular defect", "A previous episode of infective endocarditis", "Pulmonary hypertension", "A history of previous surgical repair"]
explanation_text:
Women with pulmonary hypertension should avoid becoming pregnant due to very high mortality levels

The correct answer is

Pulmonary hypertension

. Pulmonary hypertension is a contraindication to pregnancy because it significantly increases the risk of maternal morbidity and mortality. The physiological changes that occur during pregnancy, such as increased blood volume, heart rate, and cardiac output, can exacerbate pulmonary hypertension and lead to right-sided heart failure or sudden death. The European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend that women with pulmonary arterial hypertension should be counselled against becoming pregnant due to the high risk.

Aortic regurgitation

does not generally pose a significant risk in pregnancy unless it is severe. In most cases, mild to moderate aortic regurgitation can be managed conservatively throughout pregnancy. However, if the condition is severe or symptomatic, pre-pregnancy assessment and management by a cardiologist are necessary.

The location of the ventricular septal defect (VSD), whether it is

perimembranous rather than muscular

, does not significantly impact the risks associated with pregnancy. Both types of defects can be well tolerated during pregnancy if they are small and hemodynamically insignificant.

A

previous episode of infective endocarditis

does increase the risk for recurrence during pregnancy but does not represent an absolute contraindication. Prophylactic measures may be taken according to local guidelines when there is a history of infective endocarditis. Additionally, close monitoring by a multidisciplinary team involving obstetricians and cardiologists would be essential in managing these patients.

Lastly,

a history of previous surgical repair

of VSD does not contraindicate pregnancy. In fact, successful surgical repair often allows women with congenital heart disease to have safer pregnancies compared to those who have not had surgery. However, these women still require regular follow-up care and monitoring during their pregnancies by a specialist team.

He has had no recent episodes of severe chest pain and feels well today. Before starting the test his pulse is 84/min and blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg. Once the ETT has begun, which one of the following is the strongest indication for stopping the test?

question_text:
A 28-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of chest pain. He states that the pain is relieved by sitting forwards. He also has flu-like symptoms.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	144 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	162 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	14.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	66 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	14 mg/L	(< 5)
Troponin T	20 ng/l	(< 14)

What is the most specific ECG finding related to the likely underlying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Concave ST elevation", "Convex ST elevation", "PR depression", "PR prolongation", "PR shortening"]
explanation_text:
The most specific ECG finding in acute pericarditis is PR depression

PR depression

is correct. The clinical features are highly suggestive of acute pericarditis. The most specific ECG feature in this condition is PR depression. The mildly raised troponin is entirely consistent with this diagnosis. If the troponin were to be significantly elevated then a diagnosis of myocarditis would need to be considered.

Concave ST elevation

is incorrect. Although this finding is more sensitive to acute pericarditis compared to PR depression, it is a less specific finding. Other causes of this pattern include benign early repolarisation.

Convex ST elevation

is incorrect. Convex ST elevation is classically caused by an ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The character of the pain and the associated flu-like symptoms are more suggestive of acute pericarditis.

PR prolongation

is incorrect. First-degree heart block is not commonly associated with acute pericarditis.

PR shortening

is incorrect. A short PR interval is not associated with acute pericarditis. Conditions associated with PR shortening include Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and Lown-Ganong-Levine syndrome.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man is seen in the clinic after originally being referred with progressively increasing central chest pain but base level investigations, including ECGs and troponin level return within normal range.

The pain is exercise dependent with it occurring when the patient carries out activities such as climbing stairs and resolving on rest. As such the patient was started on atenolol 100mg OD along with a GTN spray and aspirin.

On review today the patient still reports symptoms of chest pain on exertion despite good compliance.

What alteration should be made to this patient's management?
options_json: ["Add diltiazem", "Add ivabradine", "Add modified-release nifedipine", "Add verapamil", "Titrate up atenolol"]
explanation_text:
If angina is not controlled with a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker should be added

This patient is suffering from symptoms in keeping with angina and has been correctly commenced on a beta-blocker along with aspirin and GTN spray as first-line therapy. As the patient is still experiencing symptoms, despite being on the maximum dose of a beta-blocker, a calcium channel blocker should be added. When used in combination with a beta-blocker a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker e.g.

modified-release nifedipine

should be used to improve symptom control whilst avoiding the risk of heart block dysrhythmias. A long-acting/modified-release version of the medication should ideally be used.

Diltiazem

may be commenced as monotherapy initially for patients presenting with angina however its use with beta-blockers should be avoided as this can lead to significant adverse effects on cardiac conduction, heart rate and contractility.

Ivabradine

is a pacemaker current or 'funny' current inhibitor that blocks the I

f

ion current present in the sinoatrial node. It can be used as a third agent if angina symptoms are not controlled with the combination of a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and beta-blocker.

Verapamil

again can be commenced as a monotherapy calcium-channel blocker in angina but should be avoided with beta-blockers as this can result in significant events including complete heart block.

This patient is already established on the maximum dose of atenolol and therefore

titrating up

the dose is not an option.

question_text: A 72-year-old man is prescribed a dipyridamole in addition to aspirin following an ischaemic stroke. What is the mechanism of action of dipyridamole?
options_json: ["Phosphodiesterase inhibitor", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor", "Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor", "Agonist of thromboxane synthase", "Irreversibly acetylating cyclooxygenase"]
explanation_text:
Dipyridamole is a non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor and decreases cellular uptake of adenosine

The correct answer is that dipyridamole acts as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor.

Phosphodiesterase inhibitor

is the primary mechanism through which dipyridamole exerts its antiplatelet effect. By inhibiting phosphodiesterase, dipyridamole prevents the breakdown of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) within platelets. Elevated levels of cAMP reduce platelet activation and aggregation. Additionally, dipyridamole blocks the cellular reuptake of adenosine, leading to increased extracellular adenosine levels, which further inhibits platelet function.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor

describes the mechanism of drugs like abciximab and tirofiban, which block the final common pathway of platelet aggregation by preventing fibrinogen binding to activated platelets. This is not how dipyridamole works.

Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor

is the mechanism of action for drugs like clopidogrel and ticagrelor, which are P2Y12 receptor antagonists. These medications prevent ADP-mediated platelet activation, but this is not the mechanism of dipyridamole.

Agonist of thromboxane synthase

is incorrect as this would promote platelet aggregation. Thromboxane A2 is a potent platelet activator, and its synthesis is actually targeted for inhibition in antiplatelet therapy, not activation.

Irreversibly acetylating cyclooxygenase

describes the mechanism of action of aspirin, which prevents the formation of thromboxane A2 by permanently inhibiting COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. While dipyridamole is often combined with aspirin for enhanced antiplatelet effect, this is not its mechanism of action.

question_text:
An 88-year-old man presents with heart palpitations. He has a past medical history of a myocardial infarction and heart failure. His daughter advises you that he has recurrent falls. He takes regular aspirin, ramipril, spironolactone, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin. Observations are as follows: heart rate 95 beats per minute, and blood pressure 155/85 mmHg.

An ECG and echocardiogram are performed:


ECG	Heart rate 95 beats per minute; irregularly irregular rhythm; absence of P waves


Echocardiogram	No valvular dysfunction. Left ventricular ejection fraction 62%

What long-term treatment is required?
options_json: ["Clopidogrel", "Edoxaban", "Low molecular weight heparin", "No treatment indicated", "Warfarin"]
explanation_text:
Risk of falls or old age alone is not sufficient reasoning to withhold anticoagulation

Edoxaban

is correct.  The ECG features confirm a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation.   The patient has a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 5. Therefore anticoagulation is required as a form of stroke prevention. The direct factors Xa inhibitors are now the first line for this purpose (e.g. edoxaban, apixaban or rivaroxaban).

Clopidogrel

is incorrect.  The patient requires anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet to reduce stroke risk.

Low molecular weight heparin

(LMWH) is incorrect. Several studies have shown that treatment with low molecular weight heparin increases the risk of hemorrhagic complications without significantly reducing the rates of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Furthermore, long-term use of LMWH can cause significant complications such as osteoporosis. In addition, daily injections have a negative effect on patients' quality of life. For all these reasons, LMWH is rarely used for long-term stroke prophylaxis.

No treatment indicated

is incorrect. Although his older age and recurrent falls will increase his bleeding risk, the significantly elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score confers a significant stroke risk. In these cases, it would be important to counsel the patient with regard to the risks and benefits of anticoagulation. In general, the balance tips towards anticoagulation since the risk of major haemorrhage is relatively low.

Warfarin

is incorrect. Warfarin has significant drug-drug, and drug-food interactions, a substantial increase in major haemorrhage (compared to DOACs) [1], and requires intensive monitoring. For all these reasons, warfarin is rarely used for stroke prevention unless the patient has a mechanical heart valve, severe mitral stenosis, or an absolute contraindication to DOACs (e.g. extreme body weight, or drug interaction). Previously warfarin may have been chosen over a DOAC in patients with substantial bleeding risk since warfarin had a highly effective reveal agent (prothrombin complex concentrate). However, DOACs now have a highly effective reversible agent (andexanet alfa) so are usually the agent of choice even in these situations. However, it is important to note that andexanet alfa is only licensed in life-threatening/uncontrolled bleeding for apixaban/rivaroxaban reversal. However, it can be considered off-license for edoxaban reversal. A more important consideration is the fact that warfarin has a much higher rate of spontaneous major haemorrhages (in particular intracerebral) compared to DOACs making DOACs the safer choice in the majority of cases.

References

[1] Y. Vinogradova, C. Coupland, T. Hill, J. Hippisley-Cox. Risks and benefits of direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in a real world setting: cohort study in primary care. BMJ. 2018; 362

question_text:
A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia complains of acute breathlessness one hour after a primary percutaneous intervention for an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. She was successfully revascularized and access was gained using a radial approach. She appeared well immediately post-procedure and a beside trans-thoracic echocardiogram demonstrated preserved left ventricular function.

On examination, she appears unwell. She is diaphoretic and clammy with a respiratory rate of 33/min, blood pressure of 80/42mmHg, heart rate of 111/minute, oxygen saturation of 96% on air and temperature of 36.2ºC. Chest auscultation demonstrates good air entry bilaterally. Cardiovascular examination demonstrates a regular pulse, elevated jugular venous pulse (JVP) and quiet heart sounds. She has cool extremities. There are no murmurs or peripheral oedema. There is no clinical evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the lower limbs.

What intervention is most likely to be life-saving?
options_json: ["Inotropic support", "Intravenous antibiotics", "Intravenous fluids", "Pericardiocentesis", "Thrombolysis"]
explanation_text:
Beck's triad of falling BP, rising JVP and muffled heart sound is characteristic of cardiac tamponade

Cardiogenic shock as a cause of hypotension is less likely as we have been told the patient was successfully revascularized and an echocardiogram post-procedure was normal. Inotropes may temporarily support a falling blood pressure but are not likely to be curative in this case.

Sepsis causing hypotension is characterized by pyrexia, bounding pulse and warm extremities in most cases. The jugular venous pulse will not be elevated. Therefore, intravenous antibiotics are the wrong answer.

Hypovolemia is not associated with an elevated jugular venous pulse and therefore intravenous fluids is not a correct answer. Additionally, radial access was used, making a retroperitoneal haematoma less likely.

Pericardiocentesis is the correct answer. The clinical features suggest Beck's triad of falling BP, rising JVP and muffled heart sounds indicating cardiac tamponade. This is a recognised complication of primary percutaneous intervention in myocardial infarction.

Thrombolysis is an incorrect answer.  While a massive pulmonary embolism could cause hypotension, elevated jugular venous pulse and tachycardia, the absence of hypoxia and clinical evidence of DVT make this less likely.

question_text:
A 57-year-old male is referred to the cardiology clinic with mild dyspnoea. He has a background medical history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, type two diabetes mellitus, and he has recently been diagnosed with a metastatic carcinoid tumour.

On examination, he has a harsh mid-ejection systolic murmur that is loudest on inspiration.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Aortic regurgitation", "Aortic stenosis", "Mitral stenosis", "Pulmonary stenosis", "Tricuspid regurgitation"]
explanation_text:
Pulmonary stenosis is louder on inspiration

Pulmonary stenosis is the correct answer. Pulmonary stenosis causes a harsh mid-ejection

systolic

murmur in the second intercostal space on the left sternal edge. It is loudest on

inspiration

. Additionally, it is associated with carcinoid heart disease (Hedinger syndrome).

Aortic regurgitation is an incorrect answer. Aortic regurgitation is inconsistent with the scenario above as it is not an ejection systolic murmur. Aortic regurgitation is a decrescendo early-

diastolic

blowing murmur. It is best heard in the third and fourth intercostal space on the left lower sternal border. It is loudest at end-expiration with the patient sitting up and leaning forward.

Aortic stenosis is an incorrect answer. Aortic stenosis causes a harsh crescendo - decrescendo ejection

systolic murmur

in the second intercostal space on the right sternal edge. However, it is louder on

expiration

as thus inconsistent with the scenario above.

Mitral stenosis is an incorrect answer. Mitral stenosis is inconsistent with the scenario above as it is not an ejection systolic murmur. Mitral stenosis is a low pitch, rumbling in character,

diastolic

murmur which is best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. It is associated with rheumatic fever.

Tricuspid regurgitation is an incorrect answer. Tricuspid regurgitation is inconsistent with the scenario above as it is not an ejection systolic murmur. It is a high pitched,

pansystolic

murmur that is best heard at the left lower sternal border.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology outpatient clinic after an incidental murmur was heard. He has well-controlled hypertension but is otherwise fit and well. He denies any chest pain, dyspnoea, or dizziness, and maintains an active lifestyle. On examination, he has a slow-rising pulse and a harsh ejection systolic murmur. An echocardiogram shows a calcified aortic valve with a mean pressure gradient of 45 mmHg and a preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Refer for aortic valve replacement", "Arrange 6-monthly echocardiogram review", "Arrange exercise stress testing", "Commence ramipril", "Refer for balloon aortic valvuloplasty"]
explanation_text:
Aortic stenosis management: AVR if symptomatic, otherwise cut-off is gradient of 40 mmHg

Refer for aortic valve replacement is the correct answer. This patient has severe aortic stenosis (AS) based on the echocardiographic finding of a mean pressure gradient >40 mmHg across the aortic valve. Although he is currently asymptomatic, UK (NICE) and European (ESC) guidelines recommend considering aortic valve replacement (AVR) for asymptomatic patients with severe AS. The rationale is that the natural history of severe AS is poor once symptoms develop, and intervention before the onset of symptoms or left ventricular (LV) dysfunction improves long-term outcomes. The risk of sudden cardiac death in asymptomatic patients with a gradient this high is significant and outweighs the procedural risk of AVR in an otherwise fit individual. The preserved LV function is a positive prognostic factor for a good outcome post-surgery. The decision between surgical AVR (SAVR) and transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) would be made by a multidisciplinary heart team based on his surgical risk, but the initial step is referral for consideration of valve replacement.

Arrange 6-monthly echocardiogram review is incorrect. This strategy, often termed 'watchful waiting', is appropriate for patients with moderate aortic stenosis or asymptomatic patients with severe AS who do not meet the criteria for intervention (e.g., mean gradient <40 mmHg, normal LV function, and no other high-risk features). Given this patient's mean gradient of 45 mmHg, he falls into a high-risk category where observation is no longer the safest option. Delaying intervention until symptoms appear could lead to irreversible myocardial damage and a significantly worse prognosis. The guidelines have shifted towards earlier intervention in such patients to prevent adverse events.

Arrange exercise stress testing is a plausible but incorrect option in this specific context. Exercise testing can be used in patients with asymptomatic severe AS to unmask 'occult' symptoms or to identify an abnormal blood pressure response to exercise, both of which are indications for AVR. However, its main utility is in patients where there is uncertainty about their symptomatic status or where the haemodynamic severity is borderline. In this case, the mean gradient of 45 mmHg is a clear marker of severe AS, which in itself is an indication for intervention according to current guidelines, regardless of the results of an exercise test. Therefore, proceeding directly to referral for AVR is the most appropriate and efficient management pathway.

Commence ramipril is incorrect and potentially dangerous. While ramipril is an ACE inhibitor used for hypertension and heart failure, its use in patients with severe AS is contraindicated. The primary haemodynamic problem in severe AS is a fixed outflow tract obstruction. Afterload-reducing agents like ACE inhibitors decrease systemic vascular resistance. In the presence of a fixed obstruction, this can lead to a critical drop in systemic blood pressure and coronary perfusion pressure, potentially causing profound hypotension, syncope, and myocardial ischaemia. While his hypertension needs management, a drug that does not cause significant vasodilation (e.g., a beta-blocker, used cautiously) would be safer, but treating the underlying valve lesion is the priority.

Refer for balloon aortic valvuloplasty is incorrect. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) is not a definitive treatment for calcific aortic stenosis in adults. It provides only temporary haemodynamic improvement and is associated with a high rate of restenosis (typically within 6-12 months) and significant procedural risk. Its role is now limited to being a 'bridge to decision' or 'bridge to surgery/TAVI' in haemodynamically unstable patients, or as a purely palliative measure for severe symptom relief in patients who are not candidates for any form of definitive valve replacement. This patient is stable in an outpatient setting and is a candidate for definitive treatment.

question_text: A 66-year-old man with no past medical history of note presents with central chest pain to the Emergency Department. An ECG shows ST elevation in the anterior leads. He is given aspirin and ticagrelor before going for a percutaneous coronary intervention. What is the mechanism of action of ticagrelor?
options_json: ["Inhibits ATP binding to its platelet receptor", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor", "Phosphodiesterase V inhibitor", "Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor", "Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor"]
answer_text: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor
explanation_text:
Ticagrelor has a similar mechanism of action to clopidogrel - inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors

The correct answer is

Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor

. Ticagrelor is an oral antiplatelet agent that works by inhibiting the binding of adenosine diphosphate (ADP) to its P2Y12 platelet receptor. This inhibition prevents platelet activation and aggregation, which is essential in the formation of blood clots. In patients with acute coronary syndromes, such as ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), ticagrelor is used along with aspirin to reduce the risk of further thrombotic events.

The first incorrect option,

Inhibits ATP binding to its platelet receptor

, is not the mechanism of action for ticagrelor. While both ADP and ATP are nucleotides involved in cellular energy metabolism, it is specifically the binding of ADP to its P2Y12 receptor on platelets that ticagrelor targets to inhibit platelet activation.

The second incorrect option,

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor

, refers to a different class of antiplatelet agents. These medications work by inhibiting the binding of fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on activated platelets, thereby preventing platelet aggregation. Examples of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors include abciximab and eptifibatide.

The third incorrect option,

Phosphodiesterase V inhibitor

, does not describe ticagrelor's mechanism of action either. Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors are primarily used for treating erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. They work by inhibiting the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), leading to smooth muscle relaxation and increased blood flow. Examples include sildenafil and tadalafil.

Lastly, the fourth incorrect option,

Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor

, is also not the mechanism of action for ticagrelor. Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitors are medications that inhibit various types of phosphodiesterases (PDEs) in the body. These drugs have a variety of uses, including bronchodilation for respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). An example of a non-selective PDE inhibitor is theophylline.

question_text: Your next patient is a 74-year-old woman who is known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her blood pressure has been borderline for a number of weeks now but you have decided she would benefit from treatment. Her latest blood pressure is 146/88 mmHg, HbA1c is 58 mmol/mol and her BMI is 25 kg/m^2. What is the most appropriate drug to prescribe?
options_json: ["Bisoprolol", "Bendroflumethiazide", "Amlodipine", "Ramipril", "Orlistat"]
explanation_text:
Hypertension in diabetics - ACE inhibitors/A2RBs are first-line regardless of age

The most appropriate drug to prescribe for this patient is

Ramipril

. This is because, according to the UK guidelines (NICE), an ACE inhibitor such as Ramipril is the first-line treatment for hypertension in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The reason behind this choice is that ACE inhibitors have been shown to reduce the risk of diabetic nephropathy and cardiovascular events in these patients.

Now let's discuss why the other options are not ideal:

Bisoprolol

is a beta-blocker, which can be used as a second-line treatment for hypertension if the first-line treatment is not effective or not tolerated. However, it should not be used as a first-line treatment in patients with type 2 diabetes because it may mask symptoms of hypoglycemia and has less evidence for reducing cardiovascular events compared to ACE inhibitors.

Bendroflumethiazide

is a thiazide diuretic that can be used as an alternative option for treating hypertension, but it's generally reserved for cases where other medications are contraindicated or not tolerated. In addition, its use may worsen glycemic control in diabetic patients due to its potential to cause hyperglycemia.

Amlodipine

is a calcium channel blocker that can be used as an alternative first-line treatment for hypertension when ACE inhibitors are contraindicated or not tolerated. However, in this case, there's no mention of any contraindications or intolerance to ACE inhibitors. Therefore, Ramipril remains the preferred choice due to its additional benefits in diabetic patients.

Finally,

Orlistat

is not a suitable option because it's an anti-obesity medication that works by inhibiting fat absorption from the gastrointestinal tract. It has no direct effect on blood pressure and would not address this patient's primary concern of hypertension.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man with a background history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with palpitations. The symptoms started suddenly, six hours prior to his attendance. There was no chest pain, dizziness or shortness of breath.

His observations were heart rate 163/min, blood pressure 155/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air and temperature 36.2ºC. On examination, his pulse was irregularly irregular. There was no clinical evidence of pulmonary oedema. His Glasgow coma scale was 15.

An ECG demonstrated atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response.

Despite treatment with IV fluids, IV metoprolol and IV digoxin, he remained tachycardic at 162 beats per minute.

Given the onset of symptoms was less than 48 hours ago, a decision was made to attempt chemical cardioversion with amiodarone. A loading dose is administered initially, followed by an infusion.

What pharmacological feature of amiodarone make a loading dose necessary?
options_json: ["Class III anti-arrhythmic activity", "Class Ia, II and IV anti-arrhythmic activity", "Renal excretion", "Long half-life", "Inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzyme family"]
explanation_text:
Amiodarone has a long half-life - it is highly lipophilic and widely absorbed by tissue, which reduces its bioavailability in serum. Therefore, a prolonged loading regime is required to achieve stable therapeutic levels

Class III anti-arrhythmic activity is the wrong answer. Amiodarone is a predominant class III anti-arrhythmic in the Vaughan-Williams classification but this is not the reason for the use of a loading dose.

Class Ia, II and IV anti-arrhythmic activity is incorrect. While amiodarone is predominantly a class III anti-arrhythmic, it does have numerous other effects, which are similar to class Ia, II and IV.

Amiodarone is not renally excreted and this is therefore incorrect. The major mechanism of excretion is hepatic.

Long half-life is correct. Drugs with a long half-life are eliminated from the body slowly and only need a low maintenance dose to maintain appropriate therapeutic concentrations. However, this means that in the absence of a higher initial dose, it would take a long time for these drugs to reach a steady-state concentration.

Inhibition of cytochrome P450 is incorrect. Amiodarone has this effect but it is not the reason to administer a loading dose.

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman presents to the cardiology clinic with frequent palpitations and episodes of dizziness on exertion. She has no prior medical history. Her father passed away at age 33 by sudden cardiac death.

Her 12-lead ECG at rest shows sinus rhythm with T wave inversion in V1-3, with a small positive deflection at the end of the QRS complexes in V1-3.

A 24-hour Holter monitor shows evidence of frequent premature ventricular complexes and runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia.

What is the most likely underlying pathological process?
options_json: ["Atrioventricular accessory pathway conduction", "Ectopic electrical foci in the pulmonary vein", "Prolongation of the ventricular action potential leading to long QT duration", "Replacement of right ventricular free wall myocardium with fibrous and fatty tissue", "Septal hypertrophy and disorganisation of muscle fiber arrangement"]
answer_text: Replacement of right ventricular free wall myocardium with fibrous and fatty tissue
explanation_text:
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is characterised by right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue

The question is alluding to an underlying diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). This is evidenced by multiple features that meet major diagnostic criteria named 'Task Force Criteria', such as her family history, ECG features and evidence of ventricular ectopy and associated tachyarrhythmia.

ARVC is a progressive myocardial disorder as described above which will usually cause ventricular tachyarrhythmia, and eventually right ventricular (and sometimes left ventricular) failure. Ultimately this patient should be considered for an implantable cardiac defibrillator and have first degree relatives clinically screened with genetic counselling.

The end-QRS abnormalities are called epsilon waves, which are seen in roughly 30-50% of patients. The only other major diagnostic feature missing from this question is right ventricular dysfunction evidenced on echocardiography.

Atrioventricular accessory pathway conduction

- is alluding to atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia as the underlying pathology. This would not be the cause of the ECG/Holter abnormalities. It is usually evidenced by delta waves with a short PR interval. Holter monitoring could show runs of narrow complex tachycardia.

Ectopic foci in the pulmonary vein

- is referring to the underlying mechanism of atrial fibrillation. Holter monitoring would likely reveal runs of irregularly irregular narrow complex tachycardia with no organised atrial activity.

Prolongation of the ventricular action potential leading to long QT duration

- is referring to the overall mechanism of long QT syndrome. This commonly presents as syncope, which classically occur during exercise or stress. It would not cause the ECG changes described, The most commonly associated arrhythmia caused is Torsades de Pointes.

Septal hypertrophy and disorganisation of muscle fibre arrangement

- is alluding to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. While it is usually asymptomatic, it typically causes exertional symptoms including dyspnoea, syncope, angina, palpitations. It fits very well with the first paragraph of the stem. Furthermore, there may be non-sustained VT on Holter monitoring. However, the resting ECG typically features left ventricular hypertrophy as opposed to the precordial changes described.

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman presents to the cardiology clinic with a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She was referred to the clinic after an ECHO demonstrated systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, with mitral regurgitation. An ECG showed sinus rhythm, with signs of LVH, and T-wave inversion in all leads beside aVR and V1. Physical examination was unremarkable besides prominent a-waves on inspecting the JVP.

Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following medications should be avoided in this patient?
options_json: ["Amiodarone", "Bisoprolol", "Loratadine", "Ramipril", "Verapamil"]
explanation_text:
ACE-inhibitors should be avoided in patients with HOCM

This woman likely has hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Ramipril will potentially worsen symptoms due to reducing preload, and therefore chamber size.

Amiodarone, bisoprolol and verapamil are often used in the treatment of HOCM.

Loratadine is not contraindicated.

Other drugs to avoid are nitrates and inotropes. Vasodilators increase the outflow tract gradient and cause a reflex tachycardia that further worsens ventricular diastolic function. Inotropic drugs worsen outflow tract obstruction, do not relieve the high end-diastolic pressure, and may induce arrhythmias.

question_text: Each one of the following is associated with right axis deviation on ECG, except:
options_json: ["Right ventricular hypertrophy", "Pulmonary embolism", "Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome with right-sided accessory pathway", "Chronic lung disease", "Left posterior hemiblock"]
answer_text: Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome with right-sided accessory pathway
explanation_text:
Left axis deviation - Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (right-sided accessory pathway)

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is associated with a short PR interval and a wide QRS complex with a slurred upstroke, termed a delta wave. Axis deviation depends on the position of the accessory pathway

question_text:
A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations that began during a night out. He reports no significant medical history but consumes 40-50 units of alcohol weekly and uses cocaine occasionally (1-2 times per month).

On examination, his pulse is irregularly irregular, although all other observations are within normal limits. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation (AF) with a heart rate of 80-90 beats per minute. An echocardiogram reveals no structural heart disease, and baseline blood tests are normal.

What is the most appropriate anticoagulation treatment to initiate?
options_json: ["6 months of warfarin and review", "Lifelong DOAC (direct oral anticoagulant)", "Lifelong aspirin", "Lifelong aspirin and clopidogrel", "No treatment required"]
explanation_text:
Young man with AF, no TIA or risk factors, no treatment is preferred to aspirin

No treatment required

is the correct answer as this patient’s CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 0, indicating a very low risk of stroke. This scoring system assesses stroke risk in patients with AF, and since this patient has no risk factors such as age over 65, diabetes, hypertension, or previous stroke/transient ischaemic attack, anticoagulation is not recommended. The patient’s presentation could be due to excessive alcohol intake or occasional cocaine use, making this a case of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. In such cases, cardioversion is unlikely to be suggested according to NICE guidelines, as the spontaneous resolution of AF is possible, especially if the trigger (alcohol or cocaine) is addressed. With regard to anticoagulation, the risks of bleeding would outweigh any potential benefits in this case.

6 months of warfarin and review

is incorrect because the patient’s CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 0, indicating no significant risk factors for stroke. Warfarin, an anticoagulant, may be considered for patients with a higher risk of stroke due to atrial fibrillation. In this case, the risk of bleeding from warfarin therapy would outweigh the minimal benefit of stroke prevention. Since the patient has no history of thromboembolic events or other risk factors, anticoagulation with warfarin is unnecessary and, therefore, would not be appropriate for short-term or long-term use. If anticoagulation were indicated, a DOAC would be the first choice. Warfarin is typically reserved only if DOACs are contraindicated or not tolerated, as per current guidelines.

Lifelong DOAC

is incorrect because the patient has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 0, meaning there are no significant risk factors for stroke. DOACs, like warfarin, are used to reduce stroke risk in atrial fibrillation patients with a higher risk profile. In this case, the patient’s risk of stroke is extremely low, and prescribing lifelong anticoagulation would expose him to unnecessary bleeding risks without providing substantial benefit.

Lifelong aspirin

is incorrect because aspirin is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, regardless of their CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. Studies have shown that aspirin provides minimal protection against stroke in atrial fibrillation and carries a significant risk of bleeding. The balance of risk versus benefit is unfavourable, particularly when the patient's stroke risk is extremely low, as in this case. If anticoagulation is indicated, DOACs are the preferred treatment, with aspirin no longer playing a role in AF management.

Lifelong aspirin and clopidogrel

are incorrect because this combination is not indicated for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. While both aspirin and clopidogrel are antiplatelet agents that can reduce the risk of thrombotic events, they do not provide adequate protection against stroke in atrial fibrillation. Furthermore, using both medications increases the risk of bleeding without a significant benefit in stroke prevention, making this approach inappropriate for this patient's clinical scenario.

question_text:
A 70-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for surgical aortic valve replacement using a bioprosthetic valve. She has no other significant comorbidities. She asks if she will need any long-term blood thinning medication after the surgery.

What is the most appropriate long-term anti-thrombotic medication for this patient?
options_json: ["Apixaban", "Clopidogrel", "Low-dose aspirin", "Warfarin", "Warfarin + low-dose aspirin"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy:

The most appropriate long-term anti-thrombotic medication for a 70-year-old woman who has had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement and no other significant co-morbidities is

low-dose aspirin

.

Bioprosthetic valves usually do not require long-term anticoagulation, unlike mechanical valves. However, low-dose aspirin is typically given for its antiplatelet effect to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.

Warfarin

may be given in addition to low-dose aspirin in the first few months after surgery depending on patient factors, but it is not typically required long-term for patients with bioprosthetic valves.

Apixaban and clopidogrel

are also not typically used in this context.

question_text:
A 79-year-old man is admitted with congestive cardiac failure. Bloods on admission show:


BNP	354 pg/ml

Which one of the following would result from elevated BNP levels?
options_json: ["Decreased sodium diuresis", "Vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries", "Inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system", "Vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels", "Increased sympathetic tone"]
explanation_text:
BNP - actions:

The correct answer is

Inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced by your heart and blood vessels. This peptide is secreted in response to changes in pressure inside the heart. These changes can occur with heart failure and other cardiac diseases. BNP promotes natriuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, thus helping to regulate blood pressure and fluid balance.

Decreased sodium diuresis

is incorrect because elevated levels of BNP actually increase sodium diuresis. BNP promotes the excretion of sodium (natriuresis), which helps decrease blood volume and thus reduce the workload on the heart.

Vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries

is also incorrect as BNP causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. The release of this hormone relaxes smooth muscle cells within vessel walls, causing dilation or increase in diameter that allows more blood flow through the vessels.

Vasoconstriction of the pulmonary vessels

is another incorrect option for similar reasons. Elevated levels of BNP would result in vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, allowing for increased blood flow and reduced pressure within these vessels.

Lastly,

Increased sympathetic tone

is not correct either. High levels of BNP do not lead directly to increased sympathetic activity; rather they work to counterbalance it by promoting vasodilation and reducing fluid volume - actions that are opposite to those brought about by sympathetic stimulation.

question_text:
A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and orthopnoea. He has a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease. His medications include aspirin, bisoprolol, ramipril and spironolactone. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol.

Observations:


Heart rate 99 beats per minute
Respiratory rate 24/minute
Oxygen saturations 92% on room air
Blood pressure 154/88 mmHg
Temperature 37C

Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles extending to the midzones. There are no murmurs. There is no peripheral oedema.

Based on the likely diagnosis, which of the following is an early sign of this condition?
options_json: ["Soft S1", "Absent S2", "Loud P2", "S3", "S4"]
explanation_text:
Gallop rhythm (S3) is an early sign of LVF

S3 is correct. The patient presents with shortness of breath and orthopnoea in association with bilateral crackles extending to the midzone with evidence of respiratory failure. On a background of ischaemic heart disease, this is likely caused by left ventricular failure. An S3 gallop rhythm is an early sign of left ventricular failure.

Absent S2 is incorrect. This is a sign of severe aortic stenosis. However, this sign will be present irrespective of whether or not this patient has developed heart failure signs and symptoms.

Loud P2 is incorrect. This is an early sign of pulmonary hypertension, which may cause right-sided heart failure. However, bilateral crackles on auscultation suggest left-sided heart failure on a background of ischaemic heart disease.

Soft S1 is incorrect. This is caused by a prolonged PR, severe mitral stenosis or mitral regurgitation. We are told there are no murmurs.

S4 is incorrect. This is an extra sound causes by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle. It is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and hypertension but not acute LVF.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine health check. During the consultation, his blood pressure is noted to be 152/86 mmHg. He is asymptomatic and examination is unremarkable. He has no significant past medical history except for mild arthritis of the knee, for which he takes paracetamol.

The blood pressure is repeated and is recorded as 155/82 mmHg.

What should be done next?
options_json: ["Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring", "Commence amlodipine", "Commence ramipril", "Recheck in clinic in one week", "Recheck later today with the nurse"]
explanation_text:
Hypertension - NICE now recommend ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to aid diagnosis

The correct answer is to

arrange ambulatory blood pressure monitoring

. Unless the blood pressure is extremely high and requires immediate treatment, NICE now recommends ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring (ABPM/HBPM), as this provides more reliable readings. In consultation, many patients experience white-coat hypertension and thus have higher-than-normal blood pressure readings. ABPM or HBPM avoids this by allowing the patient's blood pressure to be checked at home, away from the healthcare setting.

Commencing amlodipine

is inappropriate - NICE guidelines now recommend confirming a diagnosis of hypertension with ABPM/HBPM first.

Similarly,

commencing ramipril

would be inappropriate. Furthermore, ramipril would be used in patients under 55 and not of African/Caribbean descent - if this patient were to start treatment now, amlodipine would be more appropriate.

Arranging for the patient to come back in one week

for a recheck is not ideal - the same problem may occur with regards to white-coat hypertension. ABPM would be preferable to this.

Rechecking again now

would serve no purpose if the patient were experiencing white-coat hypertension.

question_text: A 62-year-old man is admitted to hospital following a myocardial infarction. Four days after admission he develops a further episode of central crushing chest pain. Which is the best cardiac marker to investigate his chest pain?
options_json: ["LDH", "Troponin I", "Troponin T", "CK-MB", "AST"]
explanation_text:
Creatine kinase (CK-MB) remains elevated for 3 to 4 days following infarction. Troponin remains elevated for 10 days. This makes CK-MB useful for detecting re-infarction in the window of 4 to 10 days after the initial insult

By day four the CK-MB levels should have returned to normal from the initial myocardial infarction. If the CK-MB levels are elevated it would indicate a further coronary event

question_text:
A 50-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with recurrent episodes of central tight chest pain for the past 3 months. The pain often occurs during physical activity but also at rest.

The following investigations are performed:


Electrocardiogram (ECG)	No signs of acute ischaemia
Echocardiogram	Unremarkable
Stress test	ST-segment depression, correlating with patient's reported symptoms
Coronary angiography	No significant coronary artery stenosis or obstructive disease; Notably the patient had chest pain at the time of the procedure

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Angina", "Coronary bridging", "Coronary vasospasm", "Syndrome X", "Takotsubo cardiomyopathy"]
explanation_text:
People with cardiac syndrome X have normal coronary angiograms despite ECG changes on exercise stress testing

Syndrome X

is correct. Based on the patient's symptoms, stress test results, and the findings from advanced imaging techniques, the most likely diagnosis is microvascular angina, also known as Syndrome X.

Angina

is incorrect. The absence of stenosis or obstructive disease on angiography makes angina a less likely diagnosis.

Coronary bridging

is incorrect. The normal coronary angiography makes coronary bridging a less likely diagnosis. During angiography, the compression of the artery can be observed, and the degree of narrowing or compression during systole can be quantified.

Coronary vasospasm

is incorrect. Coronary angiography during an episode of spasm may show transient narrowing of the coronary arteries. Since the patient was symptomatic at the time of a normal coronary angiography, vasospasm is a less likely diagnosis.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

is incorrect. Echocardiography is often used to diagnose and evaluate the extent of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. It can show characteristic changes in the heart's contraction pattern, such as a ballooning or 'apical ballooning' appearance of the left ventricle, which resembles a Takotsubo (a Japanese octopus trap, which gives the condition its name). The normal echo makes Takotsubo cardiomyopathy an unlikely diagnosis.

question_text: A 25-year-old female patient with known Bartter's disease presents to the Emergency Department with severe muscle weakness. While awaiting a potassium result from the laboratory, which of the following ECG findings would be the most consistent with severe hypokalaemia?
options_json: ["U waves, T-wave inversion, PR shortening", "U waves, ST depression, T-wave inversion", "U waves, PR shortening, ST depression", "T-wave inversion, PR shortening, ST depression", "T-wave inversion, PR lengthening, ST elevation"]
answer_text: U waves, ST depression, T-wave inversion

question_text:
A 48-year-old gentleman presents with a 3-day history of palpitations. This is on a background of recurrent atrial fibrillation with previous failed cardioversion attempts but had successful electrical cardioversion 8 months previously. An ECG confirms that he is in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 80 beats per minute. He currently takes bisoprolol and apixaban. The cardiology consultant reviews and has planned electrical cardioversion for 4 weeks time.

Until he is cardioverted, which of the following should be given in addition to his current medications?
options_json: ["Digoxin", "Amiodarone", "Flecainide", "Procainamide", "Verapamil"]
explanation_text:
If high-risk of failure of cardioversion (previous failure), offer electrical cardioversion after at least 4 weeks treatment with amiodarone

NICE recommend giving amiodarone or sotalol for at least 4 weeks prior to electrical cardioversion in cases where there is a high risk of failure (recurrent AF or previous failed cardioversion attempts).

Digoxin and verapamil can be used for rate control in AF, but the rate is already well controlled with bisoprolol.

Flecainide can be used for pharmacological cardioversion of AF in patients without structural heart disease, but the question states that electrical cardioversion is planned so there is no role for that here.

Procainamide has a role in ventricular tachycardia but is not indicated here.

options_json: ["Cardiac MRI", "Transoesophageal Echo", "Coronary angiogram", "ECG", "Nuclear perfusion scan"]
