options_json: ["Reversible direct thrombin inhibitor", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist", "Inhibits antithrombin III", "Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor", "Activates antithrombin III"]

question_text:
A 25-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit after experiencing a total loss of consciousness whilst playing football. The patient reports that his father died very suddenly in his 40s, also whilst playing football.

After an echocardiogram which demonstrated left ventricular hypertrophy and outflow tract obstruction, he is given a diagnosis of an autosomal dominantly inherited cardiac condition.

What features would be found on a cardiac biopsy of this patient?
options_json: ["Apple-green birefringent deposits when viewed under polarised light with Congo red stain", "Fibro-fatty replacement and desmosome loss/abnormality", "Inflammatory infiltrate and myocyte necrosis or damage", "Micro-granulomas and lymphatic vessel proliferation", "Myofibrillar hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, and interstitial fibrosis"]
answer_text: Myofibrillar hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, and interstitial fibrosis
explanation_text:
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy - characterized by myofibrillar hypertrophy with chaotic and disorganized fashion myocytes ('disarray') and fibrosis on biopsy

Myofibrillar hypertrophy, myocyte disarray and interstitial fibrosis

are all features of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, which we can conclude is the diagnosis the patient has been given from the echocardiogram findings and the fact the condition is said to be autosomally dominant. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the hypertrophy referred to in the name is that of the left ventricle and the interventricular septum. If this hypertrophy causes obstruction of the left ventricle outflow tract, then it is called hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, as in this case. The obstruction can limit the heart's ability to increase cardiac output, especially evident in situations of increased circulatory demand such as exercise. This hypertrophy can be seen at a microscopic level, with enlarged myofibrils that can cause displacement of the myocytes they make up (myocyte disarray) and interstitial fibrosis.

Apple-green birefringent deposits when viewed under polarised light with Congo red stain

would be typical findings on examination of a biopsy of a patient with amyloidosis. An endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis. Cardiac amyloidosis can be secondary to other conditions such as myeloma, or can be familial, with most familial forms not autosomal dominant in inheritance pattern.

Fibro-fatty replacement and desmosome loss/abnormality

would be found in arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia (ARVD). ARVD can also be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion but the echocardiogram would tend to show changes in the right ventricle rather than left ventricular hypertrophy as in the patient in the question. In ARVD, the affected gene is often one that encodes a desmosomal protein, compromising the integrity of the desmosomal links between myocytes. Over time, this can lead to replacement of these faults with fibro-fatty material. This can disrupt the normal electrical pathways of the heart, hence patients are vulnerable to life-threatening arrhythmias.

Inflammatory infiltrate and myocyte necrosis or damage

could be found in biopsy (often post-mortem exam) of patients with myocarditis. The presence of viral genomes would also support this diagnosis. A patient with myocarditis would typically report flu-like symptoms, chest pain and fever, none of which are mentioned in the question stem.

Micro-granulomas and lymphatic vessel proliferation

are histological features of cardiac sarcoidosis. Granulomas interfere with normal cardiac function and potentially lead to arrhythmia. Its inheritance is not autosomal dominant.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man presented with central crushing chest pain. Admission ECG showed ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in aVL and lead I. He was treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention and placement of a drug-eluting stent. Shortly following the procedure you are called to review him because he is bradycardic. Telemetry and a 12-lead ECG demonstrate dissociation between the P and QRS complexes with a QRS width of 150ms and a ventricular rate of 30.

He is alert in bed, orientated and pain free. He has palpable pulses throughout and a blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg. He has a catheter in place which is draining urine.

What is the most appropriate action to take?
options_json: ["Commence isoprenaline infusion", "Insert temporary transvenous pacing", "Reassure and monitor", "Return the patient to the catheter lab for further intervention", "Temporary transcutaneous pacing"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block following an inferior MI is NOT an indication for pacing, unlike with an anterior MI

The correct answer here is to reassure and monitor the patient. The patient's admission ECG demonstrates inferior myocardial infarction. The post-PCI ECG description is that of complete heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm. This may occur following inferior myocardial infarction and in a stable, asymptomatic patient does not necessarily require pacing as it often resolves spontaneously.

Isoprenaline infusion may be used to treat symptomatic bradycardia or heart block.

Transcutaneous or transvenous pacing is not currently indicated, nor is a further angiographic procedure.

question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with pleuritic central chest pain and flu-like symptoms to the Emergency Department. The pain started yesterday and is worse at night when he lies flat. Which one of the following ECG findings is most specific for the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["PR depression", "T wave inversion", "Short PR interval", "U waves", "ST elevation"]
explanation_text:
The most specific ECG finding in acute pericarditis is PR depression

The correct answer is

PR depression

. PR depression is a highly specific finding for pericarditis, which fits with the patient's presentation of pleuritic chest pain that worsens when lying flat and flu-like symptoms. Pericarditis often follows a viral illness and presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain that can radiate to the neck, shoulders, or back. The pain typically worsens when lying supine and improves with leaning forward.

T wave inversion

is not the most specific ECG finding in this case. T wave inversions can be seen in many conditions such as myocardial ischemia, left ventricular hypertrophy, bundle branch block, or even in normal variants. In the context of this patient's presentation, it would not be the most specific sign of pericarditis.

Short PR interval

is also incorrect. A short PR interval could indicate pre-excitation syndromes like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome but would not be specific for pericarditis. This patient does not present any symptoms suggestive of a pre-excitation syndrome.

The option

U waves

is incorrect too. U waves are an extra waveform that sometimes appears on an ECG after the T wave and before the next P wave. They can be seen in several conditions including hypokalaemia or hypercalcemia but again are not specific for pericarditis.

Finally,

ST elevation

is also incorrect as an answer choice because while it can be seen in acute pericarditis, it is more commonly associated with myocardial infarction (MI). Given that ST elevation in MI is usually localised whereas in pericarditis it tends to be widespread and concave upwards without reciprocal changes helps distinguish between these two conditions on ECG.

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital following an episode of dizziness and subsequent syncope while shopping with her family. She has no significant past medical history. She has cannon waves on assessment of her jugular venous pressure.

Her heart rate is 34 bpm, and her blood pressure is 128/64 mmHg.

What is the most likely finding on cardiac auscultation?
options_json: ["3rd heart sound", "Loud S1", "Quiet S1", "Quiet S2", "Variable intensity of S1"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block causes a variable intensity of S1

Variable intensity of S1

is correct. This woman has a complete heart block, manifesting as syncope. Any condition that leads to variations in the PR interval can result in beat-to-beat variation in the intensity of the first heart sound. When the PR interval is prolonged, there is more time for ventricular filling. The elevated column of blood within the left ventricle lifts the mitral valve leaflets, which then close gently in response to ventricular contraction. When the PR interval is shortened, the leaflets remain separated, with subsequent LV contraction resulting in loud closure. In complete heart block, the PR interval varies as the p-wave 'marches' through the QRS complex. This manifests during cardiac auscultation as an S1 with variable intensity.

3rd heart sound

is incorrect. A 3rd heart sound occurs shortly after S2, during the early part of diastole. It is the manifestation of rapid ventricular filling, which is commonly seen in heart failure. In the absence of known cardiac disease, it would be unusual for a complete heart block to cause acute heart failure.

Loud S1 is incorrect

. A loud 1st heart sound is most frequently encountered in mitral stenosis, where the valve leaflets are shut forcefully at the beginning of ventricular systole (which corresponds with the closure of the atrioventricular valves). In complete heart block, the intensity of S1 is variable due to beat-to-beat changes in blood flow between the atria and ventricles.

Quiet S1 is incorrect

. A quiet S1 is characteristically caused by mitral valve regurgitation, leading to poor opposition of the valve leaflets during ventricular systole. This would classically be associated with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. In complete heart block, the S1 varies between loud and quiet due to the variable position of the atrioventricular valves at the beginning of systole.

Quiet S2 is incorrect

. A quiet S2 is associated with aortic stenosis and is an indicator of disease severity. The aortic component of the second heart sound may become quieter as the disease progresses due to the valve leaflets failing to oppose each other forcefully. In a complete heart block, the second heart sound is generally unaffected.

question_text:
You are working a medical ward cover shift when a crash call is put out for a 64-year-old man arrested on the ward. He was admitted this morning with acute breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain and is being treated as a likely pulmonary embolus with treatment-dose dalteparin whilst he awaits his CT pulmonary angiogram.

When you arrive, the first cycle of cardiopulmonary resuscitation is underway. He has a laryngeal mask airway in situ with good effect. After 2 minutes of chest compressions, the defibrillator shows normal sinus rhythm. He does not have a palpable central pulse.

What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options_json: ["Intravenous fluids", "Adrenaline 1mg 1:1000", "Adrenaline 1mg 1:10000", "Alteplase 50mg", "Unsynchronised 150J shock"]
explanation_text:
ALS - give adrenaline in non-shockable rhythm as soon as possible

This patient's rhythm demonstrated on the defibrillator is pulseless electrical activity (PEA). It is a non-shockable rhythm, and therefore adrenaline should be given immediately. The cardiac arrest dose of adrenaline is 1mg 1:10000.

Adrenaline 1mg 1:1000 is incorrect. Although the dose of 1mg is correct, a 1:1000 preparation is not what is used in a cardiac arrest. A 500 microgram 1:1000 dose is used in the treatment of anaphylaxis.

Alteplase can be given if a massive pulmonary embolus is expected. However, adrenaline takes priority during a cardiac arrest scenario.

An unsynchronised 150J shock would be the next correct step if this patient were in a shockable rhythm such as pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. However, this patient's rhythm is PEA making adrenaline the correct choice.

Intravenous fluids are used in a cardiac arrest to correct hypovolaemia (one of the 4Hs and 4Ts). However, it is not the most immediate treatment to give.

question_text: A 70-year-old man with a background of ischaemic heart disease and peripheral arterial disease presents to the Emergency Department. He has been feeling generally unwell for the past two days with fever and myalgia but this morning developed a purple, cold left middle toe. On examination there are signs of early ischaemia to the toe and a faint livedo reticularis rash is seen on the foot. A diagnosis of cholesterol embolisation is suspected. Which of the following features would be most supportive of this diagnosis?
options_json: ["Lymphocytosis", "Thrombocytosis", "Neutrophilia", "Thrombocytopaenia", "Eosinophilia"]

question_text:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends clinic for hypertension review. He was started on amlodipine 10mg daily six months ago. He reports good medication adherence and has made dietary modifications. Examination reveals BMI 28 kg/m², no peripheral oedema, and normal cardiovascular examination. Home blood pressure monitoring over two weeks shows average readings of 148/92 mmHg.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Add ramipril", "Add indapamide", "Add doxazosin", "Switch to losartan", "Increase amlodipine to 15mg daily"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking a calcium channel blocker - add an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

Add ramipril

is the correct answer. This patient has poorly controlled stage 2 hypertension (HBPM 148/92 mmHg) despite maximum dose calcium channel blocker therapy. According to NICE guidelines, when a patient is already taking a calcium channel blocker and requires step 2 treatment, the options are to add either an ACE inhibitor/ARB or a thiazide-like diuretic. However, this patient has type 2 diabetes, which creates a clinical preference for ACE inhibitors due to their proven cardiovascular and renal protective benefits in diabetic patients. The 2019 NICE guidelines specifically recommend ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line agents in patients with diabetes, and when adding a second agent to a calcium channel blocker in diabetic patients, an ACE inhibitor would be the preferred choice over a thiazide-like diuretic due to the additional metabolic and renal benefits.

Add indapamide

would be an acceptable alternative according to NICE step 2 guidance, as thiazide-like diuretics can be added to calcium channel blockers. However, in a patient with diabetes, an ACE inhibitor would be preferred due to the additional cardiovascular and renal protective effects, making this a less optimal choice despite being guideline-compliant.

Add doxazosin

is premature as this alpha-blocker is typically reserved for step 4 treatment (resistant hypertension) when patients have failed optimal doses of ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blocker, and thiazide-like diuretic combinations. Using this as step 2 treatment would not follow standard NICE guidance.

Switch to losartan

would involve stopping effective calcium channel blocker therapy unnecessarily. The current approach should be to add a second agent rather than switch, as the amlodipine may be providing some benefit and combination therapy is more effective than monotherapy switching.

Increase amlodipine to 15mg daily

exceeds the maximum recommended dose of amlodipine (10mg daily). This approach would not follow BNF guidance and could increase the risk of dose-dependent side effects such as ankle oedema and flushing without proven additional efficacy.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with exertional dyspnoea and dizziness for the past 3 months. On examination, he has a slow rising pulse, blood pressure of 135/95 mmHg, and a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. An additional heart sound is heard just before S1. Echocardiogram shows a calcified aortic valve with a peak gradient of 65 mmHg.

What is the most likely significance of the additional heart sound?
options_json: ["It indicates atrial fibrillation", "It suggests severe aortic stenosis", "It is a physiological finding in the elderly", "It indicates concurrent mitral regurgitation", "It suggests left ventricular outflow tract obstruction"]
explanation_text:
Aortic stenosis - S4 is a marker of severity

It suggests severe aortic stenosis

is the correct answer. The additional heart sound heard just before S1 is an S4 (atrial gallop), which occurs during atrial contraction in late diastole. In aortic stenosis, S4 is a marker of severity and indicates decreased left ventricular compliance due to hypertrophy. This patient has several other features of severe aortic stenosis: exertional symptoms (dyspnoea and dizziness), a slow rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure (135/95 mmHg), and a high valve gradient (65 mmHg). The presence of an S4 correlates with increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and indicates that the ventricle has become stiff and non-compliant due to pressure overload, making it a valuable clinical marker of disease severity.

It indicates atrial fibrillation

is incorrect. In atrial fibrillation, there is no coordinated atrial contraction, so an S4 would not be present. In fact, the presence of an S4 requires normal sinus rhythm with effective atrial contraction. The scenario does not mention any irregular pulse or other features suggestive of atrial fibrillation.

It is a physiological finding in the elderly

is incorrect. While an S4 can sometimes be heard in elderly patients without significant cardiac disease due to age-related decreased ventricular compliance, the clinical context here strongly suggests pathological significance. The combination of symptoms, examination findings, and echocardiographic evidence of severe aortic stenosis makes a physiological explanation unlikely.

It indicates concurrent mitral regurgitation

is incorrect. Mitral regurgitation is typically associated with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not an additional heart sound before S1. The auscultatory finding of mitral regurgitation would be a systolic murmur, not an S4. While mitral regurgitation can coexist with aortic stenosis, the S4 in this case is more likely related to the severe aortic stenosis.

It suggests left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

is incorrect. While left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (as seen in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) can also cause an ejection systolic murmur, the clinical picture here is classic for valvular aortic stenosis. The calcified aortic valve on echocardiogram confirms this diagnosis. Although both conditions can produce an S4 due to decreased ventricular compliance, the overall clinical picture supports aortic stenosis as the primary pathology.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man attends the vascular outpatient clinic with worsening pain in his left calf when walking, which has limited his ability to shop and play bowls. He has a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both well controlled. He does not smoke and is already taking atorvastatin and clopidogrel. Duplex ultrasound confirms significant femoropopliteal arterial disease without critical limb ischaemia. After optimising risk factors and referring him for a supervised exercise programme, he continues to have lifestyle-limiting symptoms after three months.

Which pharmacological therapy is most appropriate to consider next?
options_json: ["Naftidrofuryl", "Cilostazol", "Pentoxifylline", "Aspirin", "Surgical revascularisation"]
explanation_text:
Naftidrofuryl is a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist which can be used for peripheral vascular disease

Naftidrofuryl

is recommended by NICE as an option for patients with intermittent claudication who remain significantly symptomatic despite best medical management (risk factor modification, antiplatelet therapy, statin) and a supervised exercise programme. It acts as a 5-HT2 receptor antagonist with vasodilatory effects. Naftidrofuryl can improve walking distance in some patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD), particularly those whose quality of life remains poor after first-line interventions have been exhausted.

Cilostazol

is a phosphodiesterase III inhibitor that also has vasodilatory properties but is not recommended by NICE due to limited efficacy data and concerns regarding side effects such as headache and palpitations. Although it may increase walking distance in some patients, UK guidelines do not advocate its use ahead of naftidrofuryl or other measures described in the scenario.

Pentoxifylline

improves erythrocyte flexibility and microcirculatory flow but evidence supporting its benefit in PAD is weak; NICE does not recommend it for routine use in intermittent claudication. It would therefore not be the most appropriate next step for this patient who has already received optimal first-line management.

Aspirin

is an antiplatelet agent previously used for PAD but current UK guidance recommends clopidogrel as first-line due to superior efficacy in reducing cardiovascular events. This patient is already taking clopidogrel so switching or adding aspirin provides no additional benefit unless there are other specific indications.

Surgical revascularisation

should be reserved for patients with severe symptoms refractory to medical therapy or those with critical limb ischaemia (rest pain or tissue loss). As this patient does not have critical limb ischaemia and still has options within medical management, surgical intervention would be premature at this stage.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the heart failure clinic. He is generally stable, although he finds the persistent oedema of his ankles particularly troublesome. He is already taking furosemide for this, but after review, the cardiologist decides to try a course of amiloride in addition to the existing medications.

What is the target of this new drug?
options_json: ["Aldosterone receptor", "Carbonic anhydrase enzyme", "Epithelial sodium channel", "Sodium-chloride transporter", "Sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter"]
explanation_text:
Amiloride selectively blocks the epithelial sodium transport channels

Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic. Specifically, it inhibits the epithelial sodium channels found in the distal convoluted tubule, making it the correct answer. It is not often used as monotherapy but is sometimes used as an adjunct to thiazide/loop diuretics to counteract the potassium loss that they can cause.

Drugs that antagonise the aldosterone receptor include spironolactone and eplerenone. These are also potassium-sparing diuretics. Amiloride does not affect the aldosterone receptor.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors include dorzolamide and acetazolamide. These are usually recognised for their use in glaucoma.

The sodium-chloride transporter is targeted by thiazide diuretics, such as bendroflumethiazide. Amiloride is not known to affect this transporter.

The sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter is inhibited by loop diuretics. This class of diuretics includes furosemide, which the patient is already taking.

question_text: What is the most appropriate dose of adrenaline to give during a cardiac arrest?
explanation_text:
Recommend Adult Life Support (ALS) adrenaline doses

Adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 in 10 000 (100 micrograms/mL) is recommended in a dose of 1 mg (10 mL) by intravenous injection repeated every 3-5 minutes if necessary

question_text:
A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a cold and blue finger. He inadvertently injected himself with adrenaline when trying to help a patient with anaphylaxis in the community.

On examination, the middle finger on his left hand is cold and blue.

What treatment should be administered?
options_json: ["Iloprost", "Intralipid", "Nifedipine", "Phentolamine", "Sildenafil"]
explanation_text:
Adrenaline induced ischaemia - phentolamine

Phentolamine

is correct. The patient has mistakenly administered adrenaline to their finger while trying to deal with a medical emergency. They now have evidence of local ischaemia in the region. The treatment for adrenaline-induced ischaemia is local infiltration of phentolamine, an alpha receptor blocker. Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction via agonism of alpha-adrenoreceptors. Phentolamine is a non-selective alpha adrenoreceptor antagonist and opposes this effect and causes vasodilation.

Iloprost

is incorrect. This stimulates prostanoid receptors resulting in vasodilation. It may help in this situation but is typically given systemically in the form of an intravenous infusion or an inhaled form. The better option in this situation is a local antidote in the form of phentolamine. Iloprost is typically used in severe Raynaud's phenomenon.

Intralipid

is incorrect. This is the antidote to local anaesthetic toxicity and is given intravenously. Lidocaine may be mixed with adrenaline in some circumstances but it is not mixed in an EpiPen, which is the most likely scenario here.

Nifedipine

is incorrect. This is a calcium channel blocker used in the treatment of primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon (which can also result in a cold blue finger). However, the clinical situation here is adrenaline-induced local ischaemia rather than Raynaud's phenomenon and therefore local infiltration of phentolamine is the better option.

Sildenafil

is incorrect. This medication (also known as Viagra) is an oral vasodilator used to manage erectile dysfunction, Raynaud's phenomenon and pulmonary hypertension. A local option (i.e. phentolamine) is a superior choice in treating regional adrenaline-induced ischaemia.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man presents with worsening peripheral oedema and shortness of breath. On examination, you note a pansystolic murmur and soft S1.

An echocardiogram confirms severe valvular disease. The cardiology consultant decides that valve replacement is required.

What would be the treatment of choice?
options_json: ["Mechanical aortic valve", "Mechanical mitral valve", "Mechanical pulmonary valve", "Prosthetic aortic valve", "Prosthetic mitral valve"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - mechanical valves last longer and tend to be given to younger patients

Mechanical mitral valve

is correct. The auscultatory findings are highly suggestive of mitral regurgitation. The cause for this should also be established, and in a patient of this age, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis and rheumatic fever would be high up the differential diagnosis list.  In general, younger patients should be provided with a mechanical heart valve since these have a significantly greater lifespan compared to bioprosthetic valves. The average lifespan of a bioprosthetic valve is estimated to be approximately 15 years. However, the major disadvantage of mechanical heart valves is the fact they need lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin. Therefore for some patients (e.g. females of childbearing potential, and those with substantial bleeding risk factors), a bioprosthetic valve is the best choice.

Mechanical aortic valve

is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Aortic stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst aortic regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.

Mechanical pulmonary valve

is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Pulmonary stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst pulmonary regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.

Prosthetic aortic valve

is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. Aortic stenosis would present with an ejection systolic murmur, whilst aortic regurgitation would present with an early diastolic murmur.

Prosthetic mitral valve

is incorrect. The clinical features suggest mitral regurgitation. As discussed above, given the patient's age, and the limited life span of a bioprosthetic valve, a mechanical valve is usually preferred in this cohort of patients.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presented with central chest pain at rest and associated difficulty in breathing. He has a background of hypertension, type-2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolaemia. He is a non-smoker. His ECG showed inferior and lateral T-wave inversion with a significant positive troponin rise in his blood test. As a result he was commenced on treatment for acute coronary syndrome with aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux. He had a normal echo-cardiogram and is discharged from hospital a few days later as his symptoms improved with a diagnosis of a non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). He presents to his general practitioner towards the end of the week with multiple short-lived episodes of difficulty in breathing.

What is the most likely cause for this patient's dyspnoea?
options_json: ["Aspirin allergy", "Heart failure", "Pneumonia", "Pulmonary embolism", "Ticagrelor-associated side effect"]
explanation_text:
Dyspnoea in ticagrelor-treated patients is due to the impaired clearance of adenosine

Ticagrelor-related dyspnoea is transient and lasts a few hours or days, generally occurring within the first week of treatment which is what this patient is experiencing. Therefore if his clinical condition allows you are able to wait 3-4 days to observe the patient and understand whether the dyspnoea is transient or more longer lasting.

Myocardial infarction is one of the most common causes of heart failure and can occur at various time frames. Given the recent normal echo-cardiogram it would be unlikely in this patient.

Pneumonia would present with other associated symptoms such as a fever, productive cough with yellow / green sputum, general malaise and chest pain during breathing.

Pulmonary embolism is unlikely as the patient has been receiving anti-platelets and anti-coagulants recently with a short hospital admission.

Allergic reactions to aspirin may present with symptoms such as itching, flushing, blocked runny nose and asthma usually within an hour of ingestion. This would make it unlikely here given the patient has already taken multiple doses.

question_text:
A 56-year-old gentleman is brought in by paramedics. The patient fainted this morning and has not regained consciousness. No injuries reported from his faint. On examination his heart rate is 37 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/minute, blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You order an ECG:

The ECG shows prolonged PR interval.

What would be the initial management?
options_json: ["IV atropine", "IV adenosine", "External pacing", "IM adrenaline", "Oral atropine"]
explanation_text:
Symptomatic bradycardia is treated with atropine

This patient is suffering from bradycardia with adverse features (syncope) likely due to his first degree heart block (prolonged PR interval). Adverse features of bradycardia are shock, myocardial ischemia, heart failure and syncope. The initial treatment is IV atropine.

IV adenosine is not used in bradycardia, it is used in supraventricular tachycardias.

External pacing is only used if there is no improvement after six doses of atropine.

IM adrenaline is indicated for anaphylaxis

Oral atropine is only indicated for GI disorders caused by smooth muscle spasms.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself.

On examination, he appears well and observations are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording.

Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
options_json: ["P wave", "QRS complex", "ST segment", "T wave", "U wave"]
explanation_text:
S4 coincides with the P wave on ECG

The correct answer is the P wave. The S4 heart sound is caused by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, occurring just before the S1 sound. It may be heard in aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or hypertension. As such, it coincides with the P wave, which represents atrial depolarisation.

The QRS complex is incorrect. This represents ventricular depolarisation, whereas the S4 heart sound is due to atrial contraction.

The ST segment is incorrect. This is simply the interval between ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation - it is not associated with a heart sound.

T waves are an indication of ventricular repolarisation - as such, the S4 heart sound is not linked to these.

U waves may not always be seen - these are small deflections following T waves. There are a number of theories regarding their origin, including delayed repolarisation of Purkinje fibres. These do not correlate with the S4 sound.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man has attended renal outpatients today for review. He has a past medical history of progressive stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD), obesity with a body mass index of 31kg/m², type 2 diabetes, hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. His regular medications include ramipril 10mg once daily, metformin 1g twice daily and liraglutide 0.6mg once daily. He sleeps on two pillows at home (which has not changed significantly) and has noticed peripheral oedema in his ankles. His blood sugar readings have been much improved since starting liraglutide three months previously.

His observations showed a blood pressure 174/100 mmHg, heart rate 85/min and he was apyrexial with oxygen saturations of 95% on room air and a respiratory rate of 17 breaths/min. His weight was 102.8kg (improved from 103kg last review). He has reduced air entry at his lung bases, with a few sparse crackles. He has pitting oedema in his ankles.

Bloods done one week previously showed:


Na+	140 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.3 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	9.0 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	165 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

Urine dipstick performed in clinic:


pH	6.0
Protein	++
Glucose	++
Leukocytes	negative
Blood	trace

He is already trying to comply with dietary salt restriction, weight loss, alcohol and caffeine reduction and exercise. He denies compliance issues.

What would be the next best step to take in managing his hypertension?
options_json: ["Add in amlodipine", "Add in doxazosin", "Add in indapamide", "Admit for close monitoring and blood pressure control", "Persist with weight loss advice alone"]
explanation_text:
Poorly controlled hypertension, already taking an ACE inhibitor - add a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic

This is a case of uncontrolled hypertension in a CKD patient with heart failure. The underlying cause for his kidney disease is not known for certain, but it is likely secondary to diabetic nephropathy and hypertension. These are two of the commonest causes of CKD in developed countries.

The clinical approach adopted should still follow the updated 2019 NICE guidelines for hypertension management. In short, the key update is that there is now a choice between a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic for second-line treatment. Given he has heart failure, hypertension and appears hypervolaemic (peripheral oedema and mild pulmonary oedema), a thiazide-like diuretic would be the best choice.

Now to look at the other options.

Amlodipine could be used, but it has peripheral oedema as a side effect and now a thiazide-like diuretic is supported as second-line treatment. This would make amlodipine the inferior choice.

Alpha-blockers like doxazosin are further down the antihypertensive treatment line.

Currently, this patient does not have any indications for admission. Clinical features necessitating admission are (adapted from oxford handbook of nephrology and hypertension by steddon and ashton, second edition):

Severe hypertension (>220/120mmHg).
Grade 3-4 retinopathy.
Hypertensive emergencies (encephalopathy, aortic dissections etc.).
Impending complications (e.g. left ventricular failure and transient ischaemic attacks).

Persisting with weight loss alone is unlikely to work given he is still hypertensive whilst losing weight.

question_text: How long should a patient stop driving for following an elective cardiac angioplasty?
options_json: ["No restriction", "1 week", "2 weeks", "4 weeks", "8 weeks"]
explanation_text:
DVLA advice following angioplasty - cannot drive for 1 week

The correct answer is

1 week

. According to the UK Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), patients who have undergone an elective cardiac angioplasty should refrain from driving for at least one week following the procedure. This guideline is in place to allow the patient sufficient time to recover from any immediate post-procedure complications, such as bleeding or vascular complications, and adjust to any new medications.

No restriction

is incorrect because it does not adhere to the DVLA guidelines. Immediately returning to driving after a cardiac angioplasty may put the patient at risk of sudden incapacitation due to potential immediate post-procedure complications.

2 weeks

,

4 weeks

, and

8 weeks

are all incorrect as they exceed the recommended duration by the DVLA. Overly prolonged abstention from driving is generally unnecessary unless there are specific medical reasons, such as ongoing chest pain or other complications. Each case should be assessed individually, but in most uncomplicated cases, resumption of driving after 1 week is considered safe.

A 52-year-old man is seen in the hypertension clinic. He was diagnosed around three months ago and started on ramipril. This has been titrated up to 10mg od but his blood pressure remains around 156/92 mmHg.

The 2019 NICE guidelines changed so that if a patient is already taking an ACE-inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor either a calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine) or a thiazide-like diuretic (e.g. indapamide). Previous guidelines suggested that only a calcium channel blocker should be added at this stage.

question_text: You are considering prescribing an antibiotic to a 28-year-old man who tells you he has Long QT syndrome. Which antibiotic is it most important to avoid?
options_json: ["Doxycycline", "Trimethoprim", "Erythromycin", "Rifampicin", "Co-amoxiclav"]
explanation_text:
Erythromycin can cause a prolonged QT interval

The correct answer is

Erythromycin

. Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that has been associated with cardiotoxicity, specifically QT interval prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. This makes it a high-risk medication for patients with Long QT syndrome, who already have an increased risk of these complications. The UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) recommends caution when prescribing drugs known to have this side effect to patients with existing QT interval prolongation.

Doxycycline

is a tetracycline antibiotic and there are no major concerns about its use in patients with Long QT syndrome. While any medication can potentially cause side effects, doxycycline is not generally associated with significant cardiac risks.

Trimethoprim

is an antibiotic often used for urinary tract infections. It does not typically affect the QT interval significantly and hence is considered safe for use in patients with Long QT syndrome.

Rifampicin

is an antibiotic commonly used in the treatment of tuberculosis. It's also not known to prolong the QT interval or induce ventricular arrhythmias, making it safe for use in these patients.

Finally,

Co-amoxiclav

, a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, is also not associated with significant cardiotoxicity or QT interval prolongation. Therefore, it too would be considered safe for use in a patient with Long QT syndrome.

In conclusion, while all antibiotics can potentially cause side effects, erythromycin poses a specific risk to those with Long QT syndrome due to its potential to further prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman who presents with progressive dyspnoea is diagnosed as having primary pulmonary hypertension. She is started on an endothelin receptor antagonist. What is the aim of this treatment?
options_json: ["Increase blood flow to the lungs", "Reduce the risk of secondary pulmonary fibrosis", "Reduce pulmonary vascular resistance leading to reduced right ventricle (RV) systolic pressure", "Decrease the pulmonary venous pressure", "Increase the oxygen saturation of venous blood flowing to the left atrium"]
answer_text: Reduce pulmonary vascular resistance leading to reduced right ventricle (RV) systolic pressure
explanation_text:
Endothelin receptor antagonists decrease pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with primary pulmonary hypertension

The aim of endothelin receptor antagonist therapy is to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and hence reduce the strain on the right ventricle. Right ventricular failure is the most common cause of death in patients with  primary pulmonary hypertension.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man presents with shortness of breath on exertion. He is reviewed by the consultant cardiologist who decides to organise cardiac catheterisation.

The cardiac catheterisation results are as follows:


	Right atrium	Right ventricle	Pulmonary artery	Left atrium	Left ventricle	Aorta
Oxygen saturation	70%	85%	85%	100%	100%	100%

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Atrial septal defect", "Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger's", "Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)", "Ventricular septal defect", "Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger's"]
explanation_text:
Cardiac catheterisation results - jump in oxygen saturation from right atrium to right ventricle → ?VSD

Ventricular septal defect

is correct. There is a jump in oxygen saturation from the right atrium to the right ventricle indicating that oxygenated blood is travelling from the left ventricle into the right ventricle. This is highly suggestive of a ventricular septal defect.

Atrial septal defect

is incorrect. An atrial septal defect would be characterised by a higher level of oxygenated blood in the right atrium (approximately 85%).

Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger's

is incorrect. Eisenmenger syndrome refers to any untreated congenital cardiac defect with intracardiac communication that leads to pulmonary hypertension, reversal of flow, and cyanosis. In the case of an atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger's, the defect is in the atria, so one would expect deoxygenated blood to travel from the right atrium to the left atrium resulting in a low oxygen saturation of blood in the left atrium (approximately 85%).

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

is incorrect.  In this case, the defect is in the ductus arteriosus, so one would expect oxygenated blood to travel from the aorta into the pulmonary artery via the ductus arteriosus, resulting in a higher-than-expected oxygen saturation of blood in the pulmonary artery (approximately 85%).

Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger's

is incorrect. Here the defect is in the ventricle, so one would expect deoxygenated blood to travel from the right ventricle to the left ventricle resulting in a low oxygen saturation of blood in the left ventricle (approximately 85%).

question_text:
A 64-year-old man attends the Emergency Department with a one hour history of central, crushing chest pain associated with nausea. His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF, and complete heart block, with a ventricular rhythm of 44/min.

His troponin T result is as follows:


Troponin T	1100ng/L	(<14)

He is managed with dual antiplatelet therapy, and proceeds to urgent PCI, where he undergoes the placement of a drug-eluting stent in the right coronary artery.

The next day, he is reviewed on the Cardiology ward. He appears well in himself, and is pain-free. His ECG shows a complete resolution of the previous ST-segment elevation, though he remains in complete heart block, with a ventricular rate of 47/min. His blood pressure is 129/77 mmHg, and he denies any dizziness.

How should his cardiac rhythm be managed?
options_json: ["Observation only", "Insertion of a temporary pacing wire", "Insertion of a permanent pacemaker", "Transcutaneous pacing", "Administer 500mcg atropine intravenously"]
explanation_text:
Complete heart block following an inferior MI is NOT an indication for pacing, unlike with an anterior MI

This patient has presented with complete heart block following an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. A proportion of inferior myocardial infarctions are complicated by complete heart block, as in the majority of patients, both the atrioventricular node and the inferior wall of the heart receive their blood supply from branches of the right coronary artery (RCA). Therefore, occlusion of the RCA can lead to both inferior wall ischaemia and ischaemic atrioventricular conduction block. This conduction block tends to resolve upon successful revascularisation of the infarcted AV nodal tissue. As such, as this patient is only one day post-PCI, and he is haemodynamically stable, the most appropriate option is to manage his heart rhythm conservatively, and avoid unnecessarily invasive interventions.

Inserting a temporary pacing wire would be an appropriate option in the context of 2nd degree or complete heart block post-anterior MI. It may also be appropriate as a bridging measure to the insertion of a permanent pacemaker in patients with symptomatic or unstable bradycardia who are unresponsive to pharmacological treatment.

The insertion of a permanent pacemaker would not be appropriate so soon after the original ischaemic insult, as there is a good chance that the patient will return to sinus rhythm upon revascularisation of the AV node.

Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency procedure reserved for patients who remain haemodynamically stable and bradycardic following treatment with atropine. It is not indicated in this stable patient.

Atropine is an antimuscarinic drug which can increase heart rate in bradycardic patients by inhibition of the vagal tone modulating the sinoatrial node. It is not likely to be effective in the context of this patient's complete heart block, as it will not improve conduction through an infarcted AV node.

options_json: ["Mitral stenosis", "Aortic stenosis", "Ventricular septal defect", "Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy", "Aortic regurgitation"]

question_text:
A 60-year-old man is referred to the cardiology clinic with recurrent exertional chest pain associated with dyspnoea. It improves with rest. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and underwent PCI to the right coronary artery five years ago. A coronary angiogram six weeks ago showed widely patent stents. His current medications include aspirin, ramipril, bisoprolol, eplerenone, and atorvastatin. Recently, his GP started him on sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. On assessment, his BP is 142/88 mmHg, and his heart rate is 70 bpm.

What medication should be added to improve his symptoms?
options_json: ["Atenolol", "Isosorbide mononitrate", "Nicorandil", "Modified-release nifedipine", "Verapamil"]
explanation_text:
If angina is not controlled with a beta-blocker, a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker should be added

Modified-release nifedipine

is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB) that can be used in combination with beta-blockers for the management of angina. If symptoms persist following the addition of a CCB, then a third agent can be added. Options include isosorbide mononitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil, or ranolazine.

Verapamil

is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker that may be used as first-line monotherapy for angina when beta blockers are not tolerated or contraindicated. However, when the patient is already receiving beta blockers, the addition of verapamil is not recommended as it can cause dangerous bradyarrhythmias, including complete heart block.

Atenolol

is a beta blocker that may be considered in the treatment of angina. However, bisoprolol is more cardio-selective and is currently the first choice beta blocker for the management of angina and heart failure. Moreover, adding a second beta-blocker is not recommended as it can cause severe hypotension/bradycardia.

Isosorbide mononitrate

is a long-acting nitrate that relieves angina by causing coronary vasodilation. It may be considered in the management of angina pectoris after the addition of a calcium channel blocker; however, concomitant use of nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil is contraindicated as it can cause severe refractory hypotension.

Nicorandil

is a nitrous oxide donor and potassium channel opener that causes coronary vasodilation. Hence it may be considered in the management of angina but only after the addition of a calcium channel blocker. Also, the concurrent use of nicorandil and PDE5 inhibitors is contraindicated as it can cause severe refractory hypotension.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man was out with his friends when he suddenly reported not feeling well. He reported he could feel his heart beating very fast and then collapsed. A bystander started CPR and an ambulance was called. Resuscitation attempts continued for an hour but were unsuccessful. A post mortem was carried out to ascertain the cause of death as the young man had no medical problems. During post mortem, the right ventricle was noticed to be thin-walled and histology of the right ventricle revealed fibro-fatty infiltration.

What is the most likely cause of death in this case?
options_json: ["Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy", "Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy", "Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome", "Cocaine ingestion", "Brugada syndrome"]
explanation_text:
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is characterised by right ventricular myocardium replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is a cause of sudden cardiac death. It is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion (there may be a history of sudden cardiac death is the family) and is characterised by fibro-fatty infiltration into the right ventricular myocardium.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and can present as sudden cardiac death. However, the ventricular wall will be thick.

Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome is a condition where there is an accessory conducting pathway that predisposes to supraventricular tachycardias. There is a small risk of sudden cardiac death, however, the histology features described in the vignette are no seen in this condition.

Cocaine is a stimulant that can cause tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia. In extreme cases, it can cause myocardial infarction and sudden death. Whilst this man is young and out with friends, there is no evidence in the history to suggest cocaine ingestion, and the post mortem findings would not be in keeping with this diagnosis.

Brugada syndrome is another cause of sudden cardiac death that is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is due to abnormalities in conduction of electrical activity.

question_text: A 47-year-old man is admitted to hospital following an acute coronary syndrome. He has a history peptic ulcer disease and his cardiologist decides to use clopidogrel. What is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
options_json: ["Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor", "Phosphodiesterase V inhibitor", "Inhibits ATP binding to its platelet receptor", "Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor"]
answer_text: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor
explanation_text:
Clopidogrel inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors

The correct answer is that clopidogrel

inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor

. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent. It works by irreversibly inhibiting the P2Y12 subtype of ADP (adenosine diphosphate) receptor, which is found on the surface of platelets. This prevents fibrinogen binding and platelet aggregation, thereby reducing the likelihood of thrombus formation.

Discussing the other options:

Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibitor

is incorrect because these drugs, such as caffeine and theophylline are primarily used for their bronchodilator effects in conditions like asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). They work by increasing cAMP levels in cells leading to smooth muscle relaxation.

A

Phosphodiesterase V inhibitor

, such as sildenafil, is also not correct. These agents are used primarily for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. They inhibit phosphodiesterase type 5 enzyme, preventing the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), resulting in smooth muscle relaxation.

The option stating clopidogrel

inhibits ATP binding to its platelet receptor

is also not correct. ATP does play a role in platelet activation but it's not directly targeted by clopidogrel.

Lastly, a

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor

, such as abciximab or eptifibatide, is also incorrect as they prevent fibrinogen from binding to its receptor on platelets, hence preventing cross-linking and aggregation. This mechanism differs from that of clopidogrel which targets ADP receptors instead.

question_text:
An 82-year-old man has been admitted to the coronary care unit after undergoing a successful transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) with a bioprosthetic valve. The patient has experienced short episodes of atrial high-rate activity (< 30 seconds) per telemetry. The nurse has asked if the patient requires anti-thrombotic or anticoagulant medication as part of his post-procedure management.

What medication should you start?
options_json: ["Abciximab", "Apixaban", "Aspirin", "Prasugrel", "Warfarin"]
explanation_text:
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy:

Bioprosthetic valves are used for TAVI procedures. Like surgically inserted bioprosthetic valves,

aspirin

is indicated to prevent valve-related thrombosis and valve-related thromboembolic events. Anticoagulation is not indicated post-bioprosthetic valve insertion unless there is an indication for oral anticoagulation such as atrial fibrillation. Atrial high-rate activity is a separate entity from atrial fibrillation. It is not recommended to start anticoagulation for these findings on ECG monitoring.

Abciximab

is a glycoprotein iib/iiia receptor antagonist used during percutaneous coronary intervention. Indications for abciximab include large intracoronary thrombus burden and no-reflow after stent deployment. Abciximab is not used for long-term anti-thrombotic therapy in patients with prosthetic valves.

Apixaban

is not indicated here as the patient does not have a concurrent indication for anticoagulation. Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor that reduces thromboembolic events in patients with atrial fibrillation or venous thrombotic diseases such as deep vein thrombosis or PE. At least a yearly review of renal function is advised for all patients taking direct oral anticoagulants.

Prasugrel

is a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor not indicated as standard anti-thrombotic therapy in patients with prosthetic valves. Prasugrel is indicated, concomitantly with aspirin, for patients, who have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention. If the patient is taking prasugrel pre-operatively, prasugrel should be stopped seven days before surgery.

Warfarin

is a vitamin K antagonist indicated for patients with metallic valves to prevent valve thrombosis formation and thromboembolic events. The addition of antiplatelets to warfarin should be reserved for patients at very high risk of thromboembolism and low risk of bleeding. Warfarin and aspirin are advised post-metallic valve insertion if coronary artery bypass grafting was concomitantly done at the time of surgery.

question_text: A 60-year-old man is transferred from the local psychiatric unit to the Emergency Department. Throughout the day he has complained of palpitations and feeling light-headed. The psychiatry consultant noted he was tachycardic and requested a transfer. An ECG taken following admission shows a broad complex tachycardia consistent with torsardes de pointes, rate 120/min. His blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg and there are no signs of heart failure. What is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Intravenous naloxone", "Intravenous magnesium sulphate", "DC cardioversion", "Intravenous amiodarone", "Intravenous verapamil"]
explanation_text:
IV magnesium sulfate is used to treat torsades de pointes

The correct answer in this scenario is

intravenous magnesium sulphate

. Torsades de pointes is a specific form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, characterized by a twisting QRS complex around the isoelectric baseline. It can be precipitated by various factors, including electrolyte imbalances, medications, and underlying cardiac conditions. Intravenous magnesium sulphate is the first-line treatment for torsades de pointes as per UK guidelines, especially when the patient is hemodynamically stable (as evidenced by their blood pressure of 122/80 mmHg and no signs of heart failure).

Intravenous naloxone

is not an appropriate management option in this case because it is an opioid antagonist used to reverse the effects of opioids such as respiratory depression. It has no role in treating torsades de pointes or other arrhythmias.

DC cardioversion

could be considered if the patient was hemodynamically unstable or experiencing ongoing ischemia due to the arrhythmia; however, given that this patient's blood pressure is stable and there are no signs of heart failure, it would not be the most appropriate initial management option.

Intravenous amiodarone

may be used to treat various types of ventricular and supraventricular tachycardias; however, it is not typically recommended as a first-line treatment for torsades de pointes due to its potential to prolong the QT interval further, which could exacerbate the condition. Magnesium sulphate remains the preferred initial treatment in this case.

Finally,

intravenous verapamil

would also not be appropriate in this situation. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker primarily used for rate control in atrial fibrillation and managing supraventricular tachycardias. It has no role in treating torsades de pointes and could potentially worsen the patient's condition by causing hemodynamic instability or further arrhythmias.

question_text:
A 30-year-old man presented with difficulty in breathing and fever. He was a known intravenous drug user. On examination, there was a pan-systolic murmur, heard loudest in inspiration over the left lower sternal edge. He had a small degree of pitting oedema bilaterally.

What is the most likely valvular condition?
options_json: ["Mitral regurgitation", "Mitral stenosis", "Mitral valve prolapse", "Pulmonary regurgitation", "Tricuspid regurgitation"]
explanation_text:
Tricuspid regurgitation becomes louder during inspiration, unlike mitral regurgitation

Tricuspid valve regurgitation is where the valve between the two right heart chambers (right ventricle and right atrium) doesn't close properly. This causes a pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border and radiates to the right lower sternal border.

Mitral stenosis has a diastolic murmur which is of low pitch, rumbling in character, and best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position. It commences after the opening snap of the mitral valve, and the duration of the murmur correlates with the severity of the stenosis.

Pulmonic regurgitation produces a soft, high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border there it is unlikely to be correct here.

Mitral regurgitation is described as a high-pitched pan-systolic murmur, best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

Mitral valve prolapse is where blood leaks backward through the mitral valve in the heart. Its produces a mid-systolic click usually accompanied by a late systolic murmur.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man has been started on amiodarone. He has been told he must first take higher doses and then continue on a lower maintenance dose long-term.

What is the reasoning behind this initial dose regime?
options_json: ["Extensive hepatic P450 breakdown of amiodarone", "Fast metabolism of amiodarone due to extensive protein binding", "Slow absorption of amiodarone via the enteral route", "Slow metabolism of amiodarone due to extensive lipid binding", "Slow renal excretion of amiodarone"]
answer_text: Slow metabolism of amiodarone due to extensive lipid binding
explanation_text:
Amiodarone has a long half-life - it is highly lipophilic and widely absorbed by tissue, which reduces its bioavailability in serum. Therefore, a prolonged loading regime is required to achieve stable therapeutic levels

Slow metabolism of amiodarone due to extensive lipid binding

is the correct answer. Lipid-bound drugs generally have longer half-lives as they are extensively distributed in tissues, primarily adipocytes. A longer half-life means that loading doses are required. The time taken to achieve stable systemic drug concentration correlates with the half-life of that drug. A long half-life means a drug is cleared more slowly. If the patient were to start taking a drug at the maintenance dose it would take much longer to reach therapeutic concentrations.

If we take the example of drug X which has a very long half-life, only 5% of the drug is cleared per day. The ideal maintenance dose would be equal to the 5% cleared per day to ensure steady concentrations. Let's say that for drug X there has to be 1000mg of this drug in the body to be within the therapeutic window. This means our maintenance dose would be 50mg per day (i.e. 5% of 1000mg, the amount cleared in 24 hours). If we started our regime by giving the 50mg once daily maintenance dose, it would take a very long time to reach the 1000mg required to achieve a therapeutic effect. A loading dose is recommended so therapeutic levels are achieved quickly before dropping down to a maintenance dose.

Fast metabolism of amiodarone due to extensive protein binding

is incorrect. Generally, drugs that are highly protein-bound are distributed extensively within tissues, this means that they are metabolised more slowly and have a longer half-life.

Extensive hepatic P450 breakdown of amiodarone

is incorrect. Although amiodarone is extensively metabolised by hepatic P450 enzymes, this is not the reason a loading regime is required.

Slow absorption of amiodarone via the enteral route

is incorrect. Amiodarone is absorbed relatively slowly but again this is not the reason a loading regime is required.

Slow renal excretion of amiodarone

is incorrect. Amiodarone is extensively metabolised by hepatic P450 enzymes rather than renally excreted.

question_text:
A 36-year-old male presents with chest pain, the chest pain is left-sided and dull in nature. It has been present for a period of five days. There is no associated shortness of breath, cough, collapse or pleuritic nature of the chest pain. He describes a recent sore throat and headache last week which has since resolved. There is no family history in a first-degree relative of sudden cardiac death and the patient has never smoked.

Blood pressure 125/89 mmHg, heart rate 95/min, temperature 37.3ºC, oxygen saturations 97% on room air. Pulsus paradoxus is not present.

Blood results reveal:



Hb	154 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	425 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	11.5 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	6.4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	100 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	40 mg/L	(< 5)
Troponin T	13 ng/L	(<14)

Electrocardiogram (ECG): ST-segment elevation in lead I, II, III, aVL, V5 and V6. PR segment elevation in aVR.

What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
options_json: ["Pericarditis", "Myocarditis", "Infective endocarditis", "Cardiac tamponade", "Myocardial infarction"]
explanation_text:
Global ST and PR segment changes: think pericarditis

This patient has pericarditis. His young age, widespread ST-segment elevation and troponin within the normal range point towards pericarditis. While typically pericarditis is associated with PR segment depression, note that the PR segment will be elevated in aVR.

Myocarditis would be diagnosed if this patient had a raised troponin.

Infective endocarditis is less likely with a normal temperature and ECG changes consistent with pericarditis.

Cardiac tamponade is a complication of pericarditis but is unlikely to be present in this case as he has normal blood pressure and pulsus paradoxus is not present.

Myocardial infarction is unlikely in this patient due to his age, lack of risk factors and uncharacteristic ECG changes. His troponin is also within the normal range.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and long-standing atrial fibrillation presents with progressive shortness of breath and lower limb swelling over several months.

On examination, there is bilateral pitting oedema and hepatomegaly, and the hepatojugular reflux test is positive.

His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated, and a prominent x-descent is observed.

An echocardiography showed right atrial and ventricular dilatation.

What mechanism is responsible for the above JVP finding, considering the clinical presentation?
options_json: ["Bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during early systole", "Fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to downward movement of the tricuspid valve", "Rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens", "Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve in late diastole", "Right atrial filling during systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed"]
answer_text: Fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to downward movement of the tricuspid valve
explanation_text:
JVP: x descent = fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole

Fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to downward movement of the tricuspid valve

is correct because the x descent in the JVP represents a drop in right atrial pressure during ventricular systole as the right ventricle contracts and pulls the tricuspid valve downward. This patient’s history of COPD and atrial fibrillation suggests chronic right ventricular strain due to pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale), which can lead to right-sided heart failure. The x descent is still present in atrial fibrillation but lacks its early component, normally due to atrial relaxation after contraction. Instead, the x descent in this patient is entirely due to the downward movement of the tricuspid valve during ventricular systole. This feature indicates that right ventricular systolic function is still relatively preserved, despite right-sided heart failure progressing.

Bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during early systole

is incorrect because this describes the c wave, which occurs as right ventricular contraction causes the tricuspid valve to briefly bulge into the atrium. While present, it is a small transient event and does not contribute to significant JVP prominence.

Rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens

is incorrect because this describes the y descent, which occurs in early diastole when the tricuspid valve opens and blood rapidly flows from the atrium to the ventricle. A prominent y descent is more characteristic of tricuspid regurgitation or pericardial disease, neither of which is indicated in this case.

Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve in late diastole

is incorrect because this describes the a wave, which is absent in atrial fibrillation due to the lack of organised atrial contraction. Since this patient has atrial fibrillation, the a wave is not present.

Right atrial filling during systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed

is incorrect because this describes the v wave, which represents venous return filling the right atrium while the tricuspid valve is closed. A prominent v wave is a hallmark of severe tricuspid regurgitation, which would also cause pulsatile JVP and a holosystolic murmur—features not present in this case.

question_text: A 13-year-old girl presents with palpitations, fatigue and dyspnoea. She has had symptoms for around a year. There is no history of syncope or chest pain. On examination she has a pan-systolic murmur associated with giant V waves in the jugular venous pulse. Auscultation of the chest is unremarkable. A resting ECG is normal but a 24 hour tape shows a short burst of supraventricular tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Atrial septal defect", "Pulmonary stenosis", "Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy", "Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy", "Ebstein's anomaly"]

question_text:
A 65-year-old male patient presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, generalised weakness, and subjective fevers. The patient's past medical history is notable for rheumatic heart disease and COPD. He reports no recent travel or unwell contacts, and reports no intravenous drug use. Last year, he had a screening colonoscopy which was unremarkable.

On physical exam, he is noted to have very poor dental hygiene with gingivitis, splinter haemorrhages, a pansystolic murmur and a mid-diastolic, rumbling murmur heard loudest at the 5th intercostal space and mid-axillary line.

An echocardiogram reveals a vegetation on the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis. Preliminary results from blood cultures reveal gram-positive cocci.

What pathogen is most likely to be responsible for this patient's illness?
options_json: ["Staphylococcus aureus", "Staphylococcus epidermidis", "Streptococcus bovis", "Streptococcus pyogenes", "Streptococcus sanguinis"]
explanation_text:
Patients with very poor dental hygiene may develop endocarditis secondary to Viridans streptococci e.g.

The vignette describes a patient with subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) which is usually caused by viridans streptococci, such as

Streptococcus sanguinis

, which are commonly found as oral flora. Poor dental hygiene, particularly in the setting of gingival disease, is a risk factor for the development of SBE. Unlike acute bacterial endocarditis which can affect healthy native valves, the viridans streptococci typically affect prosthetic valves or damaged heart valves and follows a more indolent (subacute) clinical course. In this case, the patient's rheumatic heart disease predisposed him to develop SBE affecting the diseased mitral valve.

Acute bacterial endocarditis is typically caused by

Staphylococcus aureus

. The presence of indwelling lines, particularly in combination with prosthetic heart valves and/or pacemaker leads, can provide a seeding nidus of infection for

Staphylococcus epidermidis

- a common skin commensal.

Streptococcus bovis

endocarditis has been associated with colon cancer, with some cross-sectional data to suggest that 33-50% of patients with Strep bovis bacteraemia and/or endocarditis have a colorectal adenoma or carcinoma on subsequent colonoscopy. The patient's normal colonoscopy the year prior makes this a less likely cause.

Finally, beta-hemolytic streptococci, such as

Streptococcus pyogenes

, are an uncommon cause of infective endocarditis.

question_text:
A 55-year-old female presents to hospital with worsening exercise tolerance and lethargy. She was thoroughly investigated including echocardiography and right heart catheterisation. The latter showed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 35mmhg with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8mmhg in keeping with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Ambrisentan is prescribed amongst other agents.

What is the mechanism of action of the aforementioned drug?
options_json: ["Endothelin-1 receptor antagonist", "Prostaglandin I2 (PGI2) analogue", "Prostaglandin (PGE2) analogue", "Phosphodiesterase inhibitor (PDE inhibitor)", "Nitrovasodilator"]
explanation_text:
Ambrisentan - endothelin receptor A antagonist

Ambrisentan and bosentan are endothelin receptor antagonists. In PAH the expression of endothelin-1 is increased resulting in vasoconstriction. Endothelin primarily acts upon two receptors ETA and ETB. ETA is found in vascular smooth muscle and mediate vasoconstriction. ETB is found on the endothelium and mediate vasodilation. Ambrisentan is selective for ETA receptors.

Ambrisentan has been shown to be effective for patients with PAH in reducing morbidity and mortality. It is generally well tolerated by patients and the main side effects include peripheral oedema, sinusitis, flushing and nasal congestion.

Prostacyclins such as PGI2 can be used in the management of PPH due to their vasodilatory effects and inhibition of platelet aggregation.

PGE2 is an inflammatory mediator not utilised in the treatment of PAH.

PDE inhibitors such as sildenafil decrease the activity of PED5 increasing cGMP in the pulmonary vessels, in turn, relaxing the vascular smooth muscle and reducing the pulmonary artery pressure.

Nitrovasodilators are prodrugs of nitric oxide resulting in arterial and venous dilation. Sodium nitroprusside (a nitrovasodilator) is used in hypertensive emergencies and heart failure rather than PAH.

question_text: A 60-year-old man is admitted following an acute coronary syndrome. He receives aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and morphine. His 6-month risk score is high and percutaneous coronary intervention is planned. He is therefore given intravenous tirofiban. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options_json: ["Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2", "Activates antithrombin III", "Coronary vasodilator", "Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist", "Reversible direct thrombin inhibitor"]

question_text:
A 58-year-old man presents with breathlessness and chest discomfort. He has diet controlled diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He has a weak rapid, regular pulse of 160bpm, blood pressure is 80/50mmHg, he is cold peripherally and crepitations are heard bibasally on auscultation of the chest. An ECG shows a regular broad complex tachycardia.

What is the best initial management of this arrhythmia?
options_json: ["Adenosine", "Amiodarone", "Diltiazem", "Electrical cardioversion", "Vagal manoeuvres"]
explanation_text:
In the context of a tachyarrhythmia, a systolic BP < 90 mmHg → DC cardioversion

This patient presents with a regular broad complex tachycardia with a palpable pulse and the adverse feature of shock (systolic blood pressure <90mmHg), therefore a synchronised DC cardioversion is indicated. If this patient had no adverse features an intravenous amiodarone infusion would be indicated.

Intravenous adenosine and vagal manoeuvres (e.g carotid massage, Valsalva manoeuvre) are indicated for the termination of a regular narrow complex tachycardias.

Diltiazem may be used for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

See: ALS guidelines, peri arrest arrhythmias, resuscitation council, UK.

https://www.resus.org.uk/resuscitation-guidelines/peri-arrest-arrhythmias/
